intervention_header_en: Nicolas Schmit, member of the commission
subject_of_business_title: A social Europe in a Digital world (topical debate)
paragraph: madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the digital transformation is going to have, is already having, unprecedented repercussions on our economies, our societies, our way of working, of communicating, of consuming. the question of employment is surely at the center of the questions. how many jobs will disappear, replaced by robots? what is already certain is that the majority of jobs will be transformed. new jobs will appear when others disappear or experience profound upheavals. it is expected that artificial intelligence and robotics alone will create almost 60 million jobs worldwide in the next five years and already today, it has been mentioned, almost a million jobs tic are vacant, due to a lack of candidates with the right qualifications. this is also the main concern of many companies, especially smes, which cannot find qualified personnel. it is also a major challenge for our employment and qualification policies. we have acted on the green transition by launching the just transition fund for regions and people most affected by these changes. likewise, we need to strengthen much more our employment and social policies to anticipate and manage the disruptive changes expected from digitalisation. there are – and it has already been mentioned – a lot of very good opportunities, but there are also risks of widening inequalities and more precariousness. over 90% of jobs now require some level of digital skills, as does participation in society at large, yet 43% of the eu population have an insufficient level of digital skills and 17% have none at all. next month we will propose a new skills agenda to address the skills challenges through concrete instruments and this challenge is huge because, according to a lot of forecasts, about half of the european workforce, meaning more than 120 million people have to be re—skilled or upskilled. so, we have three major aims. the first one is engaging employers to upscale their training provision, and for that purpose, we want to launch a skills pact committing companies, committing the business community to invest in their workforce. second, we have to step up public and private investment in training according to this need i just mentioned. and third, we have to empower people to invest in their own skills and qualifications. many of our post 2020 initiatives will address these challenges linked to digitalization. the european social fund plus (esf+) will support projects, such as the creation of e—schools with digitally trained teachers or training unemployed people for ict jobs. and i'm working on a reinforced youth guarantee to provide a much stronger coverage of digital skills. non—standard forms of work are on the rise, and come with flexible but also very often with inadequate working conditions, insufficient access to social protection, decreased coverage by social dialogue and absence of a right to collective representation. this challenges our labor laws and social protection systems and calls for a rethink of existing models to match the needs of old and new work arrangements and ensure decent working conditions, inclusion and high level of social protection. the digitalization is changing notions of work of employer—employee relationships and of workplaces and it is absolutely indispensable that we create some clarity in this new world of work. new technologies also blur the lines between work and private life. this creates new physical and mental health risks and, therefore, the right to disconnect has to be dealt with. the use of data in employment has led to new algorithm—based management and an increased profiling in social protection provision. these can improve productivity but also increase control on individuals and monitoring of workers’ performance. it raises questions of protection of personal data; we should pay attention to this in the context of the regulation of artificial intelligence. we need accessible and interoperable digital technologies in order to exploit the potential of digitalization to increase the autonomy of persons with disabilities and to boost their participation in society and the economy. the digital transformation must also be an opportunity in the context of the demographic challenges we face in particular in relation to our aging population and the existing rural and remote areas. we also should devote special attention to the gender gap that exists in the digital world. europe has to be a competitive and innovative player in the digital economy. new initiatives on the digital services act and artificial intelligence will play a key role, while also addressing risks of bias and discrimination. on 22 september i’m organizing together with executive vice—president vestager, a summit on platform work where we discuss how to improve working and social conditions on online platforms. beyond this, we have launched the process leading to an action plan on the european pillar of social rights, because the principles of the pillar should also fully apply to the new digital world of work. the pillar frames our social strategy to make sure that the transition towards a digital and climate—neutral society is socially fair and sustainable.

paragraph: madam president, ladies and gentlemen, a social europe in a digital world: it is astonishing that everyone here has chosen not to simply talk about social europe before tackling the digital world. does this social europe exist? i know this, because all my colleagues from the employment and social affairs committee are present here. we know, for example, that the coordination of social security systems is particularly difficult and i know that some here believe that the digitization of our data would be the panacea. i would say that indeed, artificial intelligence and robotics present risks and that it is absolutely necessary to adopt a regulatory framework. but i would like to warn you about such projects which would seriously undermine our national sovereignty. such projects where data protection is all the less assured as the european union has overlooked digital sovereignty and has made us totally vulnerable to china and the united states. i would add that the principle of consent to the collection of data from our workers, insured persons or retirees is seriously questioned. this could lead to systematic policing, commercial data traffic, or worse. so yes, we must work and move towards cooperation between states and digitization and make efforts in this direction, but my dear colleagues, today we are faced with challenges that are much more immediate and deeper, such as social dumping , fiscal dumping or the excesses of globalism. first of all, let's settle the essentials here, this is what our compatriots expect.

subject_of_business_title: Gender Equality Strategy (debate)
paragraph: madam president, we have finished the european equality strategy 2016-2019. we now face a new 2020-2024 strategy. it must be a priority for this parliament, for the commission and for the council to move forward resolutely and with a firm commitment to do what europe demands: equality for all citizens. it is a democratic question. there is no democracy without equality. there is no prosperous society with a future without human rights. equality is a human right and that is why we have to combat the salary gap, the pension gap, bet on the directive that the commissioner announced on salary transparency or the directive on reconciliation. there are still stereotypes that must be fought in order to achieve that true equality. nor is there equality in decision-making, which is why specific measures will have to be taken that are inclusive and accessible. there is gender violence — the latest statistics tell us that two out of three women have suffered violence. it is necessary to talk about artificial intelligence for the issues of cyberbullying and, above all, it is necessary to ensure that this strategy talks about disability and women. it has to have age indicators, disability indicators, female indicators. in this way, we will have managed to live up to what european values ​​demand.

subject_of_business_title: Gender Equality Strategy (debate)
paragraph: madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, we support the importance of gender equality as a common value. if we want to be consistent, let's work to promote it in all european union policies, as well as in parliament, but as a cultural revolution and not as a tax act. the barriers that prevent female participation in the world of work lead to particularly high costs of well-being and growth. removing obstacles is important. research by the european institute for gender equality proves that gender equality would foster economic growth. but does the institute also monetize the role of women in reconciling family and work? improvements in gender equality would create over ten million additional job opportunities in europe and gdp per capita would grow by almost 10% by 2050. but which balance for households? gender equality will also have to be promoted in the context of the new european union policies - digital single market, green deal and artificial intelligence - in which the employment gap is even more dramatic. now a new commissioner with exclusive responsibility for equal opportunities will have to change the management of previous policies on the matter, also because the european court of auditors will examine gender mainstreaming in the european union budget and, according to what was made public today, the audit report will be released in spring 2021. then we will see what impact the policies of the von der leyen commission will have on the world of women.

subject_of_business_title: Better internet for children (debate)
paragraph: madam president, safe internet for children is vital indeed. children should feel safe to go online, they should remain curious to discover, to learn, to innovate. however, having looked at the web page of the safer internet day, i discovered with horror that, during the safer internet day, discussions were focused on how artificial intelligence can be used to identify and remove child sexual abuse material. we, as legislators, are just about to analyse and address the opportunities and the pitfalls of these technologies. therefore, it seems to be premature indeed to consider ai a silver bullet to solve all problems. and i am glad that education was mentioned by the commission representative because i believe that future initiatives from the commission related to safer internet should focus on education and development of technical skills of kids, which should not mean promoting the use of one specific company’s tools but encouraging the use of interoperable solutions and free and open—source software.

subject_of_business_title: Road safety (debate)
paragraph: madam president, honourable members of the house, i appreciate very much your comments and your interest for this subject. as i said from the beginning, only working together and putting enough pressure on all the stakeholders on which depends the safety on the roads, will we achieve results. you were mentioning, for example the targets. we have the targets which are expiring as i said, this year, and maybe one would ask why we would have targets if we cannot achieve them? but i do believe that having a target is an important instrument, an important tool, to design policies and enter into dialogue with the stakeholders in order to have a concrete vision for the future from various areas. so i myself i’m favouring keeping a clear target which can guide our action, and we can remember and recall all the time. we don’t need .... all of you mentioned the numbers, and i mentioned the numbers at the beginning, and i said and i want to repeat that actually any number is not acceptable. and that it was said it is also not acceptable that we get used to hearing about this and numbers of deaths on the roads. so that’s why clear action is absolutely needed, and we need to be committed to that. several have mentioned the vulnerability of pedestrians or other categories involved in traffic. so when we talk about the safety of course the citizens have to be at the core of our action, and we have several categories of vulnerable road users. so we have also the pedestrians as were mentioned, but the cyclists, the motorcyclists are most at risk, especially in urban areas, and we are also looking into the urban mobility package to see ways in which we can improve the safety inside the city. the problem is, and we all know that where all the categories are meeting together, and now the evolution of the technology we see and the introduction of new ways of mobility in cities, i think these kind of risks are higher. so we have to work very early on devising a policy to accommodate all these categories which would meet in the same space. but since we are talking about that, let me refer also to a topic many of you raised. that technology and digitalisation can help us to improve road safety. many mentioned the fact that we are looking at autonomous vehicles in the future, artificial intelligence - but this comes also with lots of challenges because we have to admit that at the beginning, all these vehicles, well slowly with the introduction of the infrastructure, will need to co-habit with the traditional ones. and this is also something we have to imagine from the very beginning as being a new risk for the safety on the roads. so this is another angle we are looking at. i’m very much favouring the safe system as a system approach because it looks at all the elements which are making road safety challenging. many of you mentioned driving licensing. we are looking into this and i think in 2022 we will come up with a proposal, somewhere mentioning the speed. of course, speed is one of the most important elements, and we have also, let me give you another figure, an estimation from the edfc, that only one kilometre per year reduction in average speed in the eu would already reduce the deaths by 2000 a year. so this shows that speed is a very important factor. we are also looking and analysing to see how we can convince and cooperate with the member states in order to act in this respect. we know that in 2017 there was the valetta declaration on road safety and the transport ministers committed to engage on the possibility of reducing speed limits. so let’s see where we are after this with each member state. personalised analysis for member states is done, and i encourage you to follow, and i’m sure you’re not already, but maybe we will have another chance to discuss the subject after the annual report and statistics, which is going to be published in april. and also i would like to commit with you that after the stockholm conference, i would have probably the next day i am in the tran committee, and i can already report back to you on what was committed to in stockholm and which are the next steps to be taken together with you in the future to increase road safety in europe - and why not to the leadership for other continents, because we know and we have instruments and programmes for asia and for africa and would like to lead there, so that globally we can contribute to the reduction of deaths and serious injuries on the roads. thank you very much for this debate and i’m as always at your disposal for this topic or others for discussion in the future.

subject_of_business_title: EU coordinated action to combat the COVID-19 pandemic and its consequences (continuation of debate)
paragraph: in the context of the current crisis, one of the priorities of the itre committee is to protect europe’s 25 million small and medium enterprises, as well as the sectors of industries most affected, including those sectors that are suffering from disruption of supply chains. accordingly, i reinforce the call for a european horizontal strategy for sme recovery to support them by providing continuous access to finance, reducing red tape and fostering investments in strategic value chains. i express support for the reintegration of supply chains inside the eu and for the proposal for a health autonomy action in strategic areas such as active pharmaceutical ingredients (api). in the same context, i highlight the importance of strengthening the competences, budget and staff of the ecdc and ema, to enable these agencies to efficiently coordinate medical responses during crisis. i am conviced that the eu recovery package will have at its core enough financial resources. finally, the covid-19 crisis proved one more time the necessity to further integrate eu space programs galileo and copernicus. the added value of these systems along with the use of artificial intelligence play a decisive role in combating pandemics and crisis.

subject_of_business_title: Presentation of the programme of activities of the German Presidency (debate)
paragraph: mr president, madam president of the commission, dear colleagues in the european parliament, ladies and gentlemen! it is a pleasure for me to address the plenary session of the european parliament at the beginning of the german council presidency. like most of you, i have missed the direct encounters with people, the face-to-face conversations, and for me this is now the first trip abroad since the outbreak of the pandemic, and it leads me consciously and with complete conviction to you, to the heart of european democracy. in these times, in which the european union wants to survive this crisis stronger, the european parliament is needed in these times. the tasks before us are enormous, and they require enormous efforts. they need a parliamentary debate, they need political mediation, they need cultural translations into the different countries and regions. and for that it needs you! it is therefore a special honor for me to present the priorities of the german council presidency to you today. five topics are particularly important to me at this time: our fundamental rights, cohesion, climate protection, digitization and europe's responsibility in the world. these five issues are important because we need to change europe in a sustainable way if we want to protect and preserve europe. only then will europe be able to play its own role in a sovereign and responsible manner, even in a rapidly changing global order. we are all aware that my visit today takes place against the background of the greatest test in the history of the european union. the civil rights are the most valuable asset we have in europe. and they may only be restricted for very important reasons and only for a very short time. a pandemic must never be an excuse to undermine achievement of fundamental rights in europe that unites us. for me, who have lived in a system of bondage for thirty-five years of my life, restricting these rights during the pandemic was a decision but europe is something alive that we can shape and change. europe does not deprive us of opportunities for action, but in a globalized world europe gives us some. not without, but only with europe live out their religious beliefs, their cultural or political beliefs, that they are allowed to adhere to their respective ideas of happiness or the good life. democracy, including european democracy, – to find common solutions, if we are willing to look at the world through the eyes of others and show understanding for other perspectives. post-crisis europe will be stronger than before if we strengthen community spirit. no one can get through this crisis alone. we are all vulnerable. european solidarity is not just a humane gesture, but a sustainable investment. european cohesion is not just something that is politically imperative, but something that will be worthwhile. and that is also the leitmotif of our council presidency: “together. make europe strong again. i will devote of the mutual understanding that we need to reach compromises. they represent almost 450 million citizens in 27 countries. they are the translators of european principles. they explain europe to people and thus mediate between brussels, strasbourg and their home regions. not only do you communicate in 24 languages, you live with this diversity of perspectives and experiences. if not you, who could explain the attitude of other member states to the people of europe? that is why i am asking you, as mediators and mediators of cohesion, for your support during this difficult time. help us to deepen mutual understanding of each other. help us to strengthen europe's cohesion. the top priority of the german council presidency is for europe to come out of the crisis united and stronger. but we don't just want to stabilize europe in the short term – that would not be enough. we also want a europe that inspires hope. we want a europe that faces the challenges of the present with self-confidence and courage. we want a europe that is fit for the future, that asserts its place in the world in an innovative and sustainable way. we want a new beginning for europe. the franco-german initiative of mid-may also follows this conviction. together with french president emmanuel macron, i proposed a european recovery fund of 500 billion euros. i am pleased that the european commission is taking many aspects of this franco-german initiative into account in its proposal for the multiannual financial framework and the recovery programme. discussions are currently taking place on this basis in the european council chaired by charles michel. our common goal is to find an agreement as quickly as possible, because the depth of the economic slump reminds us to hurry. we must not waste any time. only the weakest would suffer. i very much hope that we can reach an agreement this summer. this will still require a great deal of willingness to compromise from all sides – including you. the situation is extraordinary, even unique in the history of the european union. that is why germany has also supported this extraordinary and one-time effort in this magnitude of 500 billion. now it will be important that we also come to an agreement at european level. i am convinced that the social dimension is just as important as the economic one. a socially reason, too, during our council presidency we will focus our attention particularly on young people and children. they are europe's future and have been particularly hard hit by the crisis. we also consider what individual member states can and cannot achieve – economically, socially and politically. in all of this, i am asking you, as meps, for your support today. i am convinced that is familiar, fear of the pace of change. and that's understandable. but let me be very clear: our commitment to digitization and climate protection does not mean that we are giving up everything that is established and thereby jeopardizing the jobs of millions of europeans. on the contrary, it is about a necessary change in our society that will offer more protection and more sustainability in the long term. because especially in the past few weeks and months, europe's digital dependency on third countries has once again become clear to us. many of us have undoubtedly noticed this in the course of our daily digital communication – be it in technology or in services. it is important that europe becomes digitally sovereign. we want to make progress, especially in key areas such as artificial intelligence and quantum computing, but also in building a trustworthy and secure digital infrastructure. but it is also crucial to effectively protect our democracies from cyber threats and disinformation campaigns. because a democracy needs a public in which knowledge and information can be shared, in which citizens can exchange ideas and agree on how they want to live. we are an important step on the way to giving the countries of the western balkans accession prospects - , on the other hand for our relations with our neighboring continent africa and the african union, which we want to deepen at an eu-africa summit with a view to the future. this also includes questions about our migration cooperation. there are more people fleeing than ever before. that is why we have a special responsibility to make progress on an issue that is so central to europe as asylum and migration policy. this is a question that requires a lot of political sensitivity, but we must not look the other way, but must face this humanitarian and political task together. then you need what i talked about today. then you need basic rights and cohesion. then you need answers to climate change and digitization. then europe needs responsibility in the world. then we have to make europe greener, more digital and therefore more innovative and more competitive. because internationally, europe should stand for a legal order, and internationally, europe should stand for innovation and sustainability. that is the vision for europe. let me close with a personal thought. i am a music lover, so it gives me great pleasure that our presidency marks a very special anniversary. in december 2020, the composer of the european anthem, ludwig van beethoven, would have been 250 years old. this ninth symphony fills me again and again and again. every time i listen, i discover something different in the music that hits me and impresses me, just like europe does. it can be rediscovered again and again and it still impresses me. and so let me end today with the wish that the message of this music, the idea of ​​brotherhood and unity, guides us in europe. what message could be more appropriate than this, that this europe is capable of great things if we stand by one another and stick together. subject_of_business_title: Chemicals strategy for sustainability (debate)
paragraph: madam president, with this motion for a resolution, the european parliament calls on the commission to proceed with the chemicals strategy for sustainability. chemicals are everywhere. they are in our food, in our water, in our clothes and in our cosmetics. they are in the air that we breathe. in other words, they affect all aspects of our daily life. our first priority is to upgrade the level of protection of the consumer and the environment. for this reason, we are asking for the elimination of risk-hazardous substances and substitutions to safer alternatives when it’s feasible. we call on the commission to take into account the risk posed by endocrine disrupters and the combination effect of different chemicals. commissioner, we are focusing on a very ambitious target by aiming to set the chemical safety standard for the entire world. the european chemicals agency (echa) should support the eu’s international trade policy by defining provisions and fostering regulatory systems built upon eu standards for chemical safety. this would enhance protection beyond the eu borders and extend the level playing field. chemicals are also the industry of industries. a size—based grouping approach will enable the industry, in complementarity with the ‘one substance, one assessment’ principle. this strategy must also grant sufficient time for the industry’s manufacturers in order to deliver safe and performing products and incentivise the eu industrial production and economy. in this regard, the strategy should secure adequate funding to accelerate the development of innovative and safe alternatives. the strategy should also ensure that unnecessary animal tests are avoided, incentivising the development of smart testing strategies and artificial intelligence paragraph: during commission president ursula von der leyen’s state of the european union speech, i was pleased to see ambitious and concrete actions regarding digital and technology policy. more concretely, in three main areas: increasing our industrial data cloud capacities so we can obtain the benefits of innovation and economic growth; a human-cantered approach to artificial intelligence and a new law for eu digital identity; investing in broadband infrastructure and connectivity. i welcome all of these commitments on the side of the commission, as i am a firm believer that we will not be able to achieve any of our ambitious sustainable economy goals without technology. we must work towards identifying the investment streams to cater for future breakthrough technologies to help transform existing industries, e.g. steel and cement, automotive, aviation, and more. we must also strive to identify the ecosystem of start-ups and small smes that can come up with the future clean breakthrough technology solutions and can create european technology leadership. if the european union is to meet our ambitious green goals, maintain our global position and ensure a high living standard for our citizens, we must continue to be at the forefront of technological advancements.

paragraph: mr president, mr president, dear charles, thank you again for being here. speaking of international relations, this debate that took place in the council was more than necessary. some powers have decided to complicate the situation, as if the health crisis, the economic crisis and the climate crisis were not enough. in this time when the world must stick together, some have decided to play it instead. we must therefore ensure that the union becomes a geopolitical, economic and democratic power. it is urgent to adopt a common strategic vision to become a truly geopolitical europe, to act rather than react, and to do so quickly when necessary. but this presupposes that member states understand the value of truly collective action. this is not always the case in international relations, because everyone defends their interests. and faced with china, turkey or russia, we now need a strategic vision, but also unity and firmness in action. how could one define oneself as a real geopolitical actor if it takes us two months to sanction the lukashenko regime and that, still two months later, he still has not been placed on this list. we simply lose credibility when we bring the council together just to discuss. our power must rely on new tools for action and decision-making. passing foreign policy to qualified majority voting and putting in place a human rights sanctions regime are urgent matters now. this would allow us to react quickly, for example in situations such as the poisoning suffered by alexei navalny. the council also spoke of the economic power of europe. our influence goes through our economic influence and this economic influence goes through our climate ambition and our mastery of digital technology. parliament has recently created a special committee on artificial intelligence in the digital age, we intend to make proposals in this area. our internal market, our social and democratic organization and the strategic autonomy of our economy require a real ambition to invest in digital technology. finally, democratic power. we can only be credible internationally if we ourselves are irreproachable. any strategic development must be based on solid values: freedom, democracy and the rule of law. what credibility would we have, beyond our borders, if every european could not count on an independent judiciary, free from all political pressure and clientelism. if every european could not count on an independent press, and on journalists free from any influence exerted by oligarchs close to power. if public funds, instead of fueling innovation and healthy investments, sometimes end up in the pockets of the corrupt and dark interest networks. we must therefore be lucid: without democratic values, the injection of financial liquidity will not be sufficient. we need both. if we lack a base of common values, we will not be able to solve concrete problems, such as health coordination to deal with the coronavirus. and this coordination, parliament has been asking for and demanding for months, and we see that there are still member states that do not respond to it. if it is still not in place, it is good that some want to feed health nationalism, a shock of values ​​on our continent, more than a shock of solidarity. we must not accept it, because we will all pay the price. the union must therefore be this force capable of protecting the health, employment and rights of all european citizens.

paragraph: i welcome the conclusions of the european council of october 1-2, which also include digital objectives. in the past few years, there have been successive projects that show the capabilities and challenges of the rapidly developing artificial intelligence more and more spectacularly. today, the biggest problem is hidden in the nature of ai, which is based on the intelligent processing of large data sets. the eu data strategy published in february sets out ambitious goals in the field of creating and connecting european data spaces. data is the basis of new technologies, which are of decisive importance in all areas of the economy. the goal is to have as much and better quality data as possible, which can be used by both the public and private sectors. the european commission will present the planned eu legislative act containing the data strategy only in the first half of 2021. i believe that many concepts should be clarified during this period, and at the same time priority should be given to the protection of sensitive and valuable national data sets and personal data, including health data, which is classified as special data.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Services Act: Improving the functioning of the Single Market - Digital Services Act: adapting commercial and civil law rules for commercial entities operating online - Digital Services Act and fundamental rights issues posed - Framework of ethical aspects of artificial intelligence, robotics and related technologies - Civil liability regime for artificial intelligence - Intellectual property rights for the development of artificial intelligence technologies (debate)
paragraph: madam president! dear commissioner, in recent weeks, the documentary "the social dilemma" has consistently been in the top ten most-watched films on netflix. the message of the film or documentary is scary and very powerful at the same time. social media platforms are no longer simple communication tools, but huge profit machines that significantly influence public discourse. they do this by not only deciding which information we are shown, but also deciding which content may be displayed at all and which not - unfortunately often in conflict with the law. however, i do not want the freedom of expression of users in europe to be in the hands of private companies that act as deputy sheriffs and make decisions that only courts are actually allowed to make. if we say that the law should apply online as well as offline, then there must be an end to interference with freedom of expression through overblocking and arbitrary deletion by platforms. the juri report therefore proposes establishing clear procedural rules for the notice and action system when dealing with illegal content. this is important because it creates legal certainty for the platforms on the one hand, but also creates legal certainty for users and respects their fundamental rights. our report also calls for a strong european supervisory authority that can ensure compliance with the rules and, above all, has the necessary enforcement powers to ensure the necessary transparency. an online platform must not be a black box. its actions must be transparent, justified and comprehensible, especially when it makes such important decisions about users' freedom of expression. and that brings me to a point that i'm particularly proud of in our report, that we proposed that we put in place a system that doesn't pre-check uploaded content. in fact, we specifically require the commission that the digital services act must not encourage platforms to use upload filters. even the voluntary use of technical aids by platforms must not result in content being scanned and blocked at the time of upload. and i think that's a huge success after last year's debate and a step towards an internet with no more upload filters. there is also content that is legal, but can still cause great social damage. such content as fake news, disinformation, hate speech and propaganda cannot be subject to the same rules as when dealing with illegal content, since such content is often below the level of taste, but is protected by freedom of expression. and the problem we have with such content is not so much that it exists at all, but that it spreads through the internet like wildfire and is flushed into the timelines of users by platforms because algorithms believe that attention-grabbing content is more important than democratic debate, for example. in this way, platforms can promise their actual customers – not us as users, but the advertisers – that they will provide targeted, personalized advertising in a particularly effective manner. but if algorithms exploit human curiosity for attention-grabbing content for profit reasons and fake news, hate and hate speech are the wrapping paper in which personalized advertising is packaged online, then we as legislators have to step in and take action against this business model. that's why we demand in the report that users have more control over their content. they must decide what content they see and whether they want to see targeted online advertising at all. we must not allow users to be at the mercy of algorithms that erode our shared information base in society and endanger our democracy. if that's the price to pay for enabling silicon valley companies to make more profits from personalized advertising, then the price is clearly too high, and this business model has no place in our digital single market. that is why i am expressly advocating sticking to the text of the committee on legal affairs in tomorrow's vote, despite the split vote that has been requested for advertising. the split vote on paragraph seventeen wants to undermine protection against precisely these harmful business practices - and it is clear to us that this must not happen, the business interests of the advertising industry must not take precedence over the interests of the general public. we are – dear colleagues – not yet leaders in the european union when it comes to the development of ai, but with the discussion we are having here today we are a big step ahead of both china and silicon valley. in europe, artificial intelligence and digital services have to follow our principles, our values ​​and our fundamental rights and not the other way around.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Services Act: Improving the functioning of the Single Market - Digital Services Act: adapting commercial and civil law rules for commercial entities operating online - Digital Services Act and fundamental rights issues posed - Framework of ethical aspects of artificial intelligence, robotics and related technologies - Civil liability regime for artificial intelligence - Intellectual property rights for the development of artificial intelligence technologies (debate)
paragraph: madam president, online services are everywhere, from the way we inform ourselves to the way we keep in touch with friends; from the way we buy books and clothes to the way we travel; from the way we eat to the way we make a date. some people born in a different time, like myself, might want to go back to how it was before, because it seems like a simpler time. but we can’t. we simply cannot put the genie back into the bottle. the online world with digital services, with artificial intelligence – it’s all here to stay. the future will be more digital, not less, and it brings incredible progress that we, as policymakers, should embrace. but... it also brings dangers that we cannot ignore anymore. let us be honest with each other, colleagues. the eu has done more to regulate the online world than any other continent. yet, even here, it is still the wild west! over the past decades, we have not followed up on illegal content and illegal activities online with the same rigour as we have illegal activities offline. we have not achieved any meaningful transparency over how algorithms push content to users on a massive scale. we have not grasped the impact of it on our democracies, our culture and our fundamental rights. instead, we have focused on voluntary cooperation, which is good, but not good enough. not nearly good enough. so as this european parliament discusses these six reports on the digital services act (dsa) and artificial intelligence (ai), i have one overarching message: these digital files matter a great deal more than many people think. we cannot leave this to the private sector without oversight and enforcement. we must keep this in the public debate as a priority and we must regulate, no matter how technical these files are. the difficult challenge before us is to find the balance between digital progress and respect for fundamental rights. as for the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs (libe) dsa report, i’m raising a few issues right now. the value of lawmaking is the real change it effects. if we start off with conflicting regulations and directives that undermine each other instead of complementing each other, we have lost the battle before it starts. we must respect the scope of each digital file. secondly, the fundamentals of the e-commerce directive were great, but its greatest subject_of_business_title: Digital Services Act: Improving the functioning of the Single Market - Digital Services Act: adapting commercial and civil law rules for commercial entities operating online - Digital Services Act and fundamental rights issues posed - Framework of ethical aspects of artificial intelligence, robotics and related technologies - Civil liability regime for artificial intelligence - Intellectual property rights for the development of artificial intelligence technologies (debate)
paragraph: madam president, i am going to take the floor on behalf of my colleague and rapporteur for this report, ibán garcía del blanco, who cannot be here today in plenary session and who must be thanked for the immense work he has done. the framework of ethical principles applicable to artificial intelligence is the first legislative initiative report in the artificial intelligence package, produced in parliament. the position of the european parliament that we will approve this week will undoubtedly be essential in future european regulations. the report is the result of long and complex negotiations between all the political groups, which started from very distant positions, and also of the work carried out with the seven parliamentary commissions that have issued opinions. on behalf of the speaker, ibán garcía del blanco, i would like to thank all of you for your work and your commitment to achieve a completely new regulation, which places europe at the forefront of the creation of a regulation that allows technological advances to be transformed into benefits for all. the legislative report contains a resolution proposal with recommendations for the commission and a proposal for a european regulation that establishes the ethical principles applicable to the development, implementation and use of artificial intelligence, robotics and related technologies in the union. artificial intelligence is presented to us as a technology with the potential to change the world as we know it, it offers great opportunities and carries great risks. our proposal is a balance between, on the one hand, guaranteeing citizens' confidence and security in new technologies and, on the other, supporting innovation in europe. it is a proposal that is respectful of technological neutrality and provides an adequate framework for the future to respond with solvency and responsibility to the rapidity of changes. our report is based on the creation of a regulatory framework of ethical principles that is mandatory for computer programs, algorithms and data included in artificial intelligence, robotics and related technologies that are developed, implemented or used in the european union. all technologies operating in europe must respect this anthropocentric perspective. the human dignity, autonomy and security of citizens cannot be called into question and, in the same way, we must guarantee compliance with fundamental rights and the legality of the union. technologies that imply a violation of these principles will not be able to operate in europe, regardless of where they are produced and whether they are supported or in the cloud. secondly, we have agreed on an approach based on the risks they may present. those technologies that may have a significant risk of causing harm or harm ⸺both to citizens and to society as a whole⸺, violating fundamental rights or breaking union laws will be considered high risk. to assess these risks, we have established objective criteria, taking into account the sector, the uses or purposes and the severity of the damages or losses that they may cause. this definition is intended to prevent legal loopholes from occurring. also included is an exhaustive list of sectors and uses that are considered high-risk, such as education, health, employment and worker recruitment, finance and credit granting, automated vehicle transportation, decision-making. public administration or environmental issues. when an application or technology is considered high risk, it must ensure compliance with a series of legal requirements and obligations: guarantee human control, strict security standards, transparency, explainability and responsibility, data reliability, non-discrimination and the elimination of biases in the algorithms and the results of automatic decisions, with very strict privacy guarantees in the case of remote recognition with biometric data and the requirement to apply the most rigorous governance standards. in parliament we also want to guarantee an artificial intelligence that is environmentally sustainable and socially responsible, because an ethical artificial intelligence is democratic, egalitarian, respects workers and intellectual property, cultural diversity and the right to digital illustration. and for this reason we appeal to the member states and the union so that investments in research are directed to those projects that offer a social or environmental benefit. to ensure the democratic development of technologies, both european and national authorities should maintain a dialogue with stakeholders, including civil society, trade unions, setting governance standards and parameters, as well as providing support to smes and companies. emerging. in addition to establishing the principles, we must control compliance with these obligations. our model reinforces european coordination and lists the tasks to be carried out, among others, to establish mandatory guidelines for the assessment of conformity with ethical principles. when they have been tested, a european certificate of conformity with ethical principles is awarded. this guarantee or quality seal will be voluntary for those technologies that are not high risk. each member state will appoint an independent authority in charge of applying these guidelines, granting the european certificate and carrying out continuous supervision of compliance with ethical principles, providing it with sufficient means and resources. the commission should assess which existing or future bodies and agencies can fulfill these tasks. with the rapporteur, in my group we believe that a european agency for artificial intelligence will bring added value to achieve a common goal, shared by all the members of the chamber: to make the european union the world leader in ethical artificial intelligence, which places the human being at the center of their development and guarantees our principles and values.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Services Act: Improving the functioning of the Single Market - Digital Services Act: adapting commercial and civil law rules for commercial entities operating online - Digital Services Act and fundamental rights issues posed - Framework of ethical aspects of artificial intelligence, robotics and related technologies - Civil liability regime for artificial intelligence - Intellectual property rights for the development of artificial intelligence technologies (debate)
paragraph: madam president, since we are talking about artificial intelligence and new technologies, thank you very much to the european parliament and also to the paris office for giving parliamentarians the opportunity to intervene from the offices! thanks also to the president of parliament. madam president, we are talking about artificial intelligence: it is present in our daily life, with social networks obviously, with everyday algorithms, and in our economy too, of course. by 2022, 42% of tasks will be performed by algorithms, compared to 29% today: this is an exponential measure. two out of three companies already use artificial intelligence on a daily basis. two reports have already been presented on responsibility and on ethics. first of all, i would like to thank mr voss for his important report, because it concretely addresses the question of responsibility, as well as the way to regulate the major technologies of the future, such as the autonomous car. it also makes it possible to have a law that is not fragmented and to have legislation and case law that are precisely unified at european level. i would also like to thank mr garcía del blanco, who was also unable to be with you, for his work on the question of ethics, which is first and foremost a question of trust, and in this respect transparency is not an end in itself, it is a tool of trust. i will take the example of image recognition: used by smartphones, recognition is, when it works, a good tool, but there can be deviations, such as when you see a certain number of states police use this technology. my report, madam president, is also an element of protection. after the protection of ethics, after the protection of liability, there is also the protection of innovations, which must be protected via intellectual property. we recommend that the commission review this issue and reset it. never has the planet had so many ideas, since 3.3 million patent applications were filed last year, and it is constantly increasing. the question of this report is who owns the intellectual property right of an intellectual work generated entirely by artificial intelligence. my report, without wishing to discourage human creation, gives a certain number of recommendations. i will name three. we precisely recommend not to recognize the legal personality of an artificial intelligence. we also recommend distinguishing the creation that was assisted by artificial intelligence from a creation that was entirely generated by artificial intelligence. it will also require a big data strategy. i know that margrethe vestager and thierry breton are very sensitive to these questions. this strategy is necessary, we need the big data sets for an artificial intelligence system to develop and also develop ideas. i will end, madam president, with a topical point which is perhaps outside the scope of my report, but which is also part of this joint debate on digital services legislation (dsa). french news also shows us how much we are going to have to think collectively about data regulation: i am talking about the drama we experienced in france with the beheading of a teacher who had been lynched on social networks for weeks. for my part, i think that we must put an end to the self-regulation of social networks and an end to hateful content. we have to get out of the hypocrisy on this question. who can accept that twitter accounts glorify terrorism for weeks without anyone doing anything? in my opinion, no one! who can accept such an outpouring of hate on all networks, on facebook? person. who can accept the public lynching of a teacher who was only doing his job? person. madam president, it is a question of assuming our responsibilities, with our colleagues, with the entire european representation, with the commission and with its support. it is about our values, our european values, our values ​​of democracy. it is a question of regulating social networks and going a little further than the sole question of illegal content by addressing that of harmful content. i think it's a good course of action. thank you very much for allowing us to integrate this reflection from the paris office and from other offices for other colleagues. i will intervene again if necessary in the debate.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Services Act: Improving the functioning of the Single Market - Digital Services Act: adapting commercial and civil law rules for commercial entities operating online - Digital Services Act and fundamental rights issues posed - Framework of ethical aspects of artificial intelligence, robotics and related technologies - Civil liability regime for artificial intelligence - Intellectual property rights for the development of artificial intelligence technologies (debate)
paragraph: madam president, dear vice-president vestager! first of all, my report is now about liability and artificial intelligence, and first of all i would like to thank the shadow rapporteurs very much, because we had a very cooperative spirit here, which has taken us further forward, but which ultimately also sends a strong signal, both to the commission as well as to the member states. digitization as a whole is of course extremely important and a challenge for society and for the economy, but in my opinion it is also about our economic survival. in this context, artificial intelligence is of particular importance and represents a special challenge and is of strategic relevance for our overall economic development. we will only really be able to compete if we actually manage to create a digital single market, because otherwise we would simply be too fragmented compared to other regions of the world. and that's why i think the member states have to look into themselves and sometimes go beyond their competences and say that it's for everyone's good if we also talk about liability under civil law accordingly. you can't just block and then say, that's our competence. no, this is about a digital single market, about the progress of all of us. consequently, we are basically also calling for a regulation in this regard, and we mean it really seriously, especially with regard to this digital single market. what actually led us to do this? we want the individual to also receive compensation as under normal national tort law. but we also want that he doesn't have to explain whether it was the software, the hardware, the wrong operation or wrong algorithms. we just want him to be compensated. we also want to comply with existing liability regulations from the member states. we do not want to prevent artificial intelligence and its system, and we want to move forward in a future-oriented manner. why do we think this is important? we're currently working on developing that. we therefore need a clear view of things, legal certainty, legal clarity, a fully harmonized framework, no fragmentation, in order to rule out the different applications in the internal market. we also want clarity – not only after five to eight years by the highest courts – and we want to fill legal gaps. but that is why there is no over-regulation in the end, so the whole thing is not a revolution, but merely the connection of corresponding risky artificial intelligence systems to what already exists, and we also consider this connection to the existing law to be reasonable. that's why we always have to keep in mind that we, as the legal committee, are currently unable to offer a coherent system because we simply cannot take certain things into account according to internal regulations. the goal here is actually to limit oneself to high-risk applications, because we think that only makes sense to provide appropriate liability. other risk ai systems are subject to the normal legal consequences of liability anyway. for the sake of legal clarity, we want to have a clear list of which ai system falls under this, and we want to act flexibly as legislators so that we can also quickly point out rapid changes by leaving delegated legal acts up to the commission. furthermore, non-pecuniary damages are also addressed, and we ask the commission to examine whether there is a need for harmonization here too.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Services Act: Improving the functioning of the Single Market - Digital Services Act: adapting commercial and civil law rules for commercial entities operating online - Digital Services Act and fundamental rights issues posed - Framework of ethical aspects of artificial intelligence, robotics and related technologies - Civil liability regime for artificial intelligence - Intellectual property rights for the development of artificial intelligence technologies (debate)
paragraph: madam president, madam vice president vestager! the internet was and is a place of freedom, especially in autocratic states, and preserving this freedom is our most important task. but today there is huge concern about this: misinformation is spreading at breathtaking speed, hatred and hate speech are pushing women and minorities out of public digital discourse, and this is also a threat to freedom of expression. but how could this have happened in the last 20 years? today there are a few monopoly-like companies that make the decisive decisions about what people actually see on the internet. that is why we now need new legislation for digital services and new rules for competition. what are the most urgent tasks? we must first put an end to an advertising business model that spies on people and manipulates their behavior. we must also seize this opportunity to put the financing of the quality press back on a secure footing, because we need it so urgently in times of uncertainty. today, three-quarters of digital advertising revenue – in france and germany, for example – goes to google and facebook. secondly, online platforms must disclose the principles according to which they prioritize contributions. we need to shed some light on these platforms, and users need to be able to design their timelines the way they want. thirdly, we need very clear rules for dealing with illegal content, i.e. detailed and binding notice-and-action procedures. transparency and democratic control are also our guiding values ​​for artificial intelligence. artificial intelligence must serve european priorities, and at the moment that is first and foremost the european green deal, because our most urgent task is still climate protection. but when it comes to humans, we need strict rules because we know that artificial intelligence is a good servant but a bad master. we know that artificial intelligence projects problems from the past, such as racism or discrimination against women, into the future and therefore anchors us in the past, and we don't want that. finally, we must also effectively enforce european fundamental rights in the case of artificial intelligence, and that will only work with a european body that can represent the interests of european citizens on an equal footing with global digital companies.

paragraph: madam president, commissioner, the development of computing, big data and algorithms have made artificial intelligence strategic today. but only people can guarantee that values ​​such as pluralism, solidarity and democracy inoculate us against the errors and abuses that can turn this opportunity into a pandemic of "artificial neglect". we need clear, simple, flexible and common legislation that does not harm the competitiveness of our entrepreneurs in the global market and avoids fragmentation, that controls the generation and operation processes of these tools, detects risks and corrects malfunctions through permanent evaluation and that guarantee a structured participation of the users. this global plan should encourage intense local action, focused on coordinating and learning more about technological capacities, promoting talent and supporting intra-entrepreneurship and the creation of new companies. thus, by contributing knowledge and value to the local industrial system, regions such as the basque country, recently designated as an example of innovation by president von der leyen, should help the union to gain global competitiveness. artificial intelligence needs ethical principles to prevent bias in algorithms, clarify industrial and legal aspects and establish formulas to determine and refine civil liability derived from events in which the influence of artificial intelligence is key. this is a crucial aspect in the field of mobility. from the transport and tourism commission we are committed to artificial intelligence to offer integrated services, better adapted to users and greener. but we warn that without investment in infrastructure so that data is collected and circulated properly, technology will not suffice. the changes that are coming require a holistic vision of urban and interurban transport and innovation and training to consolidate the new trades that smart mobility already demands.

paragraph: madam president, the digital age we live in today permeates our daily lives and even more so our children’s lives. can we accept that algorithms created by international corporations decide on what we can say and read online, what human rights defenders can say, what dissidents and whistle—blowers can publish? do you know that youtube’s filters suppressed a parliamentary debate on torture because they confused it with violence online? many constitutions ban ex—ante censorship. it is high time we take back control and do the same with censorship machines used by digital platforms. secondly, let’s tackle the predominant business model of surveillance capitalism. major platforms are tracking our every click, everything we read and write online, to analyse our personalities, our likes, our weaknesses, our illnesses. we cannot accept this permanent surveillance of users online, and therefore we need to make sure that we are not subject to pervasive tracking. likewise, the right to anonymity is essential to safeguard our identity online and prevent abuses and data losses and sales. finally, let’s address the gated communities on the internet. let’s make sure consumers can choose which platform to use to ensure competition and to ensure interaction across platforms, to break the dependency and the user lock—in that is predominant on the internet. let’s make sure we take back control of our digital lives. let me add one aspect regarding the ai reports. there is some mention here of biometrics surveillance that has nothing to do with the report on ai and ipr protection. let’s make sure that we do not confuse artificial intelligence with surveillance. this language on biometrics surveillance needs to be deleted.

paragraph: madam president! artificial intelligence is everyday life for us. for example, when our music streaming app suggests new songs based on our listening habits. other areas are perhaps less commonplace for most of us, but have the potential to change products, industries, even our entire lives - in medicine, in mobility or in agriculture. the eu has now set itself the goal of creating a uniform set of rules. this is pioneering work, and one simply has to say that it offers a real economic and social opportunity and can become a major locational advantage. there are three points that we must pay particular attention to: firstly, we must promote innovations instead of slowing them down. with any type of regulation, we should remain open to technology and rely on non-bureaucratic rules. second, civil rights are non-negotiable. the protection of fundamental rights is at the top of my agenda. there should be no mass surveillance through automatic facial recognition, nor should there be any obligation to upload filters. third: harmonization in the internal market. we can only increase the chance of artificial intelligence for people and the economy with uniform rules for the entire internal market. this creates the greatest possible legal certainty for companies and consumers. but we don't have to reinvent the wheel for this. in many areas we already have existing regulations, for example on the issue of liability and intellectual property. but we have to take a closer look: in which areas do we perhaps need updates that correspond to the characteristics of artificial intelligence? because our goal must be to set a framework that is smart, open to technology and sustainable and based on ethical principles and fundamental european values. then we can make it, then the european union can make it to the top of the world, to the top of the world in terms of innovation.

paragraph: madam president, artificial intelligence is an opportunity to be seized because it will improve the efficiency of most human activities. it is also a great source of jobs and economic development, especially for start-ups and small and medium-sized businesses. however, you have to be careful, because it can also constitute a danger. it is to deal with this that the three reports voss, garcía del blanco and séjourné were written. overall, these three reports have achieved their objective by requiring that artificial intelligence always remain under human control to avoid the most draconian abuses. i particularly approve of the voss report, which has the merit of avoiding any excessive centralization by asking to entrust the damage caused by artificial intelligence to national systems of civil liability for fault. it is rightly only for high-risk artificial intelligence systems that he advocates a new liability regime based on the obligation for their deployer to take out civil liability insurance, in order to guarantee their victims to obtain compensation. all is not perfect, however, and i deplore in particular that certain reports persist in considering the creation of a new european agency dedicated to artificial intelligence. from my point of view, there are already too many agencies. i also regret that the garcía del blanco report plans to use artificial intelligence to censor hate speech and false information: these incriminations are too vague and will open the way to abuses of the freedom of expression. they should be clarified, for example by removing the offense of incitement to islamist terrorism. finally, with regard to the wölken report on digital services, i agree with its main orientations, in particular the idea that the legality of content generated by their users must be determined by a national judicial authority and not by a private commercial entity. i also approve of the principle of respecting the freedom of expression of platform users, as well as the desire to fight against the most intrusive forms of targeted advertising. all in all, i am happy to have contributed to drawing up these four reports and thank the rapporteurs for having accepted some of my suggestions.

paragraph: madam president! the federal government has just introduced a chat bot that should offer us all orientation in these difficult covid times - an example of artificial intelligence on a small scale. i just tried the bot and realized one thing: normal human-like communication isn't possible outside of cue bingo. a federal government chat bot is of course not a reflection of the breathtaking developments we are facing, but it clearly shows one thing: there can be no ai without humans as creators, but also without humans as end addressees. our strategies for artificial intelligence must be human-centric. and with these reports we are taking the first real step in this direction. we enshrine human responsibility for ai. but we also state: responsibility for people. intelligence may be artificial, but we can only get ahead with real, not artificial, fundamental rights. and that is why we expressly welcome the fact that the report on ethics is not just about philosophizing about abstract ethical principles, but that this is a basis for binding european regulations and for fundamental rights. wherever algorithms cause damage - and we also welcome that in the other report - it should not just be about property that is being protected, but also about personal rights, human dignity and equality. if people don't understand the federal government's chat bot, then the technology has failed. if people are discriminated against by algorithms, then the technology has failed. if artificial intelligence changes human habitat beyond recognition and destroys our climate, then the technology has failed. and this is not an appeal for pessimism, but for optimism about progress. that's the most important thing for us. after all, ai must not be thought of without green accounting. of course we need ai for our green transition, but we can't imagine it without looking at the damage done by artificial intelligence. in frankfurt alone, 20% of the energy costs are caused by data centers. internet consumes more co2 costs in germany than air travel. we have to change that, we have to include that in the green accounting of the ai ​​- that's the only way we can make progress. no ai—technology without fundamental rights and without environmental protection.

paragraph: dear madam president! dear commissioner! creating legal regulations in the area of ​​new technologies is a race against time. innovative systems that elude standard definitions raise great hopes, but also numerous social fears. that is why people, their dignity and rights must always be at the center of digital transformation. it cannot be treated as an unconscious, passive user or – even worse – only as a source of data. the full use of the potential of the digital revolution will be possible only if we properly and transparently define the opportunities and threats brought by the full automation of many areas of our lives. however, no technology is foolproof. it is necessary to change existing regulations in areas such as enforcement of liability for accidents and failures caused by systems based on artificial intelligence. the process of pursuing claims and compensation must be transparent, and the identification of the entity responsible for the payment of compensation must not be a problem. responsibilities in this respect should be distributed in line with the ability of manufacturers, operators and users of systems using artificial intelligence to control risk. this is very important when creating the right insurance products, for example for autonomous vehicles. i am convinced that mr voss's report defines the challenges in this area well and suggests appropriate legal solutions. i hope that the commission will follow our recommendation.

paragraph: mr president, what is, basically, the issue of these various texts which we are discussing this evening? the question is: can we regain control over our digital lives? and is it possible, are we able to invent a european model which is different from that of the united states, where we really notice the pursuit of profit at all costs, and which is also different from the chinese model, where we see although technology is put to the service of mass surveillance so that the dictatorship continues? i believe it is possible, provided you respect a certain number of fundamental principles, to be able to set limits and set a framework. there are at least two points on which, in my opinion, we can go further. the first is facial recognition. i share the doubts that have been expressed by the many human rights organisations, which have warned of the use of artificial intelligence driven cctv, which will disproportionately limit the possibilities of anonymous movement and which is an intolerable invasion of privacy with additional risks, because ai is unable to avoid misidentifications based on gender, age or ethnicity. this is a real problem and we need a european moratorium on video surveillance or, in any case, on facial recognition. the second point is that of consumer protection. we must ensure respect for intellectual property, which is not the case today. platforms like amazon or alibaba market counterfeit products. nearly two-thirds of products today, according to the european consumers bureau, are illegal products. and there, europe must crack down, because it is not up to the platforms to determine what is allowed and what is not. finally, allow me, because i am speaking from paris, to tell you that it is absolutely necessary that the rights of citizens, respect for dignity and respect for human rights be ensured by the platforms, so that we escape this surge of digital hatred which resulted, the day before yesterday in france, in this abominable murder of a teacher who was really being prosecuted by a fatwa. this is also part of the debate on recovering our digital sovereignty and respecting the rights of european citizens.

paragraph: mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank the rapporteurs for their great work. quite rightly, the starting point is an ethical reflection from which adequate laws must arise. we cannot allow the ethical threshold of ai systems to fall below the human one. artificial intelligence will pose many challenges. one scenario to evaluate concerns its misuse by criminal and terrorist organizations. there is a risk that the software that manages ai will be sabotaged or tampered with. it would be naive to think that cybercrime and computer terrorism will not make a quantum leap with the evolution of artificial intelligence systems. data theft and smuggling, hacking, industrial copyright infringement, sabotage and hostage taking of ai systems. we're not talking science fiction, it's already happened. while we need to protect the patents that manage the systems, it will also be necessary to make these systems accessible to those conducting investigations, such as judges and police forces. it has already been seen in the past how companies that own encryption systems have hindered or even refused access to those investigating terrorist groups and criminal organizations. i therefore want the commission's text on the ethical aspects of ai to strike the right balance between system transparency, citizens' right to privacy, investigative needs for the fight against criminal organizations and copyright protection.

paragraph: mr. president, i am glad that we are discussing a topic that will play such a significant role in shaping the future world and europe - artificial intelligence. the penetration of artificial intelligence systems into manufacturing, services and all sectors of the economy is an integral part of the 4.0 industrial revolution, which will have fundamental and far-reaching effects. ultimately, it will not be a technological change, but a complex cybernetic-physical-social transformation. the development of artificial intelligence will have an impact on the whole society and on all parts of our lives. artificial intelligence is not only a robot, as we might imagine based on karel čapek's play and science fiction, but also software - simply an algorithm, which is often not completely obvious and can cause credibility problems. at the same time, it is absolutely essential that the systems used in europe enjoy the credibility they deserve, also based on compliance with the principle of legality and regulations and ethical principles. it has certainly been heard many times today and will be heard again that we must create a balance - this is what we are committed to.

independence depends on it.

paragraph: dear mr. president, the protection of intellectual property is an increasingly important topic at the time of the advent of artificial intelligence. it is obvious that the weight of mental work will constantly increase and its protection will thus become more and more important. until recently, the concept of intellectual property was more or less clear. someone made or created something and if someone else copied it without permission, they broke the law. however, in the age of digital technologies, more and more ambiguity enters this area. we have to answer questions that we would have recently relegated to the world of science fiction. when artificial intelligence will be able to create, who will actually be the owner of the results of this creation? who will be responsible for the autonomous decisions of the machines? and what if artificial intelligence starts creating itself? it may seem premature, but development is moving at a tremendous pace and sooner or later we will be faced with these dilemmas. and then we must already have clear rules and clear legal frameworks. the main principle we must remember is that technology always serves man and society and not the other way around. no matter how complex a machine or program is, it is always just the result of human intelligence and work. therefore, there must always be a person at the end of the decision. just as a person can always decide whether to use artificial intelligence or not, only a person must have the final say in the decision-making process. only in this way can we ensure that artificial intelligence serves us, improves our processes and improves the quality of our services.

paragraph: the types of digital services and the roles of digital service providers have changed significantly since the e-commerce directive was adopted 20 years ago. under the changed circumstances, member states have begun to define online services differently (for example, netzdg in germany, the law regulating illegal online content in france, etc.), and this would inevitably lead to the fragmentation of the european union's single market. therefore, updating the definition of network services is essential. the basic positions of the e-commerce directive should definitely be preserved during the modernization: the principle of limited liability, the principle of the country of location (coo) and the principle of the prohibition of the general obligation to monitor. regulation of digital services should not impose disproportionate new obligations on companies. nor should regulations harm innovation. i am categorically against banning the use of facial recognition systems based on artificial intelligence by the public sector. we must protect people's privacy, but we must not kill innovation. i don't think it's reasonable to ban targeted advertising. as a consumer, i prefer to receive information about goods and services that really interest me, rather than drowning in the noise of plain advertising. it was with a heavy heart that i supported the compromise proposal.
