paragraph: madam president, the european union needs to show leadership in these extremely challenging and uncertain times. our clear strategies also need to be clearly communicated. the epp group welcomes the commission’s work programme and we are ready to work together on the implementation of our priorities. now i would like to briefly walk you through the epp’s priorities, aside from the multiannual financial framework (mff) and the recovery package. first, the digital strategy. during this plenary, the european parliament is to adopt six reports on the digital services act and artificial intelligence. these files matter a lot and we are now opening up discussions on how we, as regulators, can strike the right balance between digital progress and the respect of fundamental rights and freedoms. it is up to us, as policymakers, to build a regulatory framework for where voluntary commitments from the private sector are not enough. we have to create an artificial intelligence ecosystem that serves the people first. looking to the future, we have to make education and training systems fit for the digital age. the digital revolution also requires enhanced cross-border judiciary cooperation. second, the functions of the schengen area. with the second wave of the pandemic sweeping through europe, better coordination is necessary to avoid disruption of the internal market and preserve jobs. we welcome the intention of the commission to present a new strategy for the future of schengen. however, unfortunately, we see that member states have once again adopted various national restrictions which undermine not only the right of eu citizens to free movement, but also the recovery of the eu economy. our group supports a healthy union that enables innovation, invests in the health and well-being of its citizens, and increases our resilience and preparedness to tackle cross-border health threats. an aging population, the need to ensure better access to treatment for all, the high prevalence of chronic diseases or diseases with a high social burden, such as cancer, require a more coordinated response at european level. we also believe that the eu must shape globalisation and use its trade policy to set standards internationally. our ability to conclude win-win agreements is fundamental to economic growth and recovery. however, we must not be naive. we strongly support the commission in ensuring that the interests of the eu are fully protected and that our companies do not suffer from unfair competition. this brings me to the industrial strategy, which has to remain competitive while taking into account the digital and environmental challenges of tomorrow. last but not least, the green deal. our environmental ambitions cannot be only about defending targets. the epp will focus on concrete means that will bring about a significant reduction in emissions. innovation and research will be key in this field. we ask the commission to keep this in mind when negotiating the mff and specific programmes with the council. fighting against climate change and fighting for employment in the context of the covid-19 pandemic subject_of_business_title: Towards a New Consumer Agenda beyond 2020 (debate)
paragraph: madam president! the covid-19 pandemic has irreversibly moved part of trade, both services and goods, to the digital area. in addition to many advantages, i.e. greater competition between entrepreneurs, faster shopping and access to an enlarged base of suppliers for consumers, this change entails certain risks. this is of particular importance in the context of online platforms or non-common market sellers who are not interested in complying with european union standards. such practices put consumers at risk on the one hand, and european small and medium-sized enterprises on the other. in the face of economic collapse, it is crucial to develop standards that support consumer rights, while not undermining their purchasing power. the challenge for the commission is to update the rules in response to the challenges of the pandemic while not overregulating a recovering market. the revision of the general product safety directive will be one such task. the legal framework developed for breakthrough technologies - such as artificial intelligence - can make it a driving force of the european economy and a tool supporting consumers, or make european economies in the tail of innovative solutions in a dozen or so years. the choice is ours. if only we properly use our predispositions and focus on innovation, the current crisis may be an opportunity for a developmental leap for europe.

subject_of_business_title: Towards a New Consumer Agenda beyond 2020 (debate)
paragraph: madam president, i welcome that the european commission came up with this agenda, because we need to develop the european topic of consumer protection, and it is also an economic topic, because consumer spending in our union makes up 54% of the european gdp. consumer protection takes on new dimensions in the conditions of the digital economy. it is no longer just about exchanging defective goods, poor service or refunding money. we are increasingly confronted with sophisticated fraud on the internet, with identity theft or with the new phenomenon of so-called cryptocurrencies. individual states can no longer deal with these phenomena alone. any reform of european consumer protection policy must take them into account. and it is necessary to create effective mechanisms to protect our citizens from them. this topic is also closely related to the development of artificial intelligence technologies - here we must always remember that the final decision-maker is the person. not only in the process of using products and services with elements of artificial intelligence, but also in the overall final chain with the support of artificial intelligence. a special topic that i want to draw attention to and that deserves more attention is the topic of protecting children in the online space. they are particularly exposed to deceptive or aggressive business practices and often to harassment. i believe that several measures need to be taken to protect children, such as: first, to support the promotion of media literacy, the development of critical thinking and the development of the skills necessary for analysis, which is necessary to recognize the difference between objective facts and subjective opinions. second, initiate the establishment of effective age verification and enforcement systems to ensure that children are protected from digital product, service and content and commercial exploitation. third, create an online mechanism to report illegal and inappropriate content on the internet, including a rapid intervention system, and to achieve the blocking of access to web content. at the same time, there is a need to involve internet service providers, including social networks, to play an active role in preventing and removing illegal content. i think we need a union policy for safer social networks and an extension of the use of default privacy settings for children who register on social networks to increase the safety of minors. we also need a europe-wide code of conduct for the sale of video games to minors. i believe that these measures will help to better protect children in the entire online space and contribute to a safer life for all of us.

subject_of_business_title: Towards a New Consumer Agenda beyond 2020 (debate)
paragraph: madam president, commissioner, the time when we thought that the internet was going to make the market transparent, eliminating information asymmetries, is long gone. we know that the opposite happened, the market power of the big platforms is enormous and is growing by the minute due to the network effect. it's more or less like going “naked” to the market. when we enter an online store, sellers know us better than we do and can therefore exploit our weaknesses and vulnerabilities. if we are looking for sneakers, we are recommended a gym, a personal trainer and maybe even a diet program. we therefore need to “dress up” to regain some power and privacy. consumer data should not be used for purposes other than those for which they were provided, nor should data be collected that is not essential to provide the service sought. commissioner, the digital transition has not only transformed the ways of selling and buying. it also transformed products, which are now confused with services, becoming intelligent and dynamic throughout their life cycle. from the car, which runs by itself, to a simple kitchen machine, from which i order the bolo rei for christmas, instead of going to the pastry shop, as usual. we need to prevent these digital products from becoming obsolete faster and, above all, ensure that the speed at which new products enter the market we are witnessing, european or imported, and their successive updates do not run over our security. the revision of the general product safety directive must, therefore, take into account the conclusions of the imco report, which will be presented today, and, in particular, consider the precautionary principle in relation to innovative products of greater risk, making so that the burden of proof is that they are not dangerous, not the opposite. the slowest innovation, in certain cases, may be the one that deserves the most confidence and the one that lasts without setbacks. or the use of blockchain to ensure better traceability of products, or artificial intelligence to strengthen the capacity of inspection authorities. commissioner, the new agenda, in these and other areas, must serve to give consumers the same weapons available to platforms and other service providers. in short, the new agenda must be a kind of software that updates the current legislation, that makes it bug-free, that makes it suitable for effective consumer protection, in an economy that we want to be sustainable and that we know will be increasingly digital!

subject_of_business_title: Addressing product safety in the single market (short presentation)
paragraph: madam president, i should like to thank ms walsmann very much. i’m delighted you mentioned christmas, because a lot of us have fears around christmas, but it’s nice to look on it as an opportunity, and of course when we’re buying gifts to think of safety. so thank you for your good work on this. it’s both important and timely. buying a safe product is the utmost important thing – it protects consumers and also the functioning of the single market, and all products sold on the market should be safe, but you have raised a number of very important issues when it comes to non-food products. most of these issues correspond with the main objectives of the revision of the general product safety directive, which is planned for the second quarter of next year. and this includes the safety of consumer products, linked, as you said, to new technologies, like connected products or products powered by artificial intelligence and the need to address the growth in online sales. these issues need to be tackled from different angles and we’ll carry out the revision of the general product safety directive in conjunction with other initiatives such as the digital services act, the revision of the machinery directive and initiatives on artificial intelligence. the commission is also working on delegated acts under the radio equipment directive. in your report, you underline the importance of the recently adopted regulation on market surveillance and compliance. this new regulation is a major step forward for the 70 pieces of harmonised product legislation, many of them on product safety, such as the low voltage directive and the toy safety directive. it will provide better protection for consumers, it will greatly help national inspectors, and the implementation of this regulation is ongoing. the commission will also support the eu product compliance network, providing funding from the single market programme, and we thank parliament for emphasising the importance of market surveillance in this programme. this report also calls on the commission to encourage more online marketplaces to join the product safety pledge. just two weeks ago, two new online marketplaces joined the pledge, which brings the total number of signatories to nine major online actors. the report also raises issues linked to ineffective recalls of dangerous products from consumers, and i think this is an area of deep concern. most consumers are not sometimes even aware that they own a recalled product and many others continue to use dangerous products despite seeing a recall notice. i think that is deeply concerning but important to stress. we are currently working on developing guidance on product recalls and we will also look at this issue during the revision of the general product safety directive. so thank you for this opportunity this evening, for your work and i look forward to tomorrow’s vote.

subject_of_business_title: Situation of Fundamental Rights in the European Union – Annual Report for the years 2018-2019 (debate)
paragraph: dear mr. president, the annual report for the years 2018-2019, which we are debating today, mentions many areas, such as persistent discrimination, unequal access, the rise of racism and xenophobia, poverty and migration. year after year we find the same thing, not only do people feel that the responsible institutions cannot deal with it, the situation is even getting worse despite the fact that we have legal and financial mechanisms. we must remember, and the current pandemic has confirmed it, that the freedom of an individual ends where the freedom of another begins. for example, wearing a mask is not about whether i like it or not, but about a responsible approach, when by wearing a mask i protect not only myself, but also my surroundings. so we cannot assert our right by denying the right of another. the union cannot have ambitions to be a leader in digitization, artificial intelligence or green agreements if it forgets vulnerable and endangered groups. the poor, elderly and socially excluded cannot be denied the right to a dignified life. no child can be denied the right to education. the union will only fulfill its ambitions if we get rid of the threats of terrorism. people will be safe on the streets, in schools and churches. the union must find a way to prevent disinformation and hoaxes used by extremists. our ambition must be change not only in news writing. here in europe, i must be a leader in respecting the rights of each one of us. these are interconnected areas, complex solutions, and therefore i would like the text of this report to be more balanced.

subject_of_business_title: Pharmaceutical strategy for Europe (debate)
paragraph: mr president, commissioner, one of the lessons of the covid-19 pandemic is that we have accelerated the construction of a european health union, and this new pharmaceutical strategy is an opportunity to cement one of the pillars of this new europe for health. with this strategy we must be able to face any pandemic or health threat, put the patient at the centre of all decisions, solve unmet medical needs, ensure access to medicines for all, strengthen the competitiveness of european industry and make europe a world leader in research and health care. we must invest more in the fight against antimicrobial resistance and its rapid spread, which threatens europe with more than 33 000 deaths per year. today there are more than 7,000 rare diseases, 95% of them untreated. we must respond to patients and their families in the face of this great despair. we have a huge gap in pediatric drug research and development, and our children come first. and we cannot allow a european cancer patient to have a difference of between 7% and 90% in access to approved medicines. or you have to wait 90 to 1,000 days for a drug to be marketed after it has been approved. the strategy should also strengthen the competitiveness of the pharmaceutical industry by fostering a stable and robust regulatory system, improving public procurement, speeding up approval procedures without sacrificing safety and facilitating the availability of quality medicines. technological and digital transformation must also be a reality, using artificial intelligence to improve early detection and advance innovative and personalized treatments. and we must boost production in europe and our industrial autonomy so as not to depend on third countries. there are many challenges ahead of us and we must respond to each of them. and to achieve this, the public and private sectors must work together. only in this way will we achieve the balance between innovation, accessibility to it and the sustainability of national health systems. only in this way will we protect one of the great fundamental rights, the health of all, and with great hope for all.

paragraph: mr. president, i am not going to repeat with data the importance of small and medium-sized companies for economic growth and competitiveness because it is obvious, but i am going to insist that, precisely because of this importance, the management of recovery funds must be focus to a large extent on these small and medium-sized companies. i also want to stress that it is necessary to bear in mind that, for smes, digital infrastructures, fiber optics and 5g networks are essential and, therefore, so is the proper transposition of the european code of electronic communications. but, in addition, the ability to manage data, metadata and artificial intelligence itself is decisive for small and medium-sized companies to be able to innovate and it is, therefore, of vital importance that they have the appropriate technological capacity and digital training that today , in most european countries, it is still very insufficient. the european digital program is a very good step in that direction because, among other things, it will make it possible to access supercomputers and advanced digital training. and, for all of this, we have to celebrate today the agreement that was reached this morning on this matter and was closed between parliament and the council, on the digital europe programme, for which we must truly congratulate ourselves.

subject_of_business_title: Quality of water intended for human consumption – Implementation of the EU water legislation (debate)
paragraph: madam president, while we are defending access to water in the third world all day long, allow me to remind you that our own inhabitants are finding it increasingly difficult to access it. already 11% of europeans do not have sufficient access to water. your worldview and business model have dried up groundwater and caused many streams to disappear. your progressive liberalism has already done enormous damage to agriculture. today, it is the water resource that is threatened. in this area, the institutions that know best what to apply are the states, and it is the states that must have the last word. propose a clear and logical text, without liberal ulterior motives, pseudo-humanist ulterior motives or even pseudo-ecologist ulterior motives. let us defend the common sense of the member states in the sustainable management of water. let us increase european mutual aid against fires and droughts. let's promote innovation and research. let us promote artificial intelligence in particular to help our respective countries make more profitable and above all more ecological decisions. despite these advances, too many points should be excluded from these texts. what is this obsession which consists in defending minorities all day long in all european texts? what is the link or relationship with access to water? at the same time, the most modest europeans no longer have access to it in certain regions. we denounce the inclusion in this text of any form of liberalization of the water market. and finally, let us refuse sanctions for countries that are not in compliance with the framework directive on water. the commission has no legitimacy to impose fines on sovereign and free states.

subject_of_business_title: Strengthening the single market: the future of free movement of services (debate)
paragraph: madam president! thank you, dear colleague løkkegaard, for a really excellent report. ladies and gentlemen, if around 70% of eu economic output is in services, but services are only around 20% of intra-european trade, then we have far too much wasted potential because too many member states are still creating unjustified barriers of protectionism. but we have to leverage this potential right now, also on our way out of the economic crisis. because more competition means more opportunities, more markets for companies, more choice at more competitive prices for consumers. we need that above all for the digital economy. digital business models, digital services must be able to scale much more easily across the eu. above all, the digital services act and the digital markets act must break down barriers for this. and rules for artificial intelligence and other new disruptive services, technologies have to be made at european level. i want us to put the union at the forefront of innovation in the world. and that just doesn't work with national solo efforts. this requires a common european market: the digital single market. the cornerstone of this is a really real market for services. and this report is an excellent place to start.

intervention_header: Nicolas Schmit, Member of the Commission
intervention_header_en: Nicolas Schmit, Member of the Commission
subject_of_business_title: European Skills Agenda for sustainable competitiveness, social fairness and resilience (debate)
paragraph: madam president, honourable members, first i want to thank you, and in particular the members of the committee on employment and social affairs, for this question on a very important topic. indeed the skills agenda is the centrepiece of our efforts to bring to life the principles of the un pillar of social rights and notably principle number one. this principle states that everyone, i quote, ‘has the right to quality and inclusive education, training and lifelong learning.’ we need to invest in people and in building a strong human capital to prepare and accompany the green and digital transitions, as well as to respond to the consequences of the covid-19 crisis. our goal is to empower people with education and training, with a view to boosting the creation of quality jobs and setting the conditions for a more innovative, competitive, inclusive and sustainable development model. you rightfully asked about the progress we made in implementing the european skills agenda. the agenda was adopted by the commission on 1 july 2020. it is a five-year plan to help europe develop more and better skills and to put them to good use. since last july, 7 of the agenda’s 12 flagship actions have already been launched. such actions include the council recommendation on vocational education and training which we already had the pleasure of discussing in this house. we have also launched the new europass platform. the remaining five actions will be launched in 2021, notably the initiatives on individual learning accounts and on micro-credentials. the agenda is centred around inclusive learning. it is vital to address this point across all actions, for example in the council recommendation on vocational education and training. we also underlined the importance of digital skills, and digital education and training. this is even more fundamental in the aftermath of the covid-19 pandemic. therefore the digital education plan for 2021-2027 adopted on 30 september 2020 puts forward inclusion as one of its guiding principles. we are also working on the skills for life initiatives to reach out to the most vulnerable and to create concrete opportunities for engaging with learning. our ambitions will fail to reach that goal if we collectively do not invest. we need to make the best use of the unprecedented funding of the union budget to tackle the economic and social consequences of this crisis. this includes of course the european social fund+ which can now be implemented following the agreement in trilogue between parliament and council’s negotiators very recently. additionally, the commission has encouraged member states to use the recovery and resilience facility where one of the seven flagship initiatives for reforms and investments is re-skill and upskill. the european parliament has played a central role in strengthening the position of education and skills in the legal framework of the recovery and resilience facility. i thank you for that as there can be no recovery and no resilience if we do not ensure adequate investment in skills and in quality jobs, especially also in the transition from one job to another. member states should put a strong emphasis on investment in skills in their national recovery and resilience plans, but we are working now with member states to make sure that upskilling and re-skilling is a top focus area. this is not all. skills are a shared responsibility and it is essential for everybody to play their part. this is why we will put in place a number of measures to unlock private investment in skills. we will look at how fiscal frameworks can do better to support reforms and investment in skills, and how enterprises could better report on their employees’ skills development. all these efforts culminate in the pact for skills, which commissioner breton and i launched on 10 november 2020. the pact represents a shared engagement model for skills development. partnerships should be created in order to respond to the skills challenges in different sectors and should involve social partners, too. to date, three skills partnerships are already in place and altogether eur 11 billion have been committed by partners in industrial ecosystems to upskill their workforce in the coming years. yes, the question of helping member states to align their national education systems with the labour market is an important one. of course the organisation and content of education and training is a matter for the member states, but targeted and up-to-date skills intelligence can help align training with evolving labour market needs, as well as support individuals in their choices. as part of the skills agenda the commission, in cooperation with eurostat and the eu agency cedefop, is improving and making more widely available such skills intelligence at regional and sectoral level. let me give you just one example. a big data initiative using artificial intelligence has analysed over 150 million job vacancies across europe. this is an example of assessing skills needs in real time. the results are already online and the commission is disseminating our findings with key stakeholders such as the european network of public employment services and with social partners. the skills agenda already in its name sets the path towards which we have to go: sustainable competitiveness, social fairness and resilience, and i know that i can count on this parliament to go on this path.

paragraph: president! the lack of resources, the transition to a resource-efficient, digitized and climate-neutral economy, as well as the expanding use of artificial intelligence present new challenges to the employment and labor market. new professions are created, while existing ones are transformed or disappear. this clearly indicates that a rapid change in skills and abilities is needed for the competitiveness of the european union and its member states. the covid-19 pandemic accelerated the digital transition and showed the level of digital skills of different age groups. due to security measures, most of our activities have been transferred to the digital space, remote work and distance education have become part of everyday life for millions overnight, exposing the limits of our digital preparedness. i am glad that the new european skills development agenda also intends to contribute to the management of the economic and labor market challenges caused by the covid epidemic. i welcome forward-looking proposals and it is important to show a sustainable path for future generations. in skills development, modern, innovative and high-quality education and training are very important, which are directly related to the labor market and social needs, and must also contribute to equipping young people with important skills that prepare them for real life. vocational training and lifelong learning must be given priority, as it is very important, through training and retraining, that they can always remain on the labor market, and it is very important that we think not only of young people, but also of adults and the elderly.

paragraph: mr president, the digital services act will stimulate the digital single market, which is crucial for our smes, among other things. it is good that we want to limit the omnipotence of the platforms, but the “notice and action” system will lead to censorship due to the mechanism for notification, knowledge and accountability. the platforms will run every message through their algorithm resulting in hyperpolitically correct censorship, as was the case with facebook. the eu must take freedom of expression as a starting point and impose a universal service obligation on these platforms. after all, the platforms are both the mail and the mailboxes of the twenty-first century. censorship should be limited to an exhaustive set of serious cases. it is up to the judge to judge the rest, as it should be in a constitutional state. i come from one of the few countries where censorship is constitutionally prohibited. let that also be the guiding principle for the european union.

paragraph: madam president, commissioner, my dear colleagues! the dismantling of barriers is one of the greatest achievements in the european union: only the dismantling of our internal borders and the abolition of customs controls have helped the european economy to achieve true greatness. it's about time we transferred this idea to the digital space. that is exactly the goal of the european data strategy - we want to build a schengen for data in europe. data should be able to circulate safely and easily within europe. only if we open our national data silos and link european data and make it usable, which today often still gathers dust unused in public institutions or on the hard drives of medium-sized companies, can we, for example, advance artificial intelligence made in europe. of course, we have to make sure that citizens and companies know exactly what their data is being used for. such a european internal market for data should – precisely as an alternative to the business models of the american data giants – give back control over data to citizens and companies. take health data as an example: a european medical data room could take us years forward in cancer research. for example geo and mobility data: here we can get a lot of useful information for environmental and climate protection. or, for example, all the data generated in agriculture - this also helps our farmers to manage in a more resource-efficient manner. so, we have huge opportunities if we implement the eu data strategy appropriately, and we are all called upon to do that now.

paragraph: madam president, during the first legislature of full validity of the treaty of lisbon and the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs of this european parliament - which i have the honor of chairing - consumed a lot of time and energy in exercising its role as legislator of fundamental rights in terms of data protection, approving the general data protection regulation and the directive that protects the data of europeans before the investigation of crimes. and that data protection package finally came into force in 2018, mandating that two years later, in 2020, the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs present an application report. and it does so in a context that could not be more challenging: at a time when the european union is legislating the digital package, artificial intelligence and, at the same time, is facing data protection in controlling the pandemic, in medical research and in the approval of green certificates. and this report has an overall positive assessment. companies, including small and medium-sized ones, have adapted, as well as public administrations, to the new data protection regime. and yet, there are still problems and we detect them. first, abuses of consent by online advertising or "dark employers." secondly, behind-the-scenes abuses of data protection against fundamental rights, such as freedom of expression and communication or freedom of association and collective bargaining. but, thirdly, there are also discrepancies in the way of applying it, because, above all, some countries are failing to provide their data protection agencies with material, technological and personal resources so that they can effectively clamp down on the giants. in the net. and we detect that there are national protection authorities that are not adequately fulfilling their function. therefore, a positive assessment, but at the same time a wake-up call to fully exercise the authority of the data protection authorities to fully enforce the general data protection regulation in the coming years.

paragraph: mr president, the general data protection regulation (gdpr) is not perfect, but it is groundbreaking and aims to set a global standard. in a post-covid world with the rapid development of artificial intelligence and the increased threat of cyber-attacks, a robust and phishing-resistant data legal framework that allows our economy to flourish is vital. the gdpr has the potential to play to the eu's greatest asset: mutual trust, independent oversight and a legal level playing field. but we still need to address persistent inconsistencies, non-compliance and gaps. it's not the time to break all the rules and start over. but it is time to make the regulations work as the legislator intended. we need to consider how we can make gdpr go hand in hand with changing technology. how can we help businesses grow in a digital age? how can we offer smes more guidance and support? and ultimately, how can we better protect our citizens' privacy and data? that's what it should be about!

paragraph: mr president, the gdpr has now been in force for more than two years and we cannot ignore it: the regulation is proving its usefulness. it ensures better protection of personal data and wider public awareness and sets standards worldwide. thousands of companies have done their utmost to be fully gdpr compliant to date. they have also made the necessary investments for this. i wish to make three comments today about our data policy. firstly, we must not be blind to the shortcomings and problems that have become apparent in recent years. we have to recognize that the gdpr is time consuming and expensive for smes and everyday associations. in addition, application and enforcement are not the same in every member state. this disrupts the proper functioning of the internal market. secondly, we must not hinder the exchange of data with third countries. adequacy decisions with third countries are indeed crucial to enable companies to exchange data with each other in a smooth and gdpr-compliant manner. third and last are the new technologies, which are often based on artificial intelligence and require large amounts of data to function properly. the gdpr should not hinder the european union in the global race for innovative strategic technologies. that is why, together with my group, i call on the commission, in the coming months and years, to fully assess the effects of the gdpr on these new technologies and to work out a plan so that they can continue to thrive and develop in the future.

subject_of_business_title: Control of exports, brokering, technical assistance, transit and transfer of dual-use (debate)
paragraph: mr. president, dual-use technologies, those that can be used for civil as well as military uses, are almost as old as humanity. if we go back to the paleolithic, we already find flint axes necessary for hunting, but also used for war. technology, by its very nature, is a double-edged sword. on the one hand, it is a tool to generate innovation, new economic opportunities and new jobs. that is why europe must continue to bet on new techniques such as artificial intelligence or quantum computing so as not to lose the global technological race. technology has also been consolidated in recent years as a key instrument to help the state security forces and corps to protect all citizens. but, on the other hand, there are many reasons to control and limit technology transfers and exports of these services outside the european union. if they fall into the wrong hands, these technologies can endanger our own national security or restrict the freedoms and human rights of citizens of third countries. i believe that the report that we are debating today strikes the right balance to continue advancing thanks to technology without seriously endangering rights and freedoms.

paragraph: madam president, madam minister, dear colleagues! i listened to the debate with great interest and, above all, heard the various requests for resources from different corners. i could also agree with that, because the commission is ultimately required to implement everything that was agreed in the multiannual financial framework. but i believe that we are all equally challenged - also against the background of the limited funds that are ultimately available to us - to identify potential where we can make further savings on the one hand, reallocations that ultimately enable us to actually do our job. and i would like to point out that in the area of ​​intelligence of this kind there are possibilities that have not yet been exhausted and that we all have to identify together and ultimately apply. i would like to add to what monika hohlmeier and president lehne said. if, for example, we are confronted with the fact that with shared management of funds there are around 300 programs that ultimately prevent successful interoperability: we must do everything together to enforce this interoperability - i say this quite deliberately - because if there is interoperability, then there is automatically a dramatic reduction in programs, and then there are also additional possibilities, so to speak, to rely more on artificial intelligence when processing information and data etc. and to use the people there, so to speak where it is about the interpretation, about the analysis of the corresponding data, and not that we have to waste resources - in the truest sense of the word - in order to get data physically. here, i believe, we have common tasks ahead of us, and i would also like to say that we were certainly able to achieve successes together in the negotiations on the multiannual financial framework, in terms of the possibility at european level of gaining direct access to the final beneficiaries . however, i regret that this joint resolution could not be implemented in the sectoral negotiations and that we are actually back where we were before. against the background of the limited, or not the limited, but the limited financial possibilities, we all have to think about where - as the saying goes - "efficiency gains" are possible, which we then ultimately use accordingly in our respective institutions have to bring. in any case, i gave the commission the task of looking at this in great detail for our area. this is a complex exercise, but i think we would be well advised to approach it across institutions, because ultimately we should all benefit from it and, as a first step, we should ensure interoperability within our institutions.

subject_of_business_title: Programme for the internal market, competitiveness of enterprises, the area of plants, animals, food and feed and European statistics (Single Market Programme) 2021-2027 (debate)
paragraph: mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am very proud to be able to speak here today to bring to parliament, to our citizens, the results obtained in the negotiations on the internal market programme. a program of more than 4 billion euros, which will finance the fundamental areas of what is commonly considered one of the greatest successes of our union and which is a fundamental building block of that deep integration between countries, between our economies, between our citizens, one of those concrete achievements with which de facto solidarity is built, to quote schuman, a de facto solidarity that arises precisely from these connections, from these exchanges that take place in the common market. compared to the start of negotiations in 2019, the world we knew has completely changed. the covid crisis has highlighted more than ever the importance of a well-integrated, more resilient, functioning internal market in all its aspects. indeed, all the areas financed by the program were on the front line during the crisis and will be even more so during the recovery of our economies. we recall, for example, the blockages of goods and medicines during the first months of the pandemic and how many difficulties this caused in the supply of products. let's move on to the topic of market surveillance: we have seen the numerous withdrawals by our authorities of counterfeit or unsafe goods, perhaps bought online. let's think about the theme of masks. then let's think about consumer protection: how many vulnerable consumers have stumbled upon these sales of unauthorized products and would have needed more support and information on their rights and protection? and then as regards the production of statistics at a european level, let's think about how important the exchange and coordination of information on infections and hospitalizations have been, but also data on the economy in recent months. and yet the safety of the food chain with the prevention and treatment of animal and plant diseases. covid-19 itself is a so-called zoonosis and has made it clear to everyone how fundamental this aspect is for the safety of our citizens. last, but certainly not least, the small and medium-sized enterprises and their workers who have been so seriously affected by the crisis and whose recovery, in a sustainable digital sense, is a fundamental objective on which to focus in the coming months with an eye to the future. all these areas will be funded by this program for the period 2021-2027 and it started as early as january 1st. the program will make it possible to achieve synergies with other programmes, such as digital europe, investeu, horizon europe, the structural funds, but also the funds of the national recovery and resilience plans to strengthen a common leverage effect. in particular, i want to mention the sme window which will be the heir to the old cosme program for the part of the grants to finance competitiveness support, internationalisation, digitalisation and mobility, continuing for example successful projects such as erasmus for young entrepreneurs. of course we would have preferred an even more ambitious budget but we are confident that synergies with other funds will still be able to ensure adequate support. furthermore, as the european parliament we are proud to have fought for the inclusion of business networks and social economy enterprises among the possible beneficiaries of the funds. we then placed the emphasis on environmental sustainability, on vulnerable consumers, we insisted on a specific target with its own budget line on market surveillance. the new challenges of ecommerce, new products, such as connected products and artificial intelligence applications, increasingly highlight how only effective supervision with adequate resources and sufficient staff will be able to face the many and ever new pitfalls that they can endanger the rights and protection of consumers and citizens, thus guaranteeing, instead, products compliant with european rules that circulate freely within the internal market, even when they come from outside the union. finally, i would like to thank the shadow rapporteurs of the internal market committee, my predecessor, rapporteur nicola danti in the last legislature and the draftsmen of the opinion of the industry, agriculture, economic affairs and environment committees. with five commissions involved, it was not obvious to arrive at the negotiation in a unified way; but thanks to the spirit of collaboration always shown, i had the support and confidence to always negotiate on behalf of everyone and so we arrived at a result that was able to meet, i believe, the satisfaction of each of us. i thank the german presidency which made it possible to speed up and conclude the negotiations during its semester with an always constructive attitude. last but certainly not least, let me say, thanks to the commitment of commissioner breton and the officials of dg growth, as well as of course the officials of the directorates-general involved in the negotiations together with it. i think we can all welcome the approval of this program today, which will certainly be a key cog in the engine of european recovery.

paragraph: mr president, commissioner, today, commerce is increasingly online, advertising is more personalized, products are more connected, from a simple doll to a smartwatch. they change throughout their life cycle as a result of software updates. therefore, the inspection rules to guarantee the safety of consumers have to be different. however, good rules in the official journals are not enough. without authorities properly prepared to apply them, they will be worth very little. and, for inspection authorities to respond properly to what has changed in trade and in producers, we have to invest in the skills of the people who work there and bet on the use of new block chain technologies to track products, artificial intelligence to determine risk zones . therefore, among other aspects of this excellent programme, i applaud the financial support of eur 105 million for the supervisory authorities of the member states, hoping that they will make good use of it, in the name of strengthening the internal market and the security of all of us.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Europe programme (debate)
paragraph: honorable chairman, honorable commissioner, the european parliament will give the green light to the digital europe program today. as a citizen of the european union and as a program reporter, i am very happy about that. first of all, i want to once again thank you all from the bottom of my heart for your great help and support. we made it on time and without delay. today, digital europe is getting its formal end, that is, its big operational beginning, which, honestly, we hardly all expect together. from virtual meetings and remote voting, paperless offices to supercomputers and artificial intelligence to smart homes and driverless cars. the digital revolution is happening quickly and irreversibly. at the same time, the negative economic consequences of covid-19 will be sharp and severe, and this is precisely where the digital industry plays a key role as the main tool for increasing europe's competitiveness and resilience. as a powerful tool for a better standard of citizens and their more pleasant life and daily work, as a driver of significant new sources of income based on the most modern business models and services. it's as digital as it is green. the main goal of this mandate. the main goal of this decade in our modern europe, and the wide application of digital technologies and solutions is essential to overcome the investment gap that affects both private and public. in 2021, when we nostalgically remember the distant 2019, the importance of digital is unquestionable even for the biggest skeptics. yes, we all, whether we like it or not, have become digital in the past year. our work, business, private and business communication, socializing and free time. in the past year, everything has been digitized at an enviable speed, but in order to achieve a turning point in economies, this digitization must be supported by a true digital transformation. this means a deeper change that deals with internal processes, human skills and our culture because the back of europe is reserved for those who underestimate the importance of digital transformation. that's why digital europe wants to make its contribution to strengthening europe, where digital technologies enable better healthcare and all public services in general. better education, more successful fight against climate change, digital transformation of public and private companies, transport, tourism, industry, medicine, the entire economy and the entire industry. equally important, with digital europe we want to strengthen citizens' trust in digital technologies by absolutely protecting their privacy, security and consumer rights, and increasing the transparency and speed of the services provided. with digital europe, we want to contribute to the realization of european digital independence and strengthening of competitiveness in the global digital economy, but at the same time we are also taking a responsible approach to new generations, new processes and new workplaces. the digital europe program will play a significant and powerful role in the coming years, but i want to remain absolutely realistic in my predictions. 7.5 billion euros is a lot of money. and with these funds, for example, croatia can significantly speed up its transition to an e-society. however, digital europe is only one and in itself limited aid, one program, and it is not a program for building digital capacities with the most european money. therefore, it is important that there is cooperation and synergy between european programs, that there is coordination, that it is known who is working and how. complementarity with other programs is important, for example with the horizon europe program, which with its almost 100 billion euros covers a much wider area, as well as with the multi-year financial framework 2021-2027. digital and green, respected colleagues, are therefore two indispensable items of every next european program and project, and the key priorities of the program period ahead. if europe wants to become a leader in the coming years and not remain a follower, green digital europe really has no alternative. let's take for example the field of healthcare and the development of vaccines. the challenges we have been facing in the last year due to the coronavirus pandemic are absolutely unprecedented. in such difficult times, we need a ready and strong europe more than ever before. a europe that has the most developed technologies, a europe that has top experts, a europe that can independently defy the virus, a europe that is not lagging behind the world's technological superpowers but is steadily catching up and overtaking them, a europe that is developing its own vaccines and a europe that invests huge amounts of money in research. we need that. digital europe is our greatest ally on this path and one of the most important programs that, with its activities and funding, contributes to the further development of all european countries, both today and in the future, in all aspects of life, including health and medicine. today, digital europe has its operational start, so much awaited and needed. from now on, member states such as croatia are taking on a great responsibility. digital europe offers us big money and opens up huge opportunities, and it is up to us how much we will know how to use these money and opportunities operationally. and so, finally, i want to call on the public sector, universities, educational institutions, the private sector, small, medium and large companies to prepare projects because this is a historic generational opportunity that we must not miss. the generations to come, in fact, depend on what we will do now. so let's not do today's work with yesterday's tools and expect excellent results tomorrow. very soon we will see whether europe will tap into the digital twilight or return to the favorites of the global technology race. as a reporter, as a european, i believe and am sure of the latter.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Europe programme (debate)
paragraph: mr president, mr commissioner, with this debate the end of the legislative process creating the first european digital programme. today we are fully immersed in a data economy and the stakes are high. we need to greatly improve our digital infrastructure. it must be said that, in this field, we lag behind the united states and china. steps have recently been taken to overcome these shortcomings, for example, the gaia-x program, to develop a digital infrastructure for the cloud. it is a project that is also paving the way towards a european cloud, which is precisely the objective of the recently created european alliance on industrial data and cloud. the digital europe programme, with an endowment of 7.5 billion euros, comes to reinforce these digital capacities through the acquisition of the latest generation supercomputers that the european union does not currently have, but it is also going to invest in strategic projects related to artificial intelligence , cybersecurity and advanced digital skills. in short, the first european digital program will benefit all sectors of our economy, but also research, universities and a host of other sectors. i want to make special mention of smes, because they will be able to count on the digital infrastructure, with supercomputers that allow them to process data through which they can optimize technologies that are so important, such as artificial intelligence.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Europe programme (debate)
paragraph: mr president, commissioner, dear colleagues, a digital europe is at the heart of the transformation that the european union has set out to achieve. how to make europe more digital and greener at the same time are the challenges of our generation. the digital europe program will provide strategic funding to meet these challenges in crucial areas: supercomputing, artificial intelligence, cyber security, advanced digital skills and ensuring the widespread use of digital technologies across the economy and society. geopolitically, if we succeed in the transformation today, we will have an advantage in international markets tomorrow. digitization and new technologies will change our lives and allow solutions to many of the challenges we face. for example, our ability to collect, store and process data through artificial intelligence algorithm will increase efficiency and productivity and strengthen the overall competitiveness of the european union. the digital europe program is the first financial instrument of the european union focused on bringing digital technology to citizens, industry, but also to public administrations in the member states, and this will contribute to the digital transformation of the union. for this, we in the european parliament have ensured that digital europe will be synergistic and complementary with the instruments of the new mff, such as the connecting europe facility with the horizon europe programme, and that it will receive adequate funding. with a budget of €7.5 billion and synergies with other financial instruments, it will accelerate the economic recovery and make the digital transformation of the european society and economy, bringing benefits to all.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Europe programme (debate)
paragraph: mr. president, the digital transformation affects all areas of our lives. it permeates all sectors of the economy and provides most of the communication during the pandemic. europe needs to increase its investment in digital technologies if we want to remain competitive and maintain leadership in digitalisation. a successful digital transformation is certainly a condition for a successful economic renewal of europe. we need to improve not only the digital infrastructure, but also invest more in digital skills and ensure a clear and stable legal framework. we use new digital technologies every day. even if we don't realize it, they may sometimes represent a threat, but mostly an opportunity. with the proposed balanced and systematic regulation, it can be an investment with a very quick return. new technologies bring great potential for economic growth, the creation of millions of new jobs, saving lives in the healthcare sector, but also simplifying our way of life. as part of the digital europe program, i appreciate the emphasis on the importance of educating the new generation and retraining the current workforce. investments in cybersecurity and artificial intelligence research and innovation are key areas to work on. but i want to emphasize that when we talk about new technologies, we should always keep in mind the fact that the human being must remain at the center of new technologies and always make the final decision.

subject_of_business_title: Revised industrial strategy for Europe (debate)
paragraph: madam president, madam vice-president, ladies and gentlemen, the pandemic has made clear the fragility of the european industrial system and, consequently, the need to review the industrial strategy presented by the commission a little over a year ago. the centrality of an autonomous and crisis-resilient european industry appears essential today to guarantee our future. some sensitive ecosystems - i am thinking of the health sector but not only - are heavily dependent on third countries for some materials or products which, although numerically not high, risk making our production system vulnerable. we therefore need, firstly, to diversify supply chains, especially for raw materials that we do not have; second, to ensure greater circularity by recovering resources and, finally, to make large investments in research and innovation to create compatible alternatives. this must be accompanied by adequate efforts in the energy field, investing in new energies such as hydrogen to allow the production system, and in particular those industries considered energy-intensive, to keep pace with the climate targets. digital is the other great challenge: with the digital compass we have set the goal for 2030 to reach 75% of companies that use cloud, artificial intelligence and big data and over 90% of smes with a basic level of digitalisation. ambitious goals but the only ones that will allow european industry to remain globally competitive.

subject_of_business_title: Artificial intelligence in education, culture and the audiovisual sector (debate)
paragraph: mr president, madam commissioner, dear colleagues! first of all, even at this late hour, i would like to thank my shadow rapporteurs, the secretariat, and the staff for the good working relationship, cooperation and support. through this cooperation i think a good comprehensive report was possible. we wrote a report on artificial intelligence in the fields of education, culture and audiovisual media. in this report, we call for a clear ethical framework for the use of ai technology in media to ensure people have access to culturally and linguistically diverse content. such a framework should also address the misuse of artificial intelligence to spread fake news and disinformation. we need clear rules for ai technologies so that they protect anti-discrimination, gender equality, pluralism and cultural and linguistic diversity. the use of data that reflects existing inequality or discrimination should be excluded when training artificial intelligence. instead, an inclusive and ethical framework should be developed for the use of datasets that are applied during the deep learning process. there is no doubt that artificial intelligence technologies will encounter us in all areas of life in the future and will certainly also enrich them. however, we must put people at the center of the use of all technology, and especially in the field of education, artificial intelligence technology must be geared towards the people who make the final decision and hold the responsibility in their hands. nevertheless, i think it is wrong to generally classify the education sector as a high-risk sector in the discussion about artificial intelligence. in the education sector in particular, there are all conceivable ways in which ai can be used. some carry higher risks, others far lower. here, however, a clear risk assessment is required and not a generalization of an entire sector in order to be able to classify regulation and security measures depending on the actual current risk. at this point i would also like to remind you of the importance of strengthening digital skills at union level as a prerequisite for the use of artificial intelligence in education and of the need, above all, to train teachers so that they can adapt to the realities of ai-based education can adapt and risks from misuse of technology can be reduced. teachers must always be able to correct decisions made by the ai, such as when grading students. teachers must never be replaced by ai technologies, and especially not in early childhood education. for the cultural and creative sectors, we call for a coherent vision of the use of artificial intelligence at european level and in the member states. algorithm-based content recommendations, especially for video and music streaming services, should not be able to negatively impact cultural and linguistic diversity in the european union. to this end, specific indicators will be developed to assess diversity and ensure that european works are promoted. we want to reduce filter bubbles and enable more transparency for consumers, who can then better understand algorithm decisions. we have fought for decades to establish our values ​​of inclusion, non-discrimination, multilingualism and cultural diversity, which our citizens see as an essential part of european identity. these values ​​must also be reflected in the online world, in which algorithms and artificial intelligence applications are increasingly being used. maximum transparency and the development of high-quality and inclusive data systems for the deployment of deep learning are crucial, as is a clear ethical framework to ensure access to culturally and linguistically diverse content. artificial intelligence is a technology that influences many areas of our lives and is a key driver of digital change. in my opinion, one thing is certain: ultimately, technology must serve people. the human being is the focus and has the responsibility as well as the control and the final decision.

subject_of_business_title: Artificial intelligence in education, culture and the audiovisual sector (debate)
paragraph: mr president, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs (libe), let me present the main elements from our opinion. primarily, we insist that any use of artificial intelligence in the education, culture and audiovisual sectors must fully respect fundamental rights and freedoms as set down in the treaties. ai can enhance the education process if it’s used wisely, contributing to digital skills which will be so important in the future. about 40% of children today will work in jobs that do not exist yet. i therefore welcome the commission’s intention to update the digital education action plan in this regard. we highlight the need for safeguards in the use of ai for children, who are more vulnerable and therefore deserve particular attention and protection. there must always be the possibility for human intervention to ensure that no bias is found in the systems and there are equal opportunities for all. let me conclude my remarks by calling for an open regulatory framework for artificial intelligence where benefits in the education, audiovisual and cultural sectors are maximised and risks minimised.

intervention_header: Mariya Gabriel, membre de la Commission
intervention_header_en: Mariya Gabriel, member of the commission
subject_of_business_title: Artificial intelligence in education, culture and the audiovisual sector (debate)
paragraph: mr president, ladies and gentlemen members of the european parliament, allow me first of all to thank the rapporteur sabine verheyen, chair of the committee on culture and education, and the whole of this committee for this report and for highlighting the importance of artificial intelligence in education, culture and the audiovisual sector. the european parliament and the european commission fully recognize the strategic importance of artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies for the union. artificial intelligence is already transforming our lives and it will continue to have an increasing impact on the way we learn, work and enjoy our free time. however, this change is not without risk. artificial intelligence technologies are increasingly being used to spread fake news, distort reality, hijack data or even marginalize groups of people. now is the time to seize the opportunities and meet the challenges. it is time for adaptation and this is precisely where education comes in. education can help and add a bridge between technological advances and the training needed to use them safely, effectively and ethically. the action plan for digital education exploits the possibilities offered by technologies such as artificial intelligence, virtual reality or robotics. the goal is to scale up successful practices and better understand the ethical, privacy and security implications. it will offer targeted funding and support measures and act as a catalyst to promote a strategic approach to digital education in the union. through this plan, we are strengthening digital skills and developing guidelines that will help our member states support educators, learners, researchers and future innovators, and thus contribute to the development of a successful digital education ecosystem. . for example, we will prepare ethical guidelines on artificial intelligence and the use of data in teaching and learning. i would like to tell you that at this very moment, the call for experts who will form this group has been launched since april 23. the idea is that they start their work next month, that is to say in june, and to have a first report by the end of this year. similar guidelines on digital literacy and disinformation will also be developed, to tackle the spread of fake news and disinformation online. raising awareness is equally important, which is why after the publication of the guidelines, the commission will support awareness-raising activities aimed at educators and students. at the same time, we are updating the digital skills framework of the action plan, adding artificial intelligence and data skills. this framework defines the skills required for citizens who are digitally competent in the 21st century. finally, we also support research and innovation in artificial intelligence in education. we have started to explore the use of artificial intelligence and learning analytics in education to support the education system to meet skills needs and trends. two online artificial intelligence services are being developed right now. however, as highlighted in your report, the impact of digital technologies, such as artificial intelligence, goes far beyond the education and training sector. they also have an impact on the cultural and creative sectors, as well as on the heritage sector. an obvious example is the issue of the control of online streaming services by artificial intelligence, which is mentioned in your report and which generated a lot of interest during a recent online conference entitled "diversity and competitiveness of the european sector music', which my services organized with experts from the member states and representatives of the sector. streaming will fundamentally change the way music reaches consumers. it can create opportunities to build diversity, but it can also favor some artists, languages ​​or genres over others. it is therefore essential to ensure greater transparency in the use of algorithms by streaming services, and fair financial compensation for creators and rights holders. at the same time, digital technologies, such as artificial intelligence, offer new possibilities to make cultural heritage more accessible to all audiences, and also to preserve cultural content. the crisis has also made clearer than ever the need to strengthen the link between digitization, heritage and education as digital possibilities make learning about heritage more accessible. a good example is the europeana platform, which was able to reach nearly 50,000 schoolchildren with online courses and new platforms during the pandemic. we are also exploring the relationship between digital technologies and cultural heritage, through the commission's expert group on cultural heritage, which meets in april to inform member state representatives of the possibilities offered by the application of artificial intelligence to cultural heritage. with regard to research and innovation, the new project of the program "horizon europe" includes a new fully dedicated culture cluster, which will at this time support culture and inclusive society and which will help the fields of culture and cultural heritage to benefit from projects dealing with the economic and social impact of technological applications and digital services linked to the evolution of the sector. finally and lastly, technology also has potential to promote the concept of sustainable cultural tourism. the working group of european experts on sustainable cultural tourism, within the framework of the open method of coordination and in the context of previous work plans for culture, has published a report which includes the first definition of sustainable cultural tourism , as well as recommendations and guidelines for policy makers. i think it is first of all up to us to see how all these elements can truly serve the recommendations in the report, for which i thank you once again from the bottom of my heart.

intervention_header_en: Kim Van Sparrentak, rapporteur for the opinion of the Committee on the Internal Market and Consumer Protection
subject_of_business_title: Artificial intelligence in education, culture and the audiovisual sector (debate)
paragraph: mr president, this week in the netherlands secondary schools have started their final exams, which is an important moment in their lives and for their future. last year, in the uk, not exams but artificial intelligence determined a-level exam results, which resulted in arbitrary and discriminatory results. kids who went to an expensive private school were systematically marked up and kids from state schools were systematically given a lower grade than expected. we need to protect pupils and students against situations where a computer or algorithm decides their future without human oversight. but we also have to protect them from companies harvesting their personal data through educational software. in the netherlands, 70% of all primary schools are now google schools, which is increasingly raising privacy concerns. for crucial digital infrastructure, like our education systems, we must not be dependent on a small number of large companies. we need public investment in education technology, clear public procurement rules and always human oversight on all decisions about the future of pupils and students.

subject_of_business_title: Artificial intelligence in education, culture and the audiovisual sector (debate)
paragraph: mr president, commissioner gabriel, artificial intelligence and its application are becoming more and more widespread in various areas of our lives, such as defense for example. we have witnessed a complete shift of activities from our daily lives absent, online. the same thing happened in the field of education, which showed a significant problem that needs to be solved. 42% of the population of the european union lack basic digital skills. i believe that teachers cannot and should not be replaced by machines and programs, at least in the foreseeable future, but funds should be invested in their qualification, in working with artificial intelligence, in interactive teaching. artificial intelligence also plays a role in the spread of fake news. it is important to know how to counter and use it to fight misinformation. i don't think it should be unsupervised and without people, because more than once the use of algorithms by the big social networks and online platforms leads to content being taken down, blocked, which is pure censorship. and this is a serious part, for which i thank and congratulate the rapporteur. however, there is also a very light-hearted part, and i admit, i am impressed, even in this report, when it comes to artificial intelligence, you managed to bring in your favorite topics such as gender propaganda, lgbt and gender equality, etc. even the poor robots of the future will have to deal with this propaganda, which makes their future pretty sad, i think, but what can we do, this is the version we live in.

paragraph: mr president, commissioner, thank you first of all to the rapporteur, mrs verheyen, for this very important report. artificial intelligence represents an immense opportunity for players in education, culture and the european audiovisual sector. whether it is more interactive learning devices, particularly linguistic ones, or promoting our heritage, artificial intelligence opens up many possibilities for our performance and our competitiveness. it is therefore essential, as we are asking in this group for this report, to allow everyone equitable and fair access to this digital technology. however, this also obliges us to take up several challenges: first, the strengthening of the digital skills of europeans and the adequate training of teaching staff; then, the structuring of a competitive and attractive cutting-edge research sector for european researchers; finally, the development of an artificial intelligence that is ethical from the design stage and emblematic of our european values, such as cultural diversity, gender equality or freedom of expression and information. europe therefore has its full role to play in meeting these challenges, through its “horizon europe”, “digital europe” and “creative europe” programmes. however, artificial intelligence also has its dark side: deep fakes, which make it possible to fake speeches, or the accelerated dissemination of false information. against these practices, we will have to preserve high-risk areas, such as education, and also fight even more strongly against disinformation. in this respect, we expect a great deal from the framework project proposed by the commission a few weeks ago.

paragraph: mr president, ladies and gentlemen, madam rapporteur, thank you very much for this interesting discussion. as you can see, the use of artificial intelligence in the education, cultural and creative sectors presents many opportunities, but also challenges. we want to preserve europe's cultural diversity in today's rapidly changing environment. we therefore want to ensure that the great diversity of european cultural and creative players can benefit from these developments. to explore the possibilities, the commission has launched a study which will identify inspiring case studies for all creative sectors; results are expected in december. as for the challenges, your report rightly highlights, among others, the importance of protecting privacy, combating discrimination, promoting gender equality, respecting human rights intellectual property, environmental protection, and consumer rights. all of these challenges are being examined through various ongoing initiatives and studies. creative europe also recognizes these challenges and encourages collaboration between the culture and media sectors to address these challenges, through its newly created cross-sector innovation lab. i would like to end on a subject that i find particularly important. we must ensure that these technological developments do not change our values ​​and our european way of life. progress without inclusion and equality, dissemination of news or data without ethics are just empty words. we need to ensure that no one will be left behind, that no one will feel their privacy or rights have been violated, and that everyone will have an equal opportunity to thrive. after four councils in recent days and four debates this evening, i would like to thank you once again for the extraordinary energy i felt this evening, and also tell you that you can count on my support.
