paragraph: madam president, shaping the digital future, removing barriers to the functioning of the single market and improving the use of artificial intelligence for consumers – that’s what we’ve been working on for a number of months now and i want to thank my fellow shadows and their offices, and those committees who have contributed opinions to this report. we’ve had strong cooperation, resulting in a balanced report that clearly identifies areas we believe can and should be acted on to improve the functioning of our single market in the digital area. the last 12 months and more have demonstrated to us the value of digitalisation and how it can contribute to bringing people together, to connecting businesses to consumers and connecting business to business. but we can do more to make our single market work better for citizens and businesses, make european smes, micro-businesses and larger companies more competitive, and improve their potential to compete globally. as always, we need to remove unnecessary and unjustified barriers that occur at national level and emphasise the need for a strong european approach that gives certainty to enterprise. european companies should engage with an eu approach to regulation and not have to engage with 27 member state approaches. this certainty will encourage entrepreneurs and others who want to expand and establish themselves in the european union, as they will know that the eu is a place where they can do this. they know for sure what’s expected of them. there will be no barriers, no borders, just a market of 450 million citizens and the support of european regulation that provides legal clarity. european regulation that is trustworthy, fully compliant with fundamental rights, consumer protection rules, data protection rules and is non-discriminatory. these are the traits europe has established for itself and as a leader worldwide, and the traits we also want to embed in our digital rules. of course, this approach is always essential for our public services that support our citizens, regardless of where they reside. as we continue to deal with covid and the fallout from the pandemic, as we face our ambition of implementing the eu green deal, and as we reorganise our healthcare services, digitalisation and emerging technologies such as ai can and will contribute to reaching these objectives. it is really encouraging to see that 25% of the eu rescue fund is going to be earmarked for digital and we must not waiver from that. funding for smes, innovation and tech entrepreneurs is vital if we are to facilitate the development of the eu tech space that we so badly need. if we look at our global competitors in the ai sector, like the united states or china, we can see that more private sector investment is encouraged there than it is here in the european union. yes, we have our investeu, our horizon eu and other programmes, and these are enormously successful, but we must also introduce policies that leverage private sector investment in terms of venture capital or seed capital. we need that private sector investment to ensure that we don’t have scale-ups for sale here in europe, and we don’t have start-ups that will scale up in third countries. we want eu successes. i really welcome the commissioner’s recent proposals to support artificial intelligence through regulation, proposals designed to encourage its use and, importantly, to encourage consumer confidence. ai has enormous potential to address many of the challenges that we face today in the healthcare sector, agriculture and transport, and in developing our smart cities. the list is endless and it does go on, but ai is not without its drawbacks or its risks, such as lack of transparency or traceability, or lack of human oversight, bias decision-making, etc. these need to be addressed through regulation. we already have our data protection rules, privacy rules, non-discrimination rules, paragraph: madam speaker! mr. commissioner! solutions based on advanced algorithms and using the possibilities of artificial intelligence will play a key role in the modernization of the european transport system. this applies not only to the automation of transport, but also to the creation of intelligent traffic management systems in cities and solutions that improve the safety of vehicles and drivers. without realizing the potential of the digital revolution, it will be virtually impossible to achieve the vision zero goals. one of the key barriers to the practical implementation of ai-based technologies in the transport sector is the lack of clear and consistent rules for determining the division of responsibility in the event of a breakdown or accident. another challenge is to ensure the appropriate level of cybersecurity for communicating vehicles and infrastructure. we must place particular emphasis on this issue in the work on the regulation on artificial intelligence. to create innovative products and services in the transport and tourism sectors, european companies need a huge amount of digital data. we should create a system of incentives for member states to make public data available freely and free of charge, including data falling within the spatial information infrastructure, such as geodetic and cartographic data. only in this way will our potential in the field of artificial intelligence bring real economic benefits.

subject_of_business_title: Digital future of Europe: digital single market and use of AI for European consumers (debate)
paragraph: mr president, madam rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for this impressive work and for this timely report. the pandemic has only confirmed the importance of working on digital priority, including artificial intelligence; but the pandemic is not over and i am confident that the momentum towards digitization will continue. europe is in a unique position to develop and use advanced digital technologies, such as artificial intelligence, big data and the internet of things, in an ambitious, innovative and sustainable way. the widespread integration of these digital technologies is essential for europe's economic recovery. our duty as european policymakers is to facilitate and help accelerate this process. this means removing barriers to the digital single market, empowering people to use a new generation of technologies to serve them, and addressing strategic weaknesses in our digital infrastructures. we in the commission are determined to make the 2020s europe's digital decade. we want to drive digital policies that empower people and businesses and lead to a sustainable and prosperous digital future. this european digital decade must be based on four cardinal points: talent, infrastructure, business transformation and the digitization of public administrations. for each of these four areas, we also propose clear quantified objectives to be achieved by 2030, as well as concrete actions, including for smes and start-ups. after listening to stakeholders, the commission will propose a digital policy program and a solemn declaration of digital principles. we are of course counting on the support and commitment of this house to achieve this ambition. to foster digital transformation, the commission has already proposed important legislative initiatives which are on your table, such as the digital services legislation, the digital market legislation, a new european cybersecurity strategy and the act on data governance. she also noted that artificial intelligence can strategically and crucially contribute to these goals. the key to unlocking the benefits of all this data will be processing it through artificial intelligence systems that we will be proposing in a new legislative initiative, the data act, later this year. here again, i observe that we essentially share the same concerns. your report also underlines that we must find a way to protect european values, security, fundamental rights and our european way of life, but without jeopardizing our potential for innovation. you also stress on several occasions the importance of taking into account the needs of smes. the deployment of ai by large companies alone would effectively deprive us in europe of most of the advantages linked to these technologies. the artificial intelligence package that we just proposed on april 21 reflects exactly this dual approach, which consists of developing the potential of artificial intelligence while tackling the problems that these technologies can cause. the proposed ai regulation is built so that all europeans can have confidence in the anthropocentric management of artificial intelligence. proportional and flexible rules are proposed to address the specific risks posed by ai systems in certain contexts. we also foresee a technologically neutral and evolutionary definition of the notion of ai, insofar as it can also cover techniques and approaches that are not yet known or developed. it also prohibits the use of particularly risky artificial intelligence technologies, such as social rating. for the rest, it is based on a risk-related approach, since it focuses on so-called high-risk ai use cases. only these cases must meet a set of requirements specifically designed to enhance transparency and minimize risks to security and our fundamental rights. the coordinated plan published together with the proposal for a regulation describes the policies and investments needed at european level to establish european pre-eminence in this area. we aim to encourage investment from member states and stimulate private investment, to gradually increase all public and private investment in the field of artificial intelligence to 20 billion euros per year from here at the end of the decade. the commission will invest around eur 1 billion per year in this area, in the context of the horizon europe and digital europe programs for the budgetary period of the next seven years, but without counting the investments on the cohesion policy program , which will be added to this sum. these investments aim to support research, innovation, testing, experimentation, skills development and the use of ai for smes. europe has research excellence, a vibrant robotics community and successful industrial sectors. together, they contribute to european excellence in artificial intelligence and help us to take advantage of the advantages these technologies offer us. finally, we have included measures on artificial intelligence in the field of health and on the development of green intelligence. ladies and gentlemen, allow me to conclude by emphasizing the constructive role that this parliament has played, and will continue to play, in advancing this ambitious european programme. allow me also to conclude by thanking you once again for your impressive work and by further emphasizing how convergent and compatible our approaches are.

paragraph: mr. president, the implementation of artificial intelligence brings obvious benefits, but also a number of challenges. artificial intelligence is not another technological revolution, but a mephistophelian temptation – a hostage to which our very existence as a biological species and human society will be held in the future. therefore, economic prospects and competitive pressure are not a sufficient argument for the rapid introduction of new technologies. the huge gap between our human awareness, on the one hand, and the great technological capabilities we already possess, on the other, holds risks. they require real thinking not only in the interests of business and consumers, not only by economists and scientists with a technical profile, but also by humanitarians. automation will lead to the loss of a large number of jobs. digitization creates a new type of discrimination. the success of artificial intelligence presupposes adequate education, guaranteed protection of personal data and, above all, a set of strict ethical principles that protect man and the biosphere.

subject_of_business_title: Digital future of Europe: digital single market and use of AI for European consumers (debate)
paragraph: mr president, mr vice president, dear colleagues! the report by colleague deirdre clune is a successful contribution that shows how the european parliament should make innovations possible through the new ideas of artificial intelligence. we want to promote artificial intelligence in the european union, and this promotion, ladies and gentlemen, can only succeed if we create the right and uniform foundations for it in the internal market. more specifically, this means that we must remove unjustified national barriers. especially new ideas from small and medium-sized companies must not be nipped in the bud with over-regulation. we must therefore be very careful with blanket bans on individual technologies, and this is where the european parliament's report differs very positively from the most recent proposals that we have seen from the european commission. secondly, ladies and gentlemen, we need to create legal clarity for consumers and for companies - we need regulation for the entire internal market. to ensure that robot-assisted operations or software that sorts cvs in a hiring process do not have a discriminatory effect, we need clear and uniform rules that stand up to european standards. and finally, it is also important to create trust in order to ensure that artificial intelligence and its applications work according to our european standards and bring added value in the interest of users and consumers.

intervention_header_en: Evelyne Gebhardt, on behalf of the S&D Group
subject_of_business_title: Digital future of Europe: digital single market and use of AI for European consumers (debate)
paragraph: mr president, dear colleagues, dear commissioner! artificial intelligence conquers the whole of society. artificial intelligence offers great potential for society, the internal market, the environment, can be found in all areas of our world. and that of course gives us a great deal of responsibility for what we want to shape here in this area. algorithms control intelligent vacuum cleaners – we are of course very happy about that – but they also lure consumers to buy online, make decisions in a human resources department or about creditworthiness, yes, they can even be used for automatic mass surveillance. these are then the problems that we have to tackle in order to make it clear that we want to make a policy for the people, in the interests of the people, so that the positive potential of this artificial intelligence can be used, but at the same time the damage that it causes can also actually be limited and prevented. this means that we have to support and protect consumers in particular, because if an algorithm is faulty: how is a normal person - including me - supposed to even recognize where the problems are coming from, what the reason for this problem is? if the application of artificial intelligence can result in fundamental rights, human rights and civil liberties being infringed upon, then we must also resort to prohibition, because we cannot accept such technologies being used. yes, we should use all potential, but yes, we have to ensure that the protection of citizens comes first.

intervention_header_en: Svenja Hahn, on behalf of the Renew faction

paragraph: mister president! europe's economic future depends crucially on whether we lead the digital transformation or continue to lag behind. i want us to put the eu at the forefront of innovation in the world. above all, this means that we enable the potential of artificial intelligence to develop. first of all, we need fair competition between small and big players, between small and medium-sized companies and tech giants. this works with clear rules that make it easy for the start-up to expand and the requirements are based on size. we must encourage innovation instead of holding it back. this is possible if we remain open to technology and pursue a risk-based approach. because the application and the corresponding risk belong in the focus. with face recognition as an example, we can see that quite nicely, it's handy for unlocking our phone, but biometric surveillance in public spaces is a threat to our civil liberties. as europeans, we must shape digitization with self-confidence, but not alone. independence must not become synonymous with protectionism. on the contrary: if we want to set value-based standards for the digital space, we have to do it together with democratic partners. therefore: let's start an ai alliance with the usa! i work for a digital space in europe where the credo is a desire for progress, where start-ups can become global corporations and where there is fair competition. we now have it in our hands to create a political framework for artificial intelligence in which future wishes can become reality. dear commissioner, dear colleagues, that is our job. this report is a start - but it is only a start, the real work is only beginning.

paragraph: mr. president, mr. vice president schinas, thank you very much for your presence in this important debate. first of all, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mrs clune, on this important report, which certainly sets the stage for how we should approach artificial intelligence and upcoming technologies. artificial intelligence is one of the technologies that will drive the development of our industry, of our smes, but it is not the only one. it's clear. this will give way to more developed technologies, such as quantum computing, with the potential for multiplied computing power. that is why it is important that the legislation we adopt now is prepared for the technologies that are coming and does not become obsolete in a few years. the advent of technologies such as quantum computing will allow more complex problems to be addressed, in a more agile way than current ones. in addition, it will reduce energy consumption, thus helping to meet the objectives set by the green pact. these technologies have great potential, but they also carry great risks, since they are fed by data. that is why it is very important to ensure the protection and quality of this data, both personal and non-personal. there is a very fine line between the use of personal and non-personal data once it enters the artificial intelligence system. that is why we have to be very rigorous and comply with clear transparency rules that establish red lines, if necessary. for example, we must avoid abusive or discriminatory practices towards consumers and companies caused by the biased use of data in the machine learning process. otherwise, the consumer or smes will not trust these technologies and hinder their development. as vice president vestager has said, in artificial intelligence, trust is a must, not a luxury.

then adopted by the eu.

subject_of_business_title: State of the SMEs Union – Implementation of better regulation agenda / Reduction target for administrative burden (continuation of debate)
paragraph: mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the european strategy for small and medium-sized enterprises must, in my view, be oriented around four main objectives: investment, including the creation of conditions for access to it to become a reality for all; innovation, as a facilitator of economic recovery and adaptation to the double green and digital transition; internal market, including the digital internal market - we need a cohesive internal market without fragmentation; and, finally, the fight against bureaucracy, as well as the reduction of administrative costs for companies. with regard to this last point, as the epp group, the european people's party, aims to reduce these costs for small and medium-sized enterprises by at least 30%, i ask the european commission: what will be done to make this simplification of procedures a reality in the legislative packages on artificial intelligence and on digital services and markets that are now under consideration?

subject_of_business_title: Preparation of the G7 summit of 11-13 June and the EU-US Summit (debate)
paragraph: madam president, the global pandemic provides a challenging backdrop for both the g7 and the eu—us summits. covid—19 has created a common need, our need to heal. the summit is a unique opportunity for the eu to show leadership in healing the world. to achieve this, though, we need more than feel-good media lines and carefully drafted, intentionally vapid conclusions. we need to produce tangible results. we also need to heal the transatlantic relationship, which has been wounded in recent years. it’s time to move past the blame game. it’s time to bury the hatchet. we need to resolve long-standing differences over planes, steel and data. we need to work together to combat unfair trade-distortive practices. we need to agree on a common framework for artificial intelligence and emerging technologies. the pandemic has taught us that we can no longer take anything for granted and that we must fight to preserve what we consider to be most dear to us. so we need to focus now on what brings us together, not on what could tear us apart. looking ahead, we need to safeguard our democratic principles and our common values. we need to make clear that the world’s democracies intend to stand united against autocrats, populists and demagogues. the summits are our chance to prove to the world that the eu can be a leader in the post—covid world. the world is watching. let us show them that we are ready, willing and able.

subject_of_business_title: Promoting gender equality in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) education and careers (debate)
paragraph: mr president, commissioner, caroline segui-perez, in the book “invisible women”, shows us how the world is largely built by and for men. airbags, for example, were not developed taking women's bodies into account and, therefore, initially did not adequately protect them from accidents. this is partly because there is a lack of women in technology or because the data does not reflect the characteristics of the entire relevant population. the digital transition and advances in data science and artificial intelligence make this problem even more relevant. it is therefore essential that we take measures to ensure diversity in the teams working in the digital sector and, in particular, in artificial intelligence where only 22% are women. only then will the online world reflect the world we live in, where 50% of people are women.

paragraph: the share of women in stem fields has not grown enough, therefore more girls and women must be encouraged to enter the fields of natural sciences and technology. girls perform even better than boys in stem subjects at the beginning of school, and yet only a good third of those who graduate in the fields are women. the gender gap is particularly large in newer fields such as artificial intelligence and cyber security. women must be strongly involved in shaping the technologies and science that form the services and working life of our future. strengthening the share of women in the digital world requires determined work and the change of many attitudes and habits. we need action to remove the gender stereotypes of these fields in schools, as well as the emergence of female stem role models to promote attractiveness. at the same time, inequality related to hiring and balancing work and private life must be eradicated. it is absolutely important to ensure a more equal future and a more competitive eu labor market.

subject_of_business_title: Promoting gender equality in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) education and careers (debate)
paragraph: the underrepresentation of girls and women in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (stem) is a reality that we must reverse. the gender gap that exists in all areas of digital technology is particularly evident in innovative technologies such as artificial intelligence and cyber security. in these sectors, the average presence of women at global level amounts to only 12% and 20% respectively. also, only 18% of information and communication technologies (ict) professionals in europe are women. the participation of more women can potentially add €16 billion to the gdp of the eu economy. stereotypes and the lack of female role models are some of the problems that contribute to the low percentage of women in these sectors. but the need for stem and ict skills is ever-increasing, from healthcare to manufacturing, opening up new and well-paid employment options for everyone. in this context, it is important that women and girls are encouraged to pursue educational and career opportunities in these sectors while removing barriers, combating stereotypes and improving access to finance and investment for female entrepreneurs.

subject_of_business_title: European Climate Law (debate)
paragraph: madam president! mr. commissioner! let me be the voice of reason after the manifestos. the climate law is an important document. an important document because it tries to dress our dreams, our wishes in a handful of recipes. this is not the end of the beginning, this is just the beginning. these are thoughts, unfortunately not yet combed, thoughts that we had to put in order for a year and a half. we do not yet know how they will translate into directives and regulations. let me remind you that we had to stand up for the basic values ​​that will determine whether we will implement the climate law together - including solidarity, european solidarity, co-responsibility. just a few hours before the end of negotiations on zero emissions by 2050, we did not speak at the european level, we spoke at the level of each member state. just like we didn't talk about absorbers, just like we didn't talk about the fact that we would count net, which is important after all. and i think that what peter liese said about sinks should be the subject of our concern, we should build a coalition, we should devote a lot of work to sinks, because this seems to be absolutely crucial when it comes to zero emissions. it is not difficult to close everything and destroy it, destroying human life, causing unemployment. the art of absorbing. and that's what we should focus on. commissioner, i would like to remind you how lawyers assessed both the climate law and the impact assessment. the legal services of the european parliament were merciless, they said that there were no good calculations there, that the algorithm that the commissioner wished was set at 50%, but even such calculations showed that this financial security simply does not exist. without money, we will not carry out the climate law, and these are the ones we have in the multiannual financial framework or the recovery fund. they are simply insufficient and do not correspond to a just transition. people are very important in this process. we protect water, forests and nature. yes, we must remember the man. i do not know if you know, but two weeks ago, a week and a half ago, switzerland also voted on their climate law. citizens said no. because it translated into a much higher cost of living. we must be together, we must be responsible, co-responsible and solidarity. then we will be able to implement the climate law.

subject_of_business_title: Use of technologies for the processing of data for the purpose of combating online child sexual abuse (temporary derogation from Directive 2002/58/EC) (debate)
paragraph: mister president! sexual abuse is a terrible crime, a massive violation of our children's fundamental and human rights. this applies to the real world, but also when images of abuse are repeatedly shared online. and in both worlds we have to get better - in prevention, in prosecuting the perpetrators, but also in supporting the survivors. online measures are a supplement, for example to covert investigations or the fundamentally better equipment of law enforcement and advice centers. in doing so, however, we also have to face the debate as to how much online surveillance is compatible with our free democratic basic rights and where we run the risk of installing a comprehensive surveillance system that knows the most intimate details of the communication of all people, including our children, who we are particularly want to protect. various providers are already voluntarily scanning private messages to detect child abuse. however, this threatened to become impossible due to a change in the electronic communications code. and so, last september, the commission presented the law that we are going to vote on tomorrow. an exception to current privacy rules that still allows for the scanning of private messages for child abuse without consent. the law allows different technologies. so-called hashing has been used for many years. it enables abuse depictions to be identified by matching videos and images against a predefined set of digital fingerprints, known as hashes. and when i underlined early on that i didn't want to stop this practice, i pushed for additional protective measures. clearly more controversial was and is the use of artificial intelligence to read messages to track down unknown material and possible cyber grooming. for a long time, the commission had failed to deal with the effects of the scanning that was already taking place on child abuse. there would have been plenty of time to find a good, sustainable solution to the legal challenges surrounding the scanning of private communications on the internet. but when the commission finally realized its omission, it didn't even bother to produce an impact assessment on the fundamental rights impact, when it should have done so. instead, massive pressure was put on the negotiators just to come to some kind of agreement quickly. but as legislators, we always have a duty to check all the facts and act in accordance with fundamental rights and the rule of law. i have said this several times and i will repeat it today. of course, we can have different opinions on political decisions and especially on such sensitive issues, but that never absolves us from the responsibility of a critical, comprehensive debate. the agreement that has now been reached between the council and parliament is a compromise between uncovering child sexual abuse online and protecting the privacy of users. it may not be perfect, but it's a workable interim solution for the next three years. the compromise allows for the temporary continuation of certain voluntary measures to detect sexual abuse, the images and possible cyber grooming. as parliament, we have fought hard to improve the proposal and bring it in line with existing data protection standards. we've added safeguards, such as better informing users or introducing a 12-month retention period for data. we want more direct information to european authorities and have achieved that the service providers have to work closely with the national data protection authorities. these can prohibit technologies that are hostile to fundamental rights. data protection and protection of confidentiality are not protection against offenders, but the basis of democracy. we must also protect the confidentiality of communications for the benefit of our children. this applies all the more to sensitive communications - for example between victims of abuse and their doctors and lawyers. this law is an interim solution for three years. the commission had promised to propose a new, permanent framework for detecting child abuse before the summer recess. now it's going to be september or october. i expect a significantly improved proposal for this. the long-term solution must at least be based on the data protection guarantees of the temporary solution. it is imperative that it find solutions for the more targeted scanning of private communication, otherwise it will hardly stand up in national and european courts. and yes, we expect a full impact assessment this time. and that is why it is your turn, dear ylva johansson, and also you, commission president von der leyen – because i know that you are interested in this law.

subject_of_business_title: Presentation of the programme of activities of the Slovenian Presidency (debate)
paragraph: honorable mr. president of the parliament, honorable madam president of the commission, honorable members of parliament! almost exactly thirty years ago, we slovenians created our own country. a year earlier, we won the first multi-party elections ourselves. in that period, as many as 90 percent of voters supported the dream of an independent state in a referendum. only once again in history has such a large number of our citizens supported a certain decision. and that was the decision on slovenia's entry into the european union. for us slovenians, being part of the european union has never meant just an economic opportunity. it meant returning to a family united by the values ​​of respect for human rights and fundamental political freedoms and democracy. everything that was taken from us or violated in communist yugoslavia. this return to europe coincided with the fundamental historical mission of the european union, which was dictated by the fall of totalitarian communist regimes in europe. the formation of a complete and free europe that will live in peace with itself and its neighbourhood. the european union today is much different than it was at the time of our accession and also at the time of the first presidency of the council of the european union and then also of the european council. we can say that the presidency in the first half of 2008 was the last presidency that was not marked by one of the severe crises in one way or another. what followed one after the other: the financial crisis, the migrant crisis, the occupation of crimea and the creation of frozen conflicts in our eastern neighborhood, and brexit, and since the beginning of last year, the coronavirus pandemic. and during the period of crises, we in the european union were primarily forced to respond to them and try to mitigate them as quickly as possible. we strongly hope that this semester is the time when the european union can and must start acting more strategically, more long-term, aimed at achieving the goal set by the founding fathers of the european union. europe, free, at peace with itself, whole and at peace with its neighbours. for the second time since it became a member of the european union, slovenia is taking over the helm of the country holding the presidency of the council of the european union. it will round off the work of the trio, in which we cooperated with germany and portugal, and with initiatives, some initiatives and activities we joined the work of the trio from the very beginning. at this point, we thank germany and portugal for a job well done in the very difficult conditions of the pandemic. for the second half of this year, for our semester, there are some challenges and priorities ahead of us, which arise are strong enough in the event of such a threat, given that we have common energy networks and much more. and here, only a joint plan and also joint capacities enable effective defense, because there are at least two sources of serious threat that no single country in the european union, according to the information known so far, can cope with on its own. in the national recovery plans, all countries committed to a significant share of digital and green investments. and here, when we talk about the field of digitization and the digital transition, the european union faces considerable challenges. here, in many places, we are catching up with other important players in the world. a few examples: in the european union we have companies that produce the best equipment for photolithography, which is a key technology for the manufacture of semiconductors, but less than one percent of global production is assembled and manufactured in europe. what's more, although we have prestigious universities and the most technologically advanced laboratories in europe, we only design, or in the end produce, only one percent of semiconductors on the world market, and without semiconductors there is not even a letter to digitization and the digital transition. we have the knowledge, we have the capabilities, but we need to use them and we need to decide where the line is between trade cooperation and where european autonomy begins when it comes to critical infrastructure and when it comes to critical products. and here is the fact that the european union must become as autonomous as possible. on the other hand, of course, when it comes to digitization, we want to act in accordance with our european values. among them are, of course, the right to privacy and the protection of personal data. these are values ​​that, of course, are not at the forefront of some of our competitors when it comes to digitization. the regulation of digital services, the regulation of the field of artificial intelligence and the related field of data management are therefore a bigger challenge for us than for anyone outside the european union, and these are all topics where, even during our semester, we will seek a balance between competitiveness on the one hand and respecting european values ​​on the other. and if we manage to find the right balance in our internal debate, then i believe that the european union can also take the lead in creating digital standards at a global level, which is the next very big challenge. last december, we set ourselves a very ambitious goal of a 55% reduction in emissions by 2030. with this goal, we want to encourage other countries around the world to follow our example. but this is not only a question of ambition, here it is also a question of how to convince others of the standards necessary to realize these goals. outside of europe, i think more than 90 percent of co2 is emitted, and success here can only be achieved globally. europe can be a leader, but it cannot achieve this goal on its own, and here, precisely in doing so, it is also necessary to ensure that individual parts of europe do not pay too high a price for this transition, that we do not destroy european industry, and of course, what worries us the most is our fellow citizens, that the prices of electricity and fuel will not increase disproportionately and significantly affect the decline in the quality of life. next week, the european commission will propose an important legislative package in the field of climate and energy - fit for 55. we expect a proposal that will be presented that is balanced and fair to all, and in this way we can hope to reach an agreement on how to our ambitious climate goals into binding law, can be achieved in the shortest possible time. this was also a good basis for the union's action in the international arena, especially at the climate negotiations this november in glasgow. a union of the it. it seems obvious to us, but of course it is not. the social market economy is a european invention. elsewhere in the world, they regulate economic and social relations somewhat or quite differently than we do. many people also envy our solutions. so when we talk about european legislation in the area of ​​the minimum wage or the cross-border transfer of social security rights, let's question of the rule of law, what is right and what is wrong is always decided by an independent judicial instance, not and a political body. the quality of functioning of the justice system is also important here. this must be based on an independent, impartial and non-selective judiciary that strives for justice in each member state and guarantees legal protection without delay and without unreasonably long deadlines. as far as humanity talks about law, the rule is that justice is delayed, justice is denied. we will also pay special attention to the freedom and pluralism of the media, as well as the fight against fake news. this is especially necessary in environments with media monopolies, which unfortunately also exist in the european union. at the same time, the slovenian presidency draws attention to the resolution of the parliamentary assembly of the council of europe with number 1096 and the resolution of the european parliament on european consciousness and totalitarianism. the guidelines and warnings arising from them are of permanent importance for the development of resilient, vital democracies, and especially for the realization of the historic goal of a complete and free europe that is at peace with itself. some directions and warnings of the two resolutions have not yet been implemented in some younger european democracies. it is precisely in this that we see part of the deeper reasons for mutual misunderstandings regarding the rule of law in the individual members of the european union. many are not ready and able to see cases whose standards and guarantees of the rule of law do not in fact protect the european values ​​from article 2 of the treaty on european union, but on the contrary, the institutions of the rule of law, which only formally assumed new roles with the transition to democracy, but did not internalized by them, they serve above all to defend unjustified privileges and to preserve a culture of action built in decades of undemocratic arrangements and practices that shrink the space of freedom and maintain entrenched inequalities and injustices. we will also talk about these issues at the international conference that we will organize in slovenia on the 23rd of the european day of remembrance for the victims of all totalitarian regimes. in august this year. our common responsibility and permanent task is also to keep alive the memory of the fact that the awareness of the necessity of european integration processes was formed precisely in the difficult and undemocratic historical trials of the twentieth century, which befell and marked the nations of today's european union members, although each in its own way and for varying lengths of time. a credible and safe european union, capable of ensuring security and stability in the neighborhood as well. we believe that it is time for the european union to become more strategic in its thinking and actions in its operation in the world. and this is especially true for our immediate neighborhood. slovenia, as the chairman of the council of the european union, will therefore put the european union's cooperation with the western balkans region as well as with the eastern neighborhood to the fore this semester. when we talk about the western balkans, it is a region of strategic importance for the union, which is why, together with the president of the european council, we will co-organize the european union - western balkans summit in slovenia in october. in our opinion, the enlargement of the european union is a logical answer to the strategic challenges that we have, which are ahead of us, both in the eastern neighborhood and in the western balkans. slovenia knows well from its own experience how important the european perspective is for the implementation of reforms in the process of accession negotiations. this perspective must be tangible, namely such that it is possible to believe in its realization already during the lifetime of the current generation, otherwise it is no longer an incentive. and this tangibility must inspire and be the source of the political energy needed to implement the necessary reforms at the political level, must be the source of energy and the focus of the political consciousness of citizens so that they can provide bottom-up support for these reforms. our goal is to reaffirm, revive and revitalize the european perspective of the western balkan countries, which was given at the summit in thessaloniki in 2003. and i think that if we do that, then we will prove that we are a strategic player here, if but we are not able to do this, if we do not take a step forward in the western balkans, someone else will take these steps and they have different interests and different values. the issue of migration is also closely related to the western balkan region. one of the two major migration routes to the european union takes place here, i mean illegal migration and, when it comes to migration, there is also a demanding file on the table here. i think we mostly agree on the importance of cooperation with countries of origin and transit of migration. in theory, we know what needs to be done here. there are also no differences between us regarding the importance of strengthening control over the external border, there is a high degree of agreement. there is, of course, less agreement on some parts of the migration pact, such as the issue of relocation and solidarity and responsibility. and here we are looking for solutions that will be acceptable to all countries, because only in this way can we ensure that the new system will eventually come to life in practice. illegal migration has also put a heavy burden on the operation of the schengen area in the past years. schengen is one of the most important achievements of our integration process. here, it is necessary, in our opinion, that at this time, when, hopefully, we are returning to normality, we also ask about the expansion of this space, so that it comes on the agenda. we believe that any member state that meets the conditions should be allowed to become a member of the schengen area. in our opinion, we are unnecessarily keeping bulgaria, romania and croatia in the waiting room, and this does not benefit either them or the european union. and at the very end, allow me to say a few more sentences about the conference on the future of europe. i am glad that the discussion on the organizational aspects of the conference has been concluded, that it is now time for substantive discussion, time for the voice of the europeans to be heard. on the basis of this discussion, it is possible to take very concrete conclusions in the spring of next year. i think that we are facing a great opportunity for this open discussion, that somehow it is the right time with the conference on the future of europe, that it coincides with many questions that are open or that are open again. in slovenia, as part of this year's strategic forum in bled, we will organize discussions on the future of the european union, to which many guests from the institutions of the european union, national leaders, former leaders who participated in the debates on the constitution for europe, on the treaty of lisbon, and european think tanks will be invited. , citizens and, of course, representatives of all political groups in this parliament are also invited. many questions are open here, for example, the bad demographic trends of most member states and different views on solutions to the demographic issue. then in a large part of the european union, for example, we are faced with a low voter turnout in the elections to the european parliament. other fundamental questions of european democracy are open, the question of the gap between the average european and the european institutions, the attempts of unwilling subjects to take over the role of those elected by the voters. we have more and more time to spend on mutual political arguments within the european union and therefore less time for serious discussions on strategic and development dilemmas. we are at the crossroads of many paths, but we also need some answers, or at least a discussion about which direction to set the answers regarding some strategic foreign policy and security dilemmas. for example, how to strengthen the role of the european union so that it will be able to have a stronger influence on globalization trends. when we adopted the treaty of lisbon, i myself am one of the signatories, in lisbon, we said, with this treaty, the european union will be able to guide globalization. today, we have to ask ourselves where we are actually capable of doing this, and where a lot more needs to be done in order to be. then it is necessary to reach a consensus on the question of whether the rapid expansion of the european union in the western balkans and the eastern neighborhood is a strategic answer to strategic challenges, and how to reach a consensus on this. then one has to ask whether there is any good alternative to a stronger security and also military engagement of the european union in sub-saharan africa, in the sahel region, where terrorism prevents the implementation of the most basic humanitarian, educational and development projects and this danger is spreading practically every month. then, how to define the long-term relationship between the european union and the russian federation, between the european union and turkey, which is becoming the most influential factor in the mediterranean. then, as already mentioned, where is the border between economic and trade relations between the european union and china and the necessary strategic autonomy of the european union. then, how to comprehensively and quickly strengthen relations with india, the most numerous democratic country on the planet. i think that in this debate we also need an open conversation about, for example, our responsibility for the victims and suffering that have been and will continue to be because we are withdrawing from afghanistan and leaving the people there at the mercy of the taliban. we must reach an agreement that in the future we will not participate in activities that only scatter something, but do not enable the establishment of something new, better, and permanent. we also need to sober up and realize that the great, good and indispensable, unprecedented in the global world, soft power of the european union is not enough anywhere, because we are not able to provide people with basic security and basic human rights. that the european union, if it wants to become the first regional and then an equal global power, simply needs a combination of soft and hard power. dear members of parliament, for our short-term future, the most important thing right now is to stop the pandemic and recover from it as quickly as possible, and to include the digital and green transition in the recovery. for a good future in general, and for a good future for us and future generations of europeans, the most important thing is to openly discuss open strategic dilemmas and find common solutions that enable a way forward.

subject_of_business_title: Fair working conditions, rights and social protection for platform workers - New forms of employment linked to digital development (debate)
paragraph: mr president, commissioner – dear nicolas, who has arrived at the right time –, dear colleagues, first of all i would like to thank my colleagues, more particularly the shadow rapporteurs from the various political groups, but also my colleagues from the committee on transport, who, like me, have been working on this file over the last few months in order to be able to define a common and ambitious position for the european parliament on this major subject. the porto social summit was an opportunity to identify the immediate priorities for the implementation of the european pillar of social rights, including those of platform workers. i would also like to mention the second phase of the social partner consultations, which will end on wednesday. i'm sure it will be instructive. in this context, i am delighted that the majority of political groups have so far agreed on the need for european action and on the specific needs of platform workers. i will take a few moments to outline the priorities of my report. first point: enhanced access to social protection. i would like platform workers to benefit from minimum social protection, whatever their status. this means in particular that all platform workers should have the right to receive compensation in the event of an accident at work or occupational disease and benefit from social protection including health and disability insurance coverage. we also call for social protection rights to be extended to freelance platform workers, including people transitioning or holding both statuses, to ensure the portability of rights and benefits. we already have a european instrument going in this direction: the council recommendation on the access of employed and self-employed workers to social protection. i would like to underline its importance for the member states, which must put it in place without delay. second point: improved, fair and transparent working conditions. digital work platforms should ensure the communication of essential information regarding working conditions and rules of cooperation, the method of price calculation and the allocation of tasks. they should also ensure transparency in the event of changes to the rules and have recourse to consultations. it is also important that workers have a right of recourse in the event of an account suspension. working for several platforms must also be a right for them, as well as having access to their data. third major element: collective representation. collective bargaining is a key element for improving the working conditions of these workers. platform workers, even self-employed, must be able to organize and bargain collectively. i call on the european commission to clarify that collective agreements do not fall under the prohibition of competition law, in order to ensure that these platform workers can organise, be represented and participate in collective bargaining. fourth element: more legal certainty for platform workers and platforms. this has been a big talking point for us. our objective should be to move towards more legal certainty for platform workers. this will also be favorable to the platforms which will be able to develop with more clarity, but also to the so-called traditional economy, by guaranteeing fair conditions of competition. a rebuttable presumption of a regulated employment relationship should apply to workers who challenge their status in a procedure. however, it should not lead to automatically considering all platform workers as salaried workers. truly independent workers will remain so. what is also important is that we are proposing a reversal of the burden of proof so that when a platform worker disputes their professional status, it is up to the party who is alleged to be the employer to prove that there is no employment relationship. finally, let's be clear, we do not want a third status for platform workers. fifth element: a healthy and safe workplace. platform workers, on site, must be equipped with adequate personal protective equipment and be covered by accident insurance when working in the transport and delivery sectors. they must also be able to disconnect from the platform without suffering any negative consequences. we want to protect platform workers and customers from the risk of violence and harassment by implementing effective reporting mechanisms on platforms. sixth element: skills development – ​​also a very important point. training should be provided to workers by the digital work platform itself on the use of its site or application, the tasks to be performed and occupational health and safety. platform workers, especially the less skilled, should have access to training to build skills and improve their employability. finally, the seventh element, and not the least: transparent, non-discriminatory and ethical algorithmic management. algorithmic management has revolutionized the world of work. it is clear that we want to ensure the use of algorithms that are transparent, non-discriminatory, ethical and reliable. to achieve this objective, it is necessary to ensure that the main information on the working conditions is explained in an intelligible way. these are parameters of the algorithm that influence the distribution of tasks, ratings and interactions, the deactivation procedure and pricing. moreover, it may seem obvious, but algorithmic management must be controlled by humans so that workers can challenge a decision through effective procedures. in conclusion, dear colleagues, clarifying rights, increasing protections where they are lacking, finding the balance between the advantages and disadvantages of platform work are, i believe, all objectives that have been achieved with this report . i again welcome the announcement of the european commission's legislative initiative to improve the working conditions of platform workers, scheduled for 8 december. this will represent an additional brick for the construction of social europe. we can say that the european parliament contributes to this on a voluntary basis, with this report, and we hope that the commission will take note of this when it finalizes its proposal. commissioner, let us act together to adapt the european framework to the new realities of the world of work by ensuring that european values ​​are anchored in the digital economy and so that the possibilities offered by new forms of work remain sustainable and fair. yes to “digital”, but not to the detriment of the working conditions of platform workers in europe.

intervention_header: Nicolas Schmit, membre de la Commission
intervention_header_en: Nicolas Schmit, member of the commission
subject_of_business_title: Fair working conditions, rights and social protection for platform workers - New forms of employment linked to digital development (debate)
paragraph: mr president, madam rapporteur, i would first like to thank you for this report. i would say that this parliament adopts a great many important reports which contribute to the development of our economic and social life, but also to our international action. this report is part of a new logic which is that of a particular economic development. it's digital, it's "digital", these are activities that have developed, in particular, in the context of the pandemic, with astonishing speed. so i would say that these activities and these services that the platforms provide correspond to a real demand, since practically all of us use these platforms from time to time, some more often – young people, a lot. but i also know that it is young people, precisely, since it is mainly young people who work on the platforms, with or for the platforms, who will follow our debates and who, above all, have expectations with regard to the conclusions. this commission has made a strong commitment. madam rapporteur, you said it well, it is a question of developing the digital economy, and this in conditions of respect for social rules, social protection, fundamental labor rights. and so, today, we see that many young people who travel through our cities with their bicycles, their bicycles or their motorcycles sometimes, have no protection, no guarantees. and if they have an accident – ​​and it often happens – they end up with nothing and no health protection. the pandemic, moreover, has brought to light many comparable situations in europe, but above all also outside europe. this is why what we are doing today with your report and what we are doing with a proposal on the platforms will be for europe, but it will go beyond. we see that the same problems, the same worries and the same demands are being expressed almost everywhere, including, moreover, as i said, in the part of the world where, finally, the digital economy was invented : in california. this is why now is the time to act. it is not a question of diminishing the importance of the platform economy, it is a question of giving it a framework. the first thing is to give it legal certainty, because it is not normal that, in an internal market, the rules are the same in some countries and very different in another, especially when there are also has exchanges across borders. so that's the first element. the second is to give certainty, guarantees and security to those who work for the platforms. for all those hundreds, even millions of young people who, perhaps not mainly, but occasionally, and often a lot, work for these platforms. you have listed the different dimensions which are first of all the status. and there, i agree with you. it is not about imposing a status. it is a question of guaranteeing that, whatever the status, each worker on the platforms has guarantees in social matters. and then, we cannot be objects of robots or artificial intelligence. our demand is for artificial intelligence to have a human dimension. we cannot allow workers to be steered, judged, evaluated and sometimes lose their jobs just because the algorithm is programmed in such a way. so we need a framework so that what is called management by algorithm is clear and that the rights of workers are established, that there is transparency in this regard. so these are the subjects we will have to deal with. i must tell you, madam rapporteur and all those who worked on this report, that you have helped us. you have identified the questions, the problems, and you have outlined the right solutions, such as the reversal of the burden of proof, which is an instrument to bring clarity and rights for all those who work on the platforms. thank you very much, once again. you know that we are practically, i would say, daily at work. today i had two meetings on this subject and the commission will come at the end of this year with a proposal which will surely be inspired by the work you have done.

intervention_header_en: Kim Van Sparrentak, on behalf of the Verts/ALE Group
subject_of_business_title: Fair working conditions, rights and social protection for platform workers - New forms of employment linked to digital development (debate)
paragraph: mr president, dear colleagues, commissioner, i would first like to congratulate the fnv and the dutch uber drivers on their victory today in the lawsuit against uber. uber must hire its drivers and pay back wages. this is a great result. i will now continue in english. the verdict in the netherlands adds to over 100 court cases across the eu, and with these court cases platform workers simply ask to be treated the same way as other workers, with the same social benefits and opportunities, and the cases have overwhelmingly been won by the platform workers. you might think that uber, glovo, deliveroo and other platforms would then bury the hatchet, play nice and hire their workers. but instead they do everything to keep operating outside of the law or to even change the rules in their favor with workers paying the price. and in the long run we actually all risk paying the price because this business model undermines our social security system. platform workers going to court are fighting an uphill battle against the platforms' army of lawyers and resources, and that is why we, the lawmakers, need to step in, and that is why i am very pleased with this report because we give a clear mandate to the european commission for strict rules and to once and for all tell these platforms how we protect their workers and that we have a model based on solidarity. that's why i also really would like to thank my shadow co-rapporteurs and the rapporteur for the great cooperation while writing this report, because if we stand together we can really make a social europe happen. so what do we want? we start by putting in place a presumption of employment relationship for platform workers. this may sound complicated but it simply means that it should be up to platforms to prove that someone is really an entrepreneur instead of the workers. and for me, it's quite simple. if it looks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's likely a duck. so why give workers some basic rights rather than the full rights of an employee? it shouldn't matter when you are cleaning someone's house if you've been hired through a platform or an agency: you should have the same rights. and next it is important to clarify what distinguishes these platform workers from other workers and namely the fact that an algorithm dictates what happens. a dutch judge explained today being subject to an algorithm is modern employers' control. workers are constantly tracked, monitored, evaluated and even fired by algorithms without even knowing why the algorithm assigns them certain tasks and what the price is actually based on, and as a result platform workers are under extreme stress. we need to protect workers against algorithmic management. workers must be able to know that not only does an algorithm exist, but also how it assigns tasks and sets the prices. important hr decisions should always be made by a person and not a computer. these issues are not sufficiently dealt with in the aif and have to be addressed in the directive on platform work. colleagues, it is important that we have this legislation and when it comes to the future of work and the future of a social model this is one of the first battlegrounds; the outcome will be important for how we will regulate the labor market in the future.

subject_of_business_title: Fair working conditions, rights and social protection for platform workers - New forms of employment linked to digital development (debate)
paragraph: madam president, commissioner, as we all understand, the nature of work is changing, with technology providing platform workers with flexibility in the type and timing of their work, as well as an additional income. at the same time, the use of algorithms and artificial intelligence applications create innovative services for the benefit of consumers and businesses. it seemed strange, during the pandemic, when thousands of platform workers kept several businesses afloat, such as in the catering sector. however, what must not change is our will to ensure that these workers have the same rights as those in the traditional economy. we must ensure the health and safety of platform workers, their access to medical care and social welfare services and the effective implementation of their rights to collective representation. but above all we, as legislators, should ensure that the legislation keeps pace with the speed of technological developments and also understand the breadth of platforms, through the collection of updated data on this form of employment. in conclusion, i call on the european commission to submit a legislative proposal immediately, which will clarify the existing legal uncertainties, while ensuring fair working conditions for platform workers.

paragraph: madam president, commissioner, digitization and the application of artificial intelligence in the workplace are generating new models that entail clear precariousness, hyperconnection, control and surveillance, or algorithmic decisions without human supervision. the implications at the level of mental health and emotional well-being of workers are already evident, and we now need new legislation: a directive to prevent psychosocial risks in the workplace and a directive that regulates the use of artificial intelligence in the workplace . to do this, the commission must listen and meet with all parties, companies and unions, because workers do not need psychologists, but decent working conditions, safe and quality work. the digitization of the labor context cannot be an exclusively technological process; it must be a socio-technical process, where technology and humanism go hand in hand.

subject_of_business_title: Artificial intelligence in criminal law and its use by the police and judicial authorities in criminal matters (debate)
paragraph: mr president, ladies and gentlemen, while parliament is preparing to examine the proposal for a regulation on artificial intelligence, with this report we are sending out a clear message and we are already setting out an important fixed point: in our opinion, there is no place in europe for mass biometric surveillance and security and the fight against crime cannot come at the expense of citizens' fundamental rights. identification by means of biometric data in places accessible to the public runs the risk of causing serious abuses of the right to privacy and of other principles at the basis of our democratic systems. the european data protection supervisor has said so: these systems would have a direct negative impact on the exercise of freedom of expression, assembly, association, right down to the freedom of movement itself. let us then think of what could happen in places that are not so attentive to the separation of powers or to fundamental freedoms, be they states or cities. the risk of abuse is too great. this is why we believe that the exceptions to article 5 on prohibited practices of the proposed regulation should be removed. similarly, predictive techniques for law enforcement activities carry with them a very serious risk of discrimination, in addition to the lack of evidence on their accuracy, undermining one of the fundamental foundations of our democratic systems, namely the presumption of innocence. no amount of human oversight or error-free datasets will be sufficient to ensure that decisions of this kind by artificial intelligence systems are made in compliance with constitutional guarantees and fundamental rights of the union, even where these decision-making processes are reversible. all the more reason these systems cannot undergo a mere self-assessment of conformity before being placed on the market, as proposed by the regulation in its first draft under our examination. in fact, a self-assessment exposes to unacceptable risks of errors and violations, which would only be discovered later by the supervisory authorities if they have the means to do so, and this would happen with damage that has already occurred, even irreparable, to people's lives. in the union, we already have the most advanced personal data protection laws in the world today. for us it is a model, a model that we want to bring to the rest of the world, and we cannot afford to retreat even an inch from this approach when it comes to regulating artificial intelligence. we must, also in this field, fully protect the rights of citizens. i think this is how we can do it for a europe that has its own human rights-centred model of artificial intelligence.

intervention_header_en: Dragoş Tudorache, on behalf of the Renew Group
subject_of_business_title: Artificial intelligence in criminal law and its use by the police and judicial authorities in criminal matters (debate)
paragraph: mr president, dear commissioner, dear colleagues, the use of artificial intelligence in law enforcement is a political decision, not a technical one. our duty is to apply our political worldview to determine what are the allowed uses of artificial intelligence and under which conditions. europe is built on a set of values. they constrain the realm of the possible, dictating what we cannot do. and our values also guide our way into the future, dictating what we can and what we should do. what we cannot do is to allow the use of technology to lead to a breach of our values. we must only allow ai technologies to be used with straight safeguards and oversight, and we must ensure that human rights are protected throughout. what we also cannot do is to allow authorities to use technology for mass surveillance, mass social scoring or any type of government control over citizens. we must be doubly cautious in protecting our values when dealing with law enforcement, as law enforcement is the prerogative of the state. on the other hand, what we can – and should – do is to seek to use ai to reduce the biases and discriminations plaguing our society, including in law enforcement. technology is a tool. we should invest in it until it is good enough to serve our values. what we also can and should do is ensure law enforcement is competitive and has the best tools at its disposal to fight crime. fighting crime is also a way to protect our values and should be a top priority for us. we must therefore strengthen the democratic fibre and resilience of our institutions. and tomorrow’s challenges will not come from the tools themselves but from our ability or inability to use them in accordance with our values.

paragraph: mr president, ladies and gentlemen, artificial intelligence is an admirable tool and a tremendous potential for our peoples and our nations. but as usual, the european union is spoiling it in the worst way, turning it into an instrument of ideological struggle. thus, in police and judicial matters, where information technology can allow decisive progress for the safety of our fellow citizens, in particular our children, you limit its use. you claim that artificial intelligence would reproduce and even amplify discrimination, which would force it to forbid certain conclusions and to be as blind as you in the fight against delinquency. you refuse an intelligent system for detecting lies at the borders of the european union, when 80% of so-called unaccompanied minors are in fact adults and 70% of asylum applications are rejected because they are unfounded. you claim that the american george floyd case, which does not concern us, is proof of alleged racism by the police, and demand national plans to fight against the policeman rather than against the thugs. we expected this report to talk about artificial intelligence, criminal efficiency, the safety of our fellow citizens and we only have laxity for offenders and ideological lessons for law enforcement and honest citizens . since europe does not want to seriously control its borders and fight against crime, then the member states will have to take their destiny into their own hands and decide by election or referendum on the vital questions of security and sovereignty: c is exactly what marine le pen will offer in france in march 2022.

subject_of_business_title: Artificial intelligence in criminal law and its use by the police and judicial authorities in criminal matters (debate)
paragraph: mr. speaker, i understand the concern about giving algorithms control over decisions that can seriously affect human life. for example, because algorithms can make mistakes. but i do not agree that, based on such concerns alone, we should ban the use of artificial intelligence across the board wherever it may have a legal impact on an individual, as this report suggests. we should have analytics that honestly compare the functionality and effectiveness of human and algorithmic decision-making, and decide better. there are already examples of the successful use of artificial intelligence in criminal matters that have led to a more efficient and fairer system. for example, prison reform in the state of new jersey.

paragraph: honorable chairman, commissioners, colleagues, earlier diagnosis of malignant disease, better traffic management or more rational use of energy sources are just some examples of the obvious benefits that the application of artificial intelligence brings. however, if it is not adequately regulated by law, artificial intelligence can threaten individual privacy and lead to various forms of discrimination. therefore, it is not surprising that as many as 88 percent of citizens believe that it should be carefully managed. the fight against sophisticated, well-financed and equipped terrorist and criminal groups in the 21st century cannot be imagined without the use of artificial intelligence. on the other hand, the example of artificial intelligence is particularly sensitive in the field of criminal law because it includes the possibility of geometric recognition and algorithmic decision-making. in order to protect citizens from its misuse, but also to become a world leader in smart technologies, the european union needs a new, comprehensive approach to artificial intelligence. such an approach should prohibit the concept of social evaluation, which can be used to collect a wide range of data about citizens and their behavior using algorithms. on the other hand, the use of biometric identification systems, i.e. facial recognition in public places for the purposes of criminal prosecution, in accordance with the principle of proportionality, should be limited to situations such as the search for a missing child, prevention of a specific and immediate terrorist threat, and detection, locating, identification or investigation against perpetrators of serious crimes or suspects of such crimes. we must achieve a balance between the use of artificial intelligence for the purpose of catching criminals on the one hand and protecting human rights on the other, but without spreading the hysteria and paranoia that we are unfortunately witnessing here today.

paragraph: close cooperation and strategic relations between the european union and its member states and the usa are based on shared history and shared democratic values. in the coming period, geopolitical relations will increasingly be defined by the ability to master new technologies such as artificial intelligence and setting global technological standards in accordance with shared values. the establishment of the council for trade and technology as a platform for transatlantic cooperation in the field of technology development can significantly contribute to the revitalization of relations. the incredible technological development we are witnessing brings with it a series of ethical and political issues in their application. one of the problematic examples is the application of the biometric system in the development of the chinese social scoring system designed with the aim of scoring citizens depending on their social and financial behavior. data required for scoring are collected using surveillance cameras, social networks and other databases. he believes that such practices have no place in democratic societies, and i see the transatlantic trade and technology council as the democratic core of the emerging digital future.

subject_of_business_title: Disinformation and the role of social platforms (debate)
paragraph: ms. president! finding a partner, keeping in touch, entertainment, and information are important aspects of our lives, which are determined by very complicated algorithms in the online space. however, the algorithm cannot distinguish between real and unreal, right and wrong, good and bad, since the algorithm, following capitalist logic, only sees profit in front of it. if profit is what it takes, then it decides elections. if profit is what it takes, then it chains young people to their phones without caring that it destroys their mental health. if profit is what it takes, it poisons users' minds with fake news and conspiracy theories and ultimately polarizes society. today we are at the point where algorithms determine what we read and think about. malicious actors do not hesitate to take advantage of this and spread personalized fake information and flood users' various social media platforms. my fellow representatives, we cannot stand idly by as the community is taken out of social media, so that instead of people, profit and money become the focus. it is time for the european union to take real and immediate steps to regulate the giant platforms, including in the fight against fake news. it is time to take a tougher stance against those who spread disinformation, regardless of whether they are inside or outside europe, individuals or governments, because disinformation is currently the biggest threat to a united europe. for a strong europe and above all for a democratic europe.
