subject_of_business_title: Disinformation and the role of social platforms (debate)
paragraph: madam president, two weeks ago i met a very special woman. her name is frances haugen and she is the facebook whistle-blower who spoke out sunday night on cbs. she did this because in the past she lost a friend to online conspiracy theories and did not want anyone to feel the pain that she had felt. tonight, i want to honour her courage and her moral high ground by lending my voice to her words in this high house, hoping she will soon be able to speak to us herself. i quote, ‘the thing i saw at facebook over and over again was that there were conflicts of interest between what was good for the public and what was good for facebook. and facebook, over and over again, chose to optimise for its own interests, like making more money. one of the consequences of how facebook is picking out that content today is that it is optimising for content that gets engagement, or reaction. but its own research is showing that this is content that is hateful, that is divisive, that is polarising – it’s easier to inspire people to anger than it is to other emotions. when we live in an information environment that is full of angry, hateful, polarising content, it erodes our civic trust, it erodes our faith in each other, it erodes our ability to want to care for each other. the version of facebook that exists today is tearing our societies apart and causing ethnic violence around the world. facebook has realised that if they change the algorithm to be safer, people will spend less time on the site, they’ll click on less ads, they’ll make less money. facebook, over and over again, has shown it chooses profit over safety. i’m hoping that this will have had a big enough impact on the world that they get the fortitude and the motivation to actually go put those regulations into place. that’s my hope.’ those are frances’ words. i feel gratitude and i share her hope. colleagues, she has done her bit. now let’s do ours. let’s approve a digital services act with real teeth.

subject_of_business_title: Disinformation and the role of social platforms (debate)
paragraph: madam president, for years, platforms have been profiting from the large—scale spread of disinformation and hate, and their decisions are driven by profit, image and shareholder value. any impact on society or democracy is just collateral damage. and as the courageous whistle—blower frances haugen revealed in the past weeks, facebook’s algorithms are programmed to promote and spread content that feeds anger such as hate, fake news and shocking content. people with many followers were exempted from all of facebook’s rules and could post whatever they liked, including fake news. and this while instagram is worsening one in three teenage girls’ body issues and impacting a generation’s mental health. and they know the impact of their algorithm but refuse to do anything about it. these same big corporations are acting as guardians of our online space and miserably failing, and this is why we shouldn’t look at them to fix the problem for us. incentivising platforms to delete even more only reinforces their power over our free speech. we have to tackle the root causes, which are a small number of very large and powerful platforms controlling our public debate and amplifying fake news and hate on a large scale specifically targeting certain people for profit. what we get to see online should not be up to ceos and shareholders. we need to break big tech’s power over internet users. let us ban manipulation by toxic algorithms, microtargeting and dark patterns and give people more meaningful control over recommender algorithms. how we regulate today’s tech companies can only protect and strengthen our future society if we make bold choices. we need to take the power over what we see online out of the hands of private companies and place it firmly back in the hands of the people.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Services Act (debate)
paragraph: sir. chairman! now we are taking back control from the tech giants and bringing our digital eu legislation into the 21st century. we are building on the e-commerce directive that we adopted in 2000. back then, the world looked very different. facebook didn't exist, mark zuckerberg hadn't even had the idea, and steve jobs and apple hadn't yet launched the ipod, let alone thought of the iphone. amazon was still a loss-making business, and the eu's trade with china was significantly smaller than today. it is therefore time for us to carry out a fundamental update of our digital legislation. the dsa can become the new gold standard for the tech area, not just in europe, but throughout the world. big tech nations like the us and china are watching closely what we now agree on. just like they did when we did gdpr. with the dsa, we take a fundamental stand against the wild west that digital has developed into. for far too long, illegal products and content have proliferated online. the algorithms have fostered division and the recommendation systems have destroyed the self-esteem of young people. the digital has simultaneously shortened the distance between us, but dug the ditches deeper. you can write to people from all over the world, but judging by the debate on social media, it is all too easy to forget that it is precisely a person you are writing to. you can buy products from all corners of the world, but you can no longer be sure that the product you buy actually meets the rules we have in europe. and as easy as it is to click the product into the virtual basket, it can be just as difficult to get hold of the seller if you experience problems. therefore, new strong legislation is needed. legislation that ensures that what is illegal offline will also be illegal online in the future. we are now voting on that legislation today in the european parliament. the dsa contains an incredible number of important and much-needed positive measures. i would like to emphasize here that we are improving consumer security, that we are putting a stop to the endless data harvesting, and that we are opening the black box of algorithms. specifically, we improve consumer safety in three areas: firstly, we propose that consumers and citizens should be able to contact the mediation service through a single point of contact. it will give social media users better opportunities to get in touch with the services if, for example, their content is removed illegally or if their account is blocked. at the same time, it will also allow consumers who have unknowingly bought an illegal or dangerous product online to get in touch directly with the online marketplace and not just with some chat function. second, we demand that online marketplaces do more to protect consumers from illegal products. they must quickly and efficiently remove the illegal products and contact the users who managed to buy these illegal products before they were taken down. and thirdly, we are introducing a right to seek redress directly from the platforms for both consumers and businesses if the platforms do not meet the provisions we set in the dsa. this is a significant improvement for both the consumers and the companies that make a living from the platforms and use the platforms. we are also slowing down the platforms' use of our data with a series of new rules. now there must be an end to targeted advertising for minors. minors' data must not be harvested and used for commercial purposes. here in parliament, we put an end to that. at the same time, it must be easier to withdraw your consent if you have given it to targeted advertising. so it shouldn't be more difficult to say no thank you than it is to say yes thank you to them. and finally, we would like to ban dark patterns. there must be an end to designing a dialogue box so that the citizens' choices are determined and influenced in a certain direction. all of this helps to give us users more control over our own data. then we also open the black box of the algorithms and let both the commission and the coordinator of digital services take a look at the reports on the consequences of the algorithms. going forward, the social media must make an assessment of what this means with the changes in their algorithms that they make. for example, does an algorithm promote eating disorders and self-harm? if it does, the platform needs to look into it and fix the problem. the biggest platforms can no longer hide behind a veil of ignorance. now they are forced to face the consequences of their algorithms. it is really important. so we are taking control back from the tech giants. with the european parliament's proposal for a new gold standard for the tech sector, we are sending a very, very strong signal to the council. we insist on legislation with two main objectives: we must protect users and consumers, and we must ensure that the digital economy can grow within a democratic, transparent and reliable framework. i am incredibly proud of what we have achieved with this agreement in the european parliament. therefore, there are also many who deserve a big thank you. first i would like to say a big thank you to the shadow rapporteurs for the cooperation we have had in imco, also to the associated committees and to the coordinator colleagues. thanks also to all the colleagues in my own group and other colleagues here in parliament who have contributed to proposals and to discussions, because it is such an important area. it is good that you have joined. i would also very much like to say a big thank you to the employees in the imco secretariat and in the s&d group. without their work, we would not have reached this point. and also a big thank you to the two commissioners, mrs vestager and mr breton, for an incredibly good collaboration. finally, i would also like to thank the presidency, both in portuguese, slovenian and, for the time being, also in french. we have had good cooperation so far, and i am sure that it will be very good when we start the trilogue negotiations shortly. i hope we can do it relatively quickly. european citizens deserve that we finish this legislation quickly so that we can have a safer and more secure internet. we all need that. thanks!.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Services Act (debate)
paragraph: mr president, when digital platforms emerged a decade ago, the societal challenges arising from harnessing new technologies and services seemed straightforward, and the possibilities were endless. today, our situation is totally different. those same platforms have become so big, so significant, so indispensable even for our economy, for our society, for our democracies, that they have started controlling the internet, controlling our people, controlling politics, by simply having the key and access to the online content that we read, to the online content that we watch and also that we share. for the moment, the digital world is like the wild west, without any rules, without any limits or safeguards, leaving people defenceless, exposed, and exploited for their vulnerabilities. and in the middle of all this are private companies weaponising key digital technologies for their own private gains, for their own profits. times have changed, and we can do better than this. people are demanding that we step up on their behalf and create a safe and healthier digital ecosystem. the digital services act is the right tool to answer those calls and set a gold standard in the regulation of big tech. i want to congratulate the rapporteur for her hard work. the report is preserving the general principles that are so important for us, the country of origin, no general monitoring and stay-down obligation. it is also providing better choices for our consumers and transparency measures by banning dark patterns, introducing algorithm accountability and also providing greater transparency for recommender systems. finally, yet importantly, it includes stronger protection and compensation mechanisms for consumers and people with disabilities – and our political family, the s&d group, kept in mind as a primary concern the protection of our consumers. and this is highlighted throughout the whole report. the dsa should empower people to take back control of the internet, on the kind of online content they wish to read, that they wish to watch, that they wish to share. the time has come to be ambitious and address everything from user safety to consumer protection, targeted advertisement, surveillance of users, transparency, accountability, and end the tech giants’ ability to gain the digital economy for their dividends. if we don’t act now, we will miss a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.

subject_of_business_title: Implementation of the Toy Safety Directive (debate)
paragraph: mr president, ladies and gentlemen, according to the latest report on the european notification system for dangerous products, the safety gate, toys are among the products with the most notifications by national authorities: 27% of the total in 2019. playing is a a fundamental moment for the motor and cognitive development of children, but it can also expose them to numerous health risks, not necessarily visible at the moment but also with a long-term impact. this is why the legislation on toys is a key tool. directive 2009/48/ec has certainly played a positive role so far, but there remain some problems of flexibility and inconsistencies to be corrected, as well as the need to face the new challenges that have emerged both from the most recent scientific evidence and from new technologies. in the report, we examine these points and make proposals to the commission and the member states. an important aspect is that of chemicals, where we encounter various problems. the exemptions for substances that are carcinogenic, mutagenic or toxic to reproduction provide for too high a concentration of these substances to ensure effective protection. given their high risk to children's health, we ask you to evaluate a reduction in the possibility of derogation. the limit values ​​for nitrosamines in the directive are too high, as admitted by the commission itself, and must be reduced to at least the threshold already adopted, for example in germany, by way of derogation from the directive. we also ask for a serious assessment of the possible elimination of the distinction for chemicals between toys for children under 36 months and others. a child remains vulnerable even at 37 months of age, not to mention that this distinction also makes it possible to easily circumvent the rule, declaring that a game is reserved for children over that age even when this is not the case. these points cannot currently be changed without a codecision procedure, which takes a long time. this is also why we asked for a revision of the directive, which we were pleased to see has been confirmed in the meantime by the commission itself. we therefore ask that this opportunity be used to convert the directive into a regulation, so that it is directly applicable in all member states. we ask to deliver on the commitments made also on toys by the commission with the strategy on sustainable chemicals. among others, i mention extending the generic risk management approach to endocrine disruptors, to ensure that these substances are also banned in toys. furthermore, the review can be an opportunity to explore the possibility of including elements on lifespan and reparability in the labeling, to increase the aspects of sustainability also in toys, in line with the objectives of the circular economy. as far as new technologies are concerned, the emergence of connected toys or toys that make use of artificial intelligence poses new challenges, highlighting the particular vulnerability of children to external manipulation or localization interventions. we need to take these aspects into account, in this and other legislative instruments, from cybersecurity, to connected products, to artificial intelligence, because the issue of privacy and children's mental health has become more pressing as such products are increasingly present in their lives. i conclude by addressing one of the fundamental problems for the safety of toys today, namely the proliferation of dangerous games, especially online. i want to make a premise: the toy sector in europe is made up for the vast majority of small and medium-sized enterprises that make great efforts – it must be recognized – to place only games that comply with all the rules on the market. unfortunately, however, not all other producers are so interested in respecting them. for this reason the problem will not be solved if there is not an incisive action by the so-called marketplaces in controlling their sellers and in preventing the re-emergence of unsafe games, already removed from their platforms. market surveillance authorities are working hard and certainly need to do even more, especially in some member states, coordinate better and make use of new technologies, but they need resources and cannot cover everything. so the result of the negotiations on the european digital services act, currently underway, will be crucial to improve the situation and ensure that what is illegal offline is also illegal online. these are the main questions raised in the report which we will be voting on tomorrow and which i hope will have broad support from the whole of the european parliament.

subject_of_business_title: Tackling non-tariff and non-tax barriers in the single market (debate)
paragraph: mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the single market is one of the great successes of the european project, providing 56 million jobs and generating 25% of the union's gdp. despite these achievements, its potential is yet to be achieved. a wide range of non-tariff barriers prevent us from fully achieving our objectives. the european people's party is committed to overcoming these obstacles, which are of different kinds: complex administrative procedures, lack of accessible information, legal obstacles, unequal access to public contracts and many others. as shadow rapporteur on the imco committee, i have tried to make my contribution in this report by suggesting measures to combat the growth of protectionism, which we see in many member states, and to help cut red tape, especially for smes. i welcome the report and its rapporteur, this report that we are voting on tomorrow and which results in a broad compromise. we agreed on a set of concrete recommendations addressed to the european commission and the member states. it is urgent for the european union to focus its resources on issues that affect the single market, removing all barriers. finally, allow me to refer to digitization, artificial intelligence and new technologies in general, which deserve special attention, due to their potential to reduce current obstacles and to the fact that they offer new opportunities, namely through the completion of the market digital single, to the benefit of consumers and businesses, in particular smes.

subject_of_business_title: Foreign interference in all democratic processes in the EU (debate)
paragraph: mr president, it is important to speak and act on foreign interference and its multiple facets: disinformation, manipulation of social media, cyberattacks, threats to journalists and activists, covert funding of political parties, revolving doors between politics and business, among many others. it is democracy that is at stake, as well as our rights and freedoms. this report touches on essential problems and offers important proposals to combat them, but it suffers from bias and a reduced reading of reality. yes, there are putin's maneuvers with european extreme right parties and we have to fight them. yes, there are revolving doors between politics and energy business, chinese or russian, and we have to fight them. yes, there is abuse of personal data, algorithm maneuvers and other social media scams and we have to fight them. yes, there is an attack on journalism and journalists, there are espionage schemes like the pegasus scandal and we have to fight them. let us understand, however, that disinformation and manipulation by russia and china are very real, but they are not the only ones. these schemes only work because there are actors available inside to fuel internal interference and we are well aware of the role of extreme right parties in this race to the abyss. the revolving doors between politics and business at gazprom or cfc china energy are very real, but they are far beyond energy and the financial sector remains untouched. furthermore, the maintenance of gold visas and tax havens make us accomplices in this threat to democracy, the rule of law and the rights of citizens. if there are revolving doors, it is because the rooms are contiguous between political power and financial interests. we will not vote against this report, but we regret that the work done did not have the ambition to be irreproachable from the point of view of what it claims to fight. above all, we cannot allow the fight against disinformation to be usurped as an excuse to put an end to freedom of expression and information.

subject_of_business_title: A new EU strategic framework on health and safety at work post 2020 (debate)
paragraph: mr president, mr commissioner, today we are witnessing a transformation of labor relations due to the impact of factors such as digitalisation. it is evident that the pandemic has done nothing more than highlight and increase the risks of a phenomenon that had been developing rapidly for some time: the birth of a new social, digital, market economy that has a direct impact on working conditions and, therefore, therefore, in the safety and health of workers, including mental health. the use and application of new advanced artificial intelligence systems, such as algorithms, have made working conditions more precarious, in part, due to the lack of existing regulation to date. the increase in control and surveillance of the hours worked, the lack of social interaction and separation between private and professional life are just some of the many aspects that show the pressure exerted on the worker and the risk that this entails for health. mental. the new european framework for health and safety at work must adapt to this reality and current challenges, and this also translates into the need to establish binding legal mechanisms for the prevention of psychosocial risks and to regulate the use of artificial intelligence in the workplaces. also to exercise the right to disconnect and establish minimum requirements for fair and equal teleworking conditions. depression, stress, anxiety, burnout, pathologies well known to all, as the commissioner has pointed out, present every day in our work environment as a new form of pandemic and yet not recognized as occupational diseases. we socialists are committed to ensuring that we advance towards a just modernity and social welfare. this includes protecting workers from risks derived from hyper-connectivity, macro surveillance, control and discrimination or automated digital decisions. innovation and progress were not conceived as synonymous with exploitation and job insecurity. the report we are debating here today on a new strategic framework for health and safety at work is key to ensuring that all workers in europe enjoy necessary protection and dignity in the workplace.

paragraph: mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the world of work has already been transformed by the eruption of new technologies, above all artificial intelligence, which force us, these technologies, to urgently reprogram the social and employment policies of our countries. i want to talk about this because, as rapporteur on the ai ​​regulation, i am working to shape a new european approach to artificial intelligence that puts humans at the centre, the human being, balancing the need for a regulatory framework that favors the innovation, yes, but which at the same time protects fundamental rights, including the right to healthy, safe and dignified working conditions, which are the subject of this important work that we are discussing today. increasingly, work is supervised and coordinated by algorithms, by big data, which track worker productivity, their position, their vital signs, micro facial expressions; we cannot allow the office and the factory to turn into orwellian scenario environments. the mental and physical health of workers must not be jeopardized. new rules are needed, because machines must be at the service of man and not the other way around.

subject_of_business_title: Data Governance Act (debate)
paragraph: madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, every second billions of data are generated by devices of all kinds. they represent a very important asset which, if put to good use, can make life easier for citizens, improve services or help research. a heritage that we must above all preserve from distorted or illegal use. that of data governance is therefore one of the great challenges facing politics in the digital age. we have worked in recent months, first as parliament - and i want to thank my colleague niebler, rapporteur for this provision - together with the council then - and thanks to the important mediation of the commission and commissioner breton - we have worked, i said, to provide europe with a legal tool that allows us to regulate data sharing, getting ahead of our partners and leading the way in this field. data that underlie the development of artificial intelligence and the economy of tomorrow. the goal is to create a sort of data schengen, as some call it, for the benefit of individuals and businesses and above all small and medium-sized businesses, which will have greater control over the sharing and management of the latter. we are talking about a tool that will allow operators of all sizes, especially the smallest ones, to access a market of intermediation services based on transparency and neutrality, a tool that aims to regulate the reuse of data held by the sector public, which are too often unused. finally, with this regulation, an innovation committee is created which will have various tasks, first of all that of contributing to increasing the interoperability of data in the european union and establishing guidelines for the creation of common european data spaces. in short, thanks to this important tool, we aim to have more and more data available, with more and more safeguards, being careful to balance, on the one hand, rules and principles and, on the other, not to hinder an economy that is all emerging and evolving.

subject_of_business_title: Data Governance Act (debate)
paragraph: madam president, commissioner, colleagues! a strong and harmonized legal framework for data management is an important step in alleviating existing concerns about data security and opening up wider opportunities for the use of data in the european union. thus, we would also make an additional contribution to national economies. the analogy of data as the oil of the twenty-first century undoubtedly remains relevant. the european union must therefore ensure that innovation is based on transparently obtained and good quality data. this also means that the european union must not build a fortress around itself, indirectly creating new barriers to digitization and data circulation with the rest of the world. it is international cooperation that has been the historical formula for success in this region, and this approach must continue and also promote the digital economy. likewise, the european union and its member states must direct more financial and other resources for the development and application of new technologies. in the european union, there is a distinct lack of both private and public investments in artificial intelligence and other high-tech areas. if we want to be at the forefront of the digital age, in addition to legal acts, we also need determined action, including in terms of securing funding.

paragraph: mister president! i would also like to thank you for being able to explain everything so well here, and i think it's good that you're here. but also to you, madam vice-president, thank you very much for coming, and dear colleagues, thank you very much for what we have now achieved here, and of course also the secretariat and our assistants. we have achieved a lot, but we could actually have been even bolder or more revolutionary, because artificial intelligence is a key technology. it is the key technology, basically a kind of booster for digitization, and is of great strategic relevance for us. every area of ​​our lives will be affected by this technological change, and the consequences for our competitiveness, for our prosperity, for our security should not be underestimated. and i think that with this fast-moving development, we really have to ask ourselves the question: how do we as the eu, as europe, actually want to survive in a digital and data-driven world? how do we want to keep up with other regions in the world that are far more consistent and targeted in research and development, invest, train talented people who spend a lot of money and can react much more flexibly to new developments? as europe, we also have something to offer the world by combining our values ​​with a technology. and that doesn't exist in these other regions. however, in our very complex structure, it has to happen so quickly that we are the first to come up with new ideas, so that we can also anticipate developments in the future. insisting on what was once created is the wrong way. we actually have to sit down every night and think about how we can be better tomorrow. none of this should scare us, but rather encourage us, because this change has huge opportunities for us for the benefit of society as a whole, whether it's the health sector, whether it's sustainability - these are just a few examples. it is important to take advantage of all these opportunities. we have listed them in this report, and with our human-centred, trustworthy approach to ai, which is also based on fundamental rights, on european values, we can also counteract all those risks that call our freedom and security into question. social scoring, disinformation, automated weapons or less drastic examples: that's of course what we don't want. with this european approach, however, we have the opportunity to set global standards. we have to be more active there. and we would squander this opportunity if we weren't the world leader in global competition. otherwise our standards will fall behind and instead we will end up as a kind of digital colony with the very forces who then do not share our values. the european union is currently falling behind in terms of competition, and we lack market power, research and expertise. and this is exactly where the report comes in: what still needs to happen so that we can possibly make better progress? paragraph: mr president, executive vice-president, rapporteur, dear colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, in the past, whoever ruled the waves ruled the world. in the future, i believe whoever rules artificial intelligence will dominate the world. and this is where i believe europe’s challenge lies. just as we seek to use ai for the betterment of society, we see autocracies seeking ways to weaponise it. they do so by trying to create a digital dystopia. what we notice is that when it comes to the spread of disinformation, mass hacks, the dark web, cyberattacks and autonomous weapons systems, all these phenomena can be aided by artificial intelligence. if the west loses the race to gain the social, economic and security benefits of ai, there will be a fundamental shift in global order, and this is why i believe this report seeks to shape ai in our democratic image. and it is precisely to build trust, to create an ethical framework for innovation; we have to try and be the champions for a future that ensures ai is the vessel for those ground—breaking innovations when it comes to health outcomes, when it comes to effective cybersecurity or scientific discovery or greater sustainability. we cannot let authoritarian states such as china and russia beat us to this technological punch. and i believe if we have enough political will, which i hope we show in this report, enough financial investment and legal certainty, i believe we could attract the so much needed investment, but also be able to foster world—leading innovation. so i would like to congratulate my colleague axel voss on this report, because i believe technology and democracy have to go hand in hand. and i think with this report, we set the right path in achieving that.

paragraph: mr. president, ladies and gentlemen, vice-president vestager, artificial intelligence presents numerous opportunities and potential benefits in very many fields, if used in accordance with our fundamental values, with respect for human dignity and the environment, for the good of society. this is our european model. a year and a half of work by the special commission has allowed us to explore the fundamental aspects of these technologies and the impact in the various economic sectors, the social repercussions, the geopolitical implications. implications that make a leadership role for europe necessary in affirming its own model for artificial intelligence, in the work on global standards, because the technological one will be one of the main theaters on which the future structure of international relations will be played out. this requires a united and competitive internal market, in which everyone is in a position to innovate in compliance with the rules, from privacy to competition. and this is why we are working on the regulation – which you, vice-president, also mentioned earlier – which will be a fundamental building block for the development of a true european industry in this field. among the various ideas contained in the report, i mention in particular the proposal for a legislative initiative on the use of artificial intelligence in the workplace. in fact, teleworking has accelerated and made more evident not only the advantages in terms of efficiency, but also the potentially harmful effects of the use of these technologies on workers. monitoring their performance without their consent or without their knowledge, without prior consultation of their representatives, as we unfortunately see happening, must not be allowed in europe. at the same time we will have to counter possible abuses of real-time biometric recognition in public places for security reasons. we don't want a surveillance society. i therefore thank the rapporteurs and all my colleagues for the constructive discussions of the past few months which have led to a balanced text full of proposals, very useful for the legislative work that awaits us.

paragraph: mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, first of all, thank you all for the work you have done. this work has touched on topics of great impact on the life of citizens, from transport to health, to agriculture, up to the use of artificial intelligence in the military sector. the aim was to analyze the various perspectives to provide the basis for future union legislation in this area. i don't know if we have succeeded, given the high rate of innovation in this sector, we are faced with many opportunities, but also with just as many risks. we see many improvements in the well-being and life of citizens, but also enormous risks with regard to personal freedoms and the risk of errors, with catastrophic social consequences too: i am thinking of that real estate trading platform that bought houses due to an algorithm error at a price above market value, suffering financial losses and being forced to lay off 25 percent of employees. during the proceedings, our group tabled amendments aimed at minimizing these risks, unfortunately not shared by all. it is essential for our citizens that there be as few risks as possible. in the medical field, attention must be paid to the maximum because also in this case we were faced with algorithms that reported only white patients and artificial intelligence must be free from prejudices of any kind. and especially in the military field, we consider it essential that artificial intelligence does not have the upper hand over humans in decision-making processes. it is essential that freedom of speech and expression is not jeopardized by systems that use artificial intelligence, forcing us to use the so-called algospeak, a coded language to bypass algorithms and online censorship. we are not opposed to progress, we are not thinking of a luddite revolt. we don't want to destroy machines, we simply want a future of this technology that is driven by ethics and a desire to protect our citizens.

paragraph: artificial intelligence ignites the imagination of both technology enthusiasts and opponents of faster and faster automation in the economy and social life. reconciling these two approaches and building a broad compromise is a difficult but possible task. unfortunately, in our view, this report has not quite succeeded. we appreciate the rapporteur's effort and commitment to the report, but as ecr we will abstain. the final text lacks a clear, coherent and strong message that europe wants to seriously join the global technological race and be a place where innovations are not only consumed, but above all created. artificial intelligence is a huge opportunity for our companies, including small and medium-sized ones, which can develop modern products and services if they receive the right support. that is why spending on research and development as well as close cooperation in the field of ethical, legal and technical standards with international partners who can and want to share their knowledge and experience in the field of ai with us are so important. we cannot allow our strategy for developing artificial intelligence and the data economy to fall victim to long and futile discussions. especially that we are working on the ai ​​act regulation, which above all should create an innovation-friendly legal framework. i hope that we will take advantage of this opportunity and not build another bureaucratic corset for companies, including european ones, operating in the new technologies sector.

paragraph: mr president, my colleague axel voss was right: artificial intelligence is an opportunity to be seized. the benefits of this technology are numerous. they can be applied, for example, to medicine and help save many lives. however, the machine only makes sense if man retains absolute control of it. the reflexes, which the most advanced technologies make it possible to program, will always be worth less than the discernment, the free will and the sensitivity inherent in the human being. it's all about usage. example of a good use of artificial intelligence: the regulation of the internet using algorithms to end the anarchy that reigns there. we have just reached a historic political agreement in europe: the dsa (digital services act, legislation on digital services) will make it possible to combat the most inadmissible abuses of social networks. the principle? it's simple: anything that's illegal offline must become illegal online. no more no less. no, messages of hate and harassment do not constitute opinions that would be part of freedom of expression. they are even the opposite, because they impose silence on all those who fear becoming its victims. are those who harassed and called for the internet murder of samuel paty, are they, were they vectors of freedom of expression? asking the question is already providing an answer. as planned, this new regulation should apply to search engines and all the major social networks. and as brilliant and innovative as it is, elon musk, will have to subject twitter to it like any digital giant. protecting citizens from online hate is a great use of the most advanced technologies. and here is also a very appropriate use of the european union.

paragraph: mr president, we are debating a report that is indeed key, which concludes an eighteen-month job, and which also represents a very notable exercise in dialogue in the european parliament. i want to especially thank the coordinators of this special commission, also the president and the bureau, for the work they have done, in particular the numerous debates and conferences and a total of fourteen public hearings and eight seminars. a joint effort, in short, of the entire european parliament, which ranges from transport to agriculture, health and the fight against cancer, the economy, competitiveness, finance, the green pact and the data strategy. and we have also talked about the impact on democracy, disinformation, the risks of fundamental rights, discrimination, including gender equality, and the role that women must also play in the development of european artificial intelligence. there are two aspects that should be highlighted: firstly, that this has been a fully democratic debate. various points of view have been advocated with the participation of stakeholders from industry, civil society, academia and also users, as well as national parliaments. second, there has been a necessary balance to favor innovation and limit risks in artificial intelligence. from the group of socialists and democrats i would also like to thank the work of the rapporteurs and shadow rapporteurs in articulating the report, which is a very balanced report, with more than a thousand amendments, many of them, by the way, from the group of socialists and democrats , which perfectly responds to the task entrusted to us. it indicates a majority position of the european parliament on all aspects relating to the development and diffusion of artificial intelligence in europe. it also emphasizes very specific aspects, with examples, in each case, of the potential benefits or risks that the use of artificial intelligence may present. to give some examples, in health, it highlights the benefits in the treatment of diseases and new medicines; in the green deal, it highlights the need to create artificial intelligence so that it is sustainable and supports the environmental transition; in foreign and security policy, he makes a geostrategic analysis; in competitiveness, we highlight the need to improve our research and the support of small and medium-sized companies; in the labor market, we call for a specific legislative initiative that can regulate use at work and that respects the rights of workers and workers and ends surveillance in the workplace; also at school, promoting digital illustration. in short, i think that this is a report that will be, above all, very useful for future work and i want to thank all those who have participated in it.

paragraph: mr president, first and foremost, my congratulations to you, axel voss, and to the shadow rapporteurs for the very important work that you’ve done with this report. it was my privilege to serve as chair of the aida committee for the duration of this mandate, and i am very proud about the way in which we have achieved our objectives. as chair, and even before, when negotiating the mandate of the committee, i imagined aida as a place where we, as parliament, think politically about the future of artificial intelligence, a place where we have an honest, introspective and forward—looking assessment of our technological competitiveness on the global stage, and a place where we think beyond the status quo, where we look at the next steps to 2030 and even past that threshold. the aida report captures this vision. so here are three main points i will take away from our work in the aida committee and from this report. first, artificial intelligence is no longer a technical subject. ai is a political or rather – as i have said many times – a geopolitical issue. i am happy that in our work in aida and in this report, we did not shy away from making this point very clearly. we need closer cooperation with our like—minded democratic partners in setting the rules of the digital future. we need to make strategic choices based on our values, and this may come at odds with how other players on the global stage view the role and future of ai in their societies. second, artificial intelligence is, no doubt about it, an opportunity. it is not only an opportunity to improve efficiency in every sector of our economy, it is an important opportunity for us to correct historical biases and discrimination in our societies and, quite literally, build a better future. this leads me to the last, but very important, conclusion. at the end of the aida mandate and after working on this report, parliament is better equipped to regulate the use of technology to work on acts such as the artificial intelligence act, the first legislation of its kind worldwide. we have explored, we have learned and we have defined our political vision. now it’s time to write the laws. once again, congratulations to you, rapporteur, to the coordinators and to the shadow rapporteurs for the work we’ve done together.

subject_of_business_title: Artificial intelligence in a digital age (debate)
paragraph: mr president, madam commissioner, dear colleagues! artificial intelligence is seen by many, including me, as a promise of a better future in many areas. but without clear rules, we risk a "back-to-the-future" effect, like marty, the film hero, who ambitiously starts into the future in 1985 with his future machine and then ends up in 1955. and that is what we are experiencing today: when, for example, with apple pay, the man's credit limit is 20 times greater than that of his wife with the same creditworthiness and the same income. this has nothing to do with intelligence, with innovation or with progress, because this is artificial intelligence without clever rules, a technology that is based on data from the past and therefore does not carry us into the future by itself. and so that it can really develop its potential, we need clear rules, clear ex ante rules against discrimination. this means high-quality data sets, mixed teams and, above all, verifiability. and that's why the ai ​​act, i.e. the current regulation that is on the table, has to make a quantum leap for artificial intelligence. it is not enough to have a product certification or product safety regulation. what we need is a true law implementing fundamental rights in the age of artificial intelligence. and that can also be a competitive advantage for european companies, because the companies, the tech giants that are currently dominating the market, cannot do that. and what's also notable about this report is the recognition that the business of data profiling-based online advertising is the foundation for the market dominance of the big big tech companies - the same companies we're regulating in the dsa and dma right now - also in the artificial intelligence space . and i wish that the european union would no longer sell out the soil – because data is also the soil on which the digital economy thrives and grows – that it would finally till it itself.

subject_of_business_title: Artificial intelligence in a digital age (debate)
paragraph: mr president, ladies and gentlemen, a technological revolution is taking place. the development of artificial intelligence will transform our lives in ways that most men and women can hardly imagine. the european union must encourage this new manifestation of human creativity, because it holds tremendous promise for economic progress. it is high time, because faced with competition from the united states and china, we europeans have already fallen far behind. if we do not want to become a digital colony of external powers, we must support european research, encourage the emergence of start-ups in our member states and avoid market concentration by ensuring access for smes to the economy of artificial intelligence. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr axel voss, for having taken care to recall these priorities. of course, artificial intelligence is not without danger. in the hands of authoritarian regimes, it can lead to mass surveillance and a serious restriction of freedoms, of which the questionable generalization of the health pass gave us a first idea. this is why its use must be regulated by obliging it to respect human rights, and in particular the rights of patients in terms of health. as the author of the report of january 20, 2021 on the use of artificial intelligence in the military and sovereign domains, i would also like to reaffirm the need to regulate, under the aegis of the un, the use of lethal autonomous weapon systems, more commonly known as killer robots. here again, mr voss's report has the merit of reminding us of this. the identity and democracy group particularly insists on the risks of censorship and negation of pluralism that this technology could promote. under no circumstances should the use of artificial intelligence, in particular to filter online content, hinder freedom of expression, in particular freedom of political expression. as a famous french revolutionary said: “the storms of political discussions are only the birth pangs of freedom”. a final danger lies in the temptation to use artificial intelligence to aggravate the social segregation of which rural inhabitants are victims in several member states, such as france, to the benefit of inhabitants of metropolitan areas. to counter this, we will have to demand an equitable deployment of 5g in all of our territories: the issue is fundamental, because if we succeed in this, we will even be able, thanks to this democratization of access to artificial intelligence , reduce inequalities and make this technology an instrument of social progress.

subject_of_business_title: Artificial intelligence in a digital age (debate)
paragraph: mr president, in 2020 the eu has not achieved its target of spending three percent of gdp on research and development. the recent private investment figures are very alarming: 80% in the us and china, compared to less than 5% in the eu. the strategic relevance of artificial intelligence (ai) cannot be denied. the eu must therefore show more ambition to stimulate ai and offer european companies opportunities. we need to attract talent to keep pace with the us and china to prevent the brain drain to the us and to grow and unlock new technologies for our citizens and businesses. on behalf of geert bourgeois, who is shadow rapporteur for this report, i would like to thank rapporteur voss for the good work he has done. we support efforts to create a legal framework for safe, accountable, ethical and trustworthy ai. in doing so, we must adopt a reasonable and proportionate approach that focuses on high-risk systems and allows us to remain true to our standards and reach our full potential. at present, too much eu funding goes to small, short-term and often overlapping projects. the eu should focus on the long term and on cooperation between member states and make targeted investments in a number of strategic areas. in addition, the eu must not sideline itself by adopting too rigid regulations and must be aware of the need for international cooperation. the risk of bias and discrimination that ai entails must also be addressed. however, the emphasis has mainly shifted to fundamental rights and regulations rather than the whole. finally, accessing and sharing data are critical to ai development. the gdpr was enacted before ai appeared on the radar and currently leads to too much uncertainty among companies because it is not progressive enough. we advocate a pragmatic and progressive no-nonsense approach, as we believe it will lead to growth, innovation and open strategic autonomy. on the other hand, too much and too rigid regulation will deter companies and prevent us from becoming a leader on the global stage.

paragraph: mr president, i want to thank axel voss and the chair of the committee for bringing us to this point. we look forward to dealing with the regulation on artificial intelligence. ‘what is it and what is it about’ is a topic that has so many answers and so many approaches, but it does have so many potential benefits for our societies, for our economy and for development. climate can be addressed there, and how we can help to meet our green targets and green ambitions, how to make more efficient decisions based on high—quality inputs. in agriculture, again, efficient approaches measuring inputs to maximise outputs, improving levels and quality of food production. in health we have seen the benefits in the development of the covid-19 vaccine, and also in appropriate care and treatments for patients. so we’ve seen much activity in areas such as the dsa and the dma – and thanks to the commissioner for leadership in that area – and they regulate current practices. now we move to the opportunity to shape ai and its future so we can use it in the way that we want, which is trustworthy, if we are to gain citizens’ confidence. we need human oversight with transparency and strong regulatory bodies. we need clear standards for a human—centred approach to ai that is based on our core european ethical standards. we don’t want to stop ai, we want to use it and harnesses it for its enormous potential. investment from public to encourage private sector in artificial intelligence needs to be encouraged. we need to send a message that europe is a place to invest, to innovate and to know that you can do so with legal certainty, to know that there is a regulation in place in europe that applies across the union. the proposed ai regulation will put europe at the forefront internationally in the area of artificial intelligence. we’d be the first to regulate it and other nations will follow. so we have done so with our leadership before and we can now do it again. so the proposed legislation would be future—proofed, which i think is really important, with the ability to react so that we’re not always coming from behind, but we are prepared to deal with this very important technology as it evolves.

subject_of_business_title: Artificial intelligence in a digital age (debate)
paragraph: mr president, dear commissioner, dear colleagues, getting artificial intelligence right is one of the key questions for the future – also for the european union. this technology will shape the way value is created in our economy and who wields the power in our societies. we cannot look away from this development and just let it happen. that became clear from our work. we need to sail not drift in technological development. the work of the aida committee was a european push to get artificial intelligence right. i had the honour to serve as the first vice—chair, and i thank the chair and the rapporteurs for this work. i think we worked hard and i am proud of the results. for 18 months, aida organised 12 public hearings on different aspects of ai, from tackling the bias of the data to the role of ai in achieving the green deal objectives. we debated, different political groups worked together to bring the whole spectrum of ai—based values on the table. like we condemned ai surveillance in the working place and are concerned that is happening in schools also. in the end, we delivered. the report we are voting on today is a good report that takes steps towards the european approach to ai. we consider, for example, that the imbalance in powers might have negative effects for democracies. if there’s one conclusion i can draw from this work, it is that ai can only be a tool, not an end itself. we should not focus on the specific technologies, but we should focus on what kind of societies we want to see. it is crucial that we see ai as a stepping stone towards inclusive, socially responsible and environmentally sustainable societies. this requires a political effort in directing technological developments towards these goals and help investing in them. i see the report as a sign of europe taking an active role in the global development of ai. the current ai act gives the world’s first legal framework for the development of ai, and parliament has now shown a sign, a strong signal where we want to go. in terms of ai, europe will no longer be a bystander. europe will no longer be a battleground. in the future, the eu will be an ecosystem of excellence, trust and purpose that delivers ai to take us to the future we want.

paragraph: mr president, ladies and gentlemen! the final report of the special committee presents nothing less than a vision for artificial intelligence for europe. this is so important if we want to play in the top tech league. because we shouldn't always just hyperventilate the worst-case scenarios, but very, very urgently wake the eu up from its slumber. we have to find our european way into the technological future, a way beyond the totalitarian surveillance state à la china and the absolutely risky anything goes of a us market that is unregulated in many respects. the framework for the use of artificial intelligence must always be our fundamental rights. mass state surveillance or discrimination are unacceptable, especially if we want to weatherproof our european democracies for the future. then we will lay the foundation for the innovation continent of europe, and then we can tap into an incredible potential for our society and open up completely new scope for ideas for our companies: research into new medicines, the smart cities of tomorrow, a modern industry. the potential of ai is so great that we can hardly imagine it today. we must therefore also manage the political balancing act – i would almost like to say – of not over-regulating what is already there and, above all, not over-regulating what could be there tomorrow. because first of all we need courage. more courage to see opportunities and to encourage those who seize them, so that we don't put tumbling stones in the way of our developers, but rather build stepping stones. i want the eu to become a global innovation leader in tech. artificial intelligence needs the digital single market for this, as do many other technologies. if our civil rights are the cornerstone of this, then we are giving the digital future the face of europe and democracy. thanks to rapporteur voss and my group colleague andrus ansip for their work, and to our chairman dragoș tudorache for his leadership.

paragraph: honorable chairman of the session, dear colleagues! the special committee of the parliament, which was launched last year and analyzed and made proposals on the issue of artificial intelligence, has concluded its work today. i highly appreciate the initiative taken by the parliament by creating a special committee. the development of artificial intelligence and the technology based on its use is extremely fast, and there are obviously many important issues related to artificial intelligence, which were also dealt with in this report. in my view, looking forward, we need to consider the following important factors regarding the implementation and regulation of artificial intelligence. we also need a balanced approach to legislation and must avoid over-regulation that stifles innovation and the deployment of artificial intelligence in security and defence. over-regulation limits our possibilities in the technological development of artificial plants, especially considering that our competitors have no restrictions. attention must certainly be paid to close transatlantic cooperation in the field of artificial intelligence. the usa is the most serious cooperation partner of the european union in this field. we must avoid regulations that interfere with our cooperation with each other. i am convinced that the european commission needs to plan more resources in the field of artificial intelligence. any technological development requires significant investment. in my opinion, emerging and disruptive technologies in general, including artificial intelligence, could become a common area of ​​work for the european union and nato. nato is working on the development of a defense artificial intelligence strategy. i would expect from the european union, above all, funding for the implementation of the protection of artificial plants through the protection fund and other relevant financial instruments. i would like to once again thank my colleagues from the special committee on artificial intelligence. and i really hope that the conclusions of the commission and also the issues i emphasized will receive enough attention in the european union in the future. on the topic of artificial intelligence, we must definitely keep up with our competitors and avoid being left behind - this is a matter of our competitiveness.

paragraph: madam president, commissioner, we are human beings and not just numbers. although artificial intelligence has created several opportunities, increased capital, productivity, innovation, sustainable development, created a number of new jobs, we must not ignore a number of difficulties. ethical, legal difficulties, difficulties related even to the world of work, to the rights of our workers. digital technologies are affecting the quality of life of our workers and are creating an imbalance. an imbalance that is mostly affecting those workers who are vulnerable. ai and digital technologies have reorganized, in particular, the future of our world of work and are also threatening a number of particular work sectors, due to outsourcing, also due to a number of other realities. they have also created a number of new tools to spy on our workers, spy on their personal lives, the use they make of a number of digital platforms, and this is also creating various realities. realities also related to abusive practices that are often taking place without the workers knowing; this without any moral standard, without any ethical standard. the companies and these digital tools are also controlling the way the workers also work and this is also being done on a european level. and that is why it is important, it is fundamental that we see that ai is used in a way that in the end it is also surrounded by the fundamental rights of our human beings, it is more human centric, and that is why i believe that this report is a step in the right direction in order to call for a legislative act at a european level to control these realities that are also affecting our world of work. therefore it is important that these realities ultimately take their knowledge of the world of work, in order to see and ensure that we really have a balance, work-life balance, and as well as other rights also respected, among others , that of the right to disconnect. therefore it is important that we act today before tomorrow and i believe that this is a step in the right direction that should also lead us to the act on artificial intelligence. thank you very much.

paragraph: madam president, dear vice president vestager, colleagues, we are at risk of european values ​​being superseded globally, our businesses marginalized and our living standards drastically reduced. these, as you know, are not my words, but those contained in the report that we approved today after months of work in the special commission on artificial intelligence. fighting for technological leadership in the european union is not an option. not only because our competitiveness depends on it, but because we cannot run the risk that others who do not share our values ​​end up imposing the rules on us. europe is brave and is setting the global standards for artificial intelligence: trustworthy ethics, at the service of citizens and centered on our democratic values. the challenge will be not to overregulate, to avoid duplication and in a governance system that avoids a fragmented market with twenty-seven different interpretations. our companies, especially the small ones, need a single market, without bureaucracy, that allows them to innovate and grow in europe. that being said, the report we are adopting today is more than a wake-up call. it is a roadmap with clear proposals that must accompany the legislation if we want to compete for leadership. i am speaking, for example, of the creation of a stock market similar to the nasdaq, which helps our digital companies to be quickly financed with european capital. i am talking about increasing public and private investment to reach at least 20 billion euros per year. i am talking about investing in training to reduce the shortage of qualified personnel, but also so that workers know how to integrate technology into their day-to-day lives and free them from repetitive jobs that machines can do. and, above all, i am talking about a european interoperable data space that frees us from foreign dependencies. it is urgent to make up for lost time to ensure that the enormous advances in artificial intelligence benefit all of society. and today we take a big step.

paragraph: madam president, madam vice-president of the european commission, dear colleagues! artificial intelligence can be a great enrichment for our society and for our economy. today we can already see that artificial intelligence is used in many different ways in everyday life: artificial intelligence is used in music streaming platforms, for example, and artificial intelligence is used in online language translators. if you look at medicine alone: ​​what advances are there in the diagnostic field through the use of artificial intelligence and big data! image data is evaluated, disease patterns are recognized earlier. there are also a number of ways of using geodata for climate protection. with the help of ai systems, agriculture can work in a more targeted manner here, and also in the household: what efficiency increases there can be - tremendous. it is very, very important that we deal with the topic of “artificial intelligence”. artificial intelligence is the future and has huge potential. but: where there are opportunities, there are usually also major risks. i always say: curse and blessing at the same time. the topic of "social scoring" was raised, for example, and the fear that ai systems would be used to carry out comprehensive surveillance, be it in the work area or elsewhere. that's why i think we have to think carefully about how we will continue to shape regulation here in the future. i think it is important for us as europeans that whatever we are now considering in terms of regulation – and the proposals are on the table – digital technologies must always serve people. so when it comes to the question of how things are regulated here, we have to focus on people. this is the most important thing so that we prevent discrimination and other things. i would like to thank my colleague axel voss for his great report and all the colleagues who have really dealt with the most diverse questions relating to the use of ai in this special committee for many months. and i am now looking forward to the further discussions and debates when it comes to the specific regulatory proposals. i believe that we europeans can really put another scent mark here and create regulation in this digital environment that at the end of the day serves our citizens across europe.

subject_of_business_title: Artificial intelligence in a digital age (debate)
paragraph: madam president! colleagues, commissioner! what do you imagine when you hear the term artificial intelligence? robots taking over the world? a dystopia of orwellian proportions? or perhaps an app that can diagnose skin cancer as accurately as experts? or the machine bluedot that predicted the covid-19 pandemic before the who did? artificial intelligence, like everything else, has at least two sides. used responsibly, it can benefit us all. but if it is misused, it can have disastrous consequences. it is therefore important that we in the eu become leaders when it comes to the development of artificial intelligence, because we have a completely unique approach to technological development. we put people at the center and insist that technology must be reliable. it goes hand in hand with high innovation, economic growth and greater competitiveness. but right now it is the usa and china who have taken the lead, and if we don't catch up with them, it will be them who will set the standard for how artificial intelligence should be and should be used. it shouldn't be like that! the eu really needs to do it. the challenges with artificial intelligence today must not be made into machine storms. they must not become an excuse for being against progress and against technological development. the decisive thing is that we set certain requirements for the artificial intelligence. it must be developed and used in a transparent, ethical and responsible manner. that is what the european way is. here we have the opportunity to take back the leader's jersey. i thought the aida report is really good because it strikes exactly this balance. we are increasing investments in artificial intelligence, we are ensuring that european legislation is harmonized and we are addressing the risks inherent in the use of artificial intelligence. i hope that in the future we can use artificial intelligence more in europe. but this presupposes that it is human-centred and that we have legislation which ensures reliability in the way we use artificial intelligence. with that, i warmly welcome the report.

paragraph: madam president, madam vice-president, congratulations to the rapporteur axel voss and the shadow rapporteurs and also to the president, who has played a fundamental role in the development of this special committee. artificial intelligence has become a key driver for any economy that wants to be globally competitive and is therefore of decisive strategic importance. its impact is economic and also social and, of course, geopolitical. for this reason, this report that we are discussing today offers us an all-encompassing vision of the potential, the needs and the risks that artificial intelligence poses. it analyzes central aspects for its development, ethical principles and, in particular, the centrality that people should have, the need to increase our investment in r&d, cybersecurity, the ability to train and retain talent in europe or the future of employment. i am going to refer specifically to two conditions that are sine qua non for its development: data and infrastructure. it is essential to eliminate legislative fragmentation in the field of data and to promote equal access to such data. some secure data, some reliable data, some data that can be shared. in this sense, we have recently approved the regulation on european data governance and in this sense we are now also beginning to discuss the data law, whose focus is on the internet of things and industrial data. but, in addition, we must put an end to our shortcomings in digital infrastructures in the european union. we continue to depend not only on processors from third countries, but also the cloud infrastructure market is in the hands of five non-european providers. in short, the development of artificial intelligence in europe is going to have a great impact on the competitive capacity of our economy and on the progress of society in all areas: education, health, transport, energy, etc. it is an opportunity that we must make the most of and we, in the european union, have an enormous responsibility for it.

paragraph: madam president, in the world only about 22% of artificial intelligence professionals are women. unfortunately, this gender inequality is also reflected here in the european parliament. all those responsible for this report from the various political groups were men. it must be very important... there are, however, several women interested in this topic, as can be seen even in this debate, who submitted amendments and, fortunately, in its final version, the report recognizes the importance of adopting a gender perspective when we talk about artificial intelligence. we have to prevent the data on which the algorithms are built from being biased and discriminatory. but artificial intelligence can also be used to combat this discrimination. for example, artificial intelligence makes recruitment processes more objective, basing decisions on predefined criteria and reducing the space for subjective analyzes that often discriminate against young women due to the risk of becoming pregnant. we have to invest in retraining and improving skills, placing emphasis on underrepresented groups, such as women. the way we use artificial intelligence has to be based on democratic values ​​and ensure that men and women benefit equally from this technology.

subject_of_business_title: Artificial intelligence in a digital age (debate)
paragraph: madam president, the report of the aida special committee set out the direction of the eu’s approach to artificial intelligence. on an unparalleled scale, europe can establish its own leadership in the area of ai by creating a regulatory environment that gives both private and business users the most appropriate and complete rights and the widest possible protection. this report can be – and confidentially will be – used as a compass during the ai-related process ahead. faced with the rapid technological development of ai and a global policy context where more and more countries are investing heavily in ai, the eu must act to harness the many opportunities and address the challenges of ai in a future-proof manner. we have to set the appropriate standards – neither more nor less than is necessary to achieve our goals. we can pave the way to ethical technology worldwide and ensure that the eu remains competitive all along the way. on artificial intelligence, trust is not an option but a must. that is what human-centred artificial intelligence is all about. the primary purpose of the development and the use of algorithms, sensors and robots is not to produce technology or create scientific knowledge, but to support the quality of human life, the preservation of health and the organisation of social relations. ai should be used at the service of people, families and businesses, and not the other way around. i would like to thank mr axel voss for his excellent work and congratulate him on this very good report.

paragraph: madam president, after a year and a half of work, the special commission on artificial intelligence concludes with this document that the european parliament is examining today and that impacts all the matters and legal bases on which the european parliament legislates regarding the content of the industry, energy, trade and, of course, employment. this document must also respect the european standard for the protection of fundamental rights, which happens to be the highest in the world, established not only in the data protection regulation, but also in the directive addressed to agencies that investigate crimes, law enforcement agencies. this standard has to be very present in the legislation, which should place the european union at the forefront of the reference in regulations on artificial intelligence. when we talk about predictive policing, we have to know what impacts the presumption of innocence. when we talk about biometric recognition we have to know that it impacts on the principle of non-discrimination enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. and when we talk about potentially as abrasive content on fundamental rights as the one that has to do with the handling of personal data, the european data protection standard has to be respected. therefore, that is the commitment: to place the european union at the head of the legislation on artificial intelligence, but in no case give in to the siren songs that claim that this would be in contradiction with the maintenance of the european standard for the protection of personal data and respect for fundamental rights. so, congratulations, yes, to the speakers. but, above all, alert to the european legislation on artificial intelligence so that it maintains respect for the fundamental rights protected by the charter.

subject_of_business_title: Artificial intelligence in a digital age (debate)
paragraph: artificial intelligence plays an increasingly important role in the economy and in democracy. we encounter solutions based on artificial intelligence more and more often in our daily work and life. the use of this technology has the potential to significantly improve productivity, innovation and economic growth in many european countries in the future. during this mandate, we will regulate artificial intelligence horizontally for the first time, and the voss report, which is the result of the work of a special committee set up to consider the union's future policy needs in this field, is another step forward. nevertheless, i would like to point out that we need an even more innovation-friendly approach that recognizes the role of protecting intellectual property rights, as well as an experimental approach, such as dedicated regulatory environments. at the same time, we must ensure a balance between the need to implement new technologies and the implementation of environmental policy. i believe that the green deal and technology policy should complement each other. presuming that the green deal should prevail over all is not a sensible solution, because such an assumption threatens the future of our economies and the overall ability to achieve our goals, both in terms of technology and ecology. i believe that in the near future we will be able to develop regulations that will seek to maximize the possibilities of using this technology, while protecting citizens from the risks associated with it.

paragraph: artificial intelligence is developing at an extraordinary speed and will affect all areas of our lives in the future, so it is crucially important in which direction the development of this technology will go and, last but not least, who will control the operation and use of this technology. this is how we could summarize the main message of the final report of the european parliament's special committee on artificial intelligence in the digital age, which we mps adopted at the may plenary session. the report contains recommendations and directions that the european union will have to follow if it wants to catch up with the currently leading technological superpowers - china and the united states of america - in the development of artificial intelligence. there are many areas in which artificial intelligence can improve our lives; from the fight against climate change and faster and more accurate medical diagnoses, to improving labor standards and accelerating innovation. but we must be aware that the development of new technologies also brings new dangers. autocratic regimes are already exploiting artificial intelligence for mass population control and systematic curtailment of human rights. therefore, it is crucial that in the future the european union will be the one that will set the normative framework in the field of artificial intelligence and thus ensure that it will be developed and used in accordance with european principles.
