paragraph: artificial intelligence (ai) is no longer science fiction, but is already a reality today – also in everyday life. ai applications determine which music you listen to and which videos you see online. they ensure that the food you eat has not been treated unnecessarily with pesticides and help decide on the loan for your dream home and the determination of your cancer diagnosis. with large amounts of data to fuel, strong algorithms and large computing power, ai has the potential in virtually every industry to provide answers to the challenges we face today: on social media, in agriculture, in the of financial services, in healthcare and for the police and judiciary. of course we should be aware of the possible side effects. we cannot blindly rely on an algorithm that cannot be adequately explained, cannot be monitored, and which is fed with extremely flawed or clearly erroneous data and can potentially lead to discrimination. ai will only succeed with a balanced legal framework that allows ai systems to develop and refine using large amounts of data, while providing safeguards that enable us to deal with the possible negative side effects.

subject_of_business_title: The follow up of the Conference on the Future of Europe (debate)
paragraph: dear madam president. on the one hand, we must be pleased that, despite the covid, it was possible to involve a lot of people from all over europe in the conference on the future. on the other hand, we cannot be happy that we did not manage to involve the poorest and most vulnerable in this activity to a greater extent. on the one hand, we can be pleased that the huge number of people who participated in the conference on the future feel that they are europeans. on the other hand, we have to admit that there is a large group of people in europe who do not even feel that they are full citizens of their own countries, let alone europeans. on the one hand, we can be pleased with the shift and visions in areas such as digitization, artificial intelligence or the environment. on the other hand, let's face it, a huge number of poor people in europe do not have access to drinking water. people want certainties, such as quality education, well-paid work, affordable housing and quality healthcare. europeans want europe to be fairer, more democratic, to be a safe territory where everyone has space to realize their dreams. today, our most important task is to turn all the conclusions from the conference on the future of europe into reality. so that every child, every young person, has the opportunity to develop not only themselves, but also their surroundings. we have before us many of the recommendations calling for extensive reforms. we cannot afford to ignore them. europeans want a more social, dignified europe, a europe where people live in prosperity and not in poverty.

subject_of_business_title: Use of the Pegasus Software by EU Member States against individuals including MEPs and the violation of fundamental rights (topical debate)
paragraph: mr president, ladies and gentlemen, technology allows us to do wonderful things today. the development of artificial intelligence then led humanity to unprecedented discoveries. sharing is now a key concept of any real or virtual experience. unfortunately, sometimes, technology allows for silent sharing by gathering information. pegasus is an algorithm born in israel capable of collecting information from deputies, journalists or citizens from any device connected to the internet. many computer scientists have defined pegasus as an information technology jewel with unprecedented discretionary autonomy. photos, e-mails, everything on your mobile phone are targets that pegasus uses for social, military and political purposes. pegasus, like any other advanced spyware, is a serious threat to the rule of law. as recalled by our spanish colleagues, when a government is threatened in its constitutional integrity, this government has the right to defend itself against these threats. spying is what we were taught not to do in school, yet knowing ahead of a potential threat is the best possible survival strategy. pegasus could become the vile deformation of a technology useful to few and which lives thanks to our daily lives. an excess that, i must say, has teased global social realities, albeit in a different way. someone has even spoken in this chamber. the work of the pega commission will be very complicated. on the table are the freedoms of 500 million europeans, their governments and the challenges of the future between search algorithms and ultra-artificial intelligence. however, the time has come to ask ourselves essential questions: how much is our freedom worth?

paragraph: mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the abuse of software such as pegasus for espionage is only part of a much greater threat to the fundamental rights of european citizens. seduced by the luxury of smartphones and home appliances that can be given voice commands, we have allowed private individuals to create the largest spy program ever seen. every day, 500 million europeans are unknowingly monitored and plundered of myriads of personal data by companies that analyze their behaviour, tastes and opinions for commercial, but also social and political purposes. advances in artificial intelligence and the metaverse are leading to solutions to enable full control and predictions over people's feelings, thoughts and actions to determine their every choice. many think that surveillance is just a tool of capitalism to maximize its profits. but the reality is that governments and public institutions are increasingly using it as a weapon to control and limit the freedom of their citizens, just like in china. a nightmare that we thought existed only in science fiction films and which is now a reality. a nightmare against which this parliament must fight to avoid turning europeans into guinea pigs and europe into a horrible big brother.

intervention_header_en: Franco Roberti, draftsman of the opinion of the Committee on Legal Affairs
subject_of_business_title: Commission’s 2021 Rule of Law Report (debate)
paragraph: madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, respect for the rule of law must be our absolute political and institutional priority. for this reason it is regrettable that the passivity of the bodies which have the duty to supervise the protection of the rights of european citizens has led the situation to deteriorate to such a worrying degree in hungary and poland. our task is to defuse, with regulatory and persuasive tools, the attacks, including in the media, against magistrates, journalists, ngos and lgbt people, who unfortunately circulate insistently on our continent. the rule of law is the foundation of the european union, we are also seeing it these days, and it strengthens citizens' trust in the institutions. however, it is fragile, because it is based only on the rule of the law, it claims the exclusive rule of the law. this is possible only when the powers of the state are separated and well balanced, so that none of them can overwhelm the others. other indispensable conditions for guaranteeing equality and the protection of citizens' rights before the law are the efficiency of judicial systems and the independence of magistrates, since the efficient management of justice can only be achieved where independent judges and prosecutors operate, that there is availability of adequate human and financial resources and permanent and professional training of the magistrates themselves: we are also seeing this in recent days with the topic under discussion of the application of artificial intelligence to judicial systems. furthermore, and finally, an efficient and transparent public administration, with codes and management procedures such as to prevent illicit conduct, is extremely important for an effective fight against corruption; we must aim at strengthening measures aimed at limiting the duration and costs of disputes and trials, as well as the funds available for legal assistance and means of redress for needy citizens such as to favor access to justice for all.

subject_of_business_title: Minimum level of taxation for multinational groups (debate)
paragraph: dear chairperson, the world is further and further away from economic balance and fairness. on the one hand, corporations led by investment funds such as avantgard, blackrock, state street and others, and on the other hand, from year to year, from crisis to crisis, increasingly indebted states, indebted to banks whose owners are again these funds. in recent years, we have seen a large allocation of capital flowing towards the top. corporations climb a mountain of capital, and countries climb a mountain of debt. with the help of algorithms and artificial intelligence and supported by enormous money printing, the funds turned into monsters and even started buying private family houses. if these trends continue, in a few decades there will be nothing left to buy. democracy itself is threatened. this directive on ensuring a global minimum level of taxation for multinational groups is a feeble attempt to strike this balance. i am the first to tax the big ones. they have to give back part of what they get because the system works on cooperation. facebook has no value without your scrolling. it's time for a change and all the subcontractors in this system deserve dividends, not just the team from blackrock and their ilk.

subject_of_business_title: Digital Services Act - Digital Markets Act (debate)
paragraph: mrs. chairman! new technology has always changed the world. it has created fantastic benefits and lots of opportunities, but with new opportunities come new challenges. this also applies to our mediation services. the digital has simultaneously made the distance between us shorter, but also dug the ditches deeper. you can write to people from all over the world, but judging by the debate on social media, it's all too easy to forget that it's people you're writing to. the algorithms on social media all too often promote hatred and division rather than hope and unity, and disinformation spreads like wildfire and reinforces echo chambers that reduce dialogue and understanding and challenge our democracy and our social model. and dangerous and illegal products find their way all too easily to european consumers via online marketplaces that take advantage of loopholes in our legislation. for far too long, there have been far too few rules in our online world. digital has developed somewhat into a wild west, where the biggest players decide the rules of the game. but with the dsa, there's a new sheriff in town. now we tame the tech giants, give users better rights and look after our democracy. we open the black box of the algorithms so that we can look into the engine of the platforms' money machine. from now on, it will be a requirement that the largest platforms must risk assess their algorithms. does the algorithm spread illegal content? does it promote eating disorders and self-harm? does it promote disinformation and conspiracy theories? if there is a risk that this affects us negatively, then the platforms must rectify the problem, just as they must provide access to their algorithms to authorities, to the eu commission as well as to researchers and ngos, so that they can contribute to to look over the shoulder of the tech giants. we demand that the platforms take responsibility for their algorithms. algorithms and not just neutral mathematical formulas. they are designed to keep us engaged on the platform for as long as possible. it is a central part of the platform's money model. the longer we are online, the more data the platforms collect about us and the more money they can make from targeting advertising to us. now we are dealing with the platform's business model. they may make money, but not at the expense of our health or our social model. first and foremost, we prohibit targeted advertising to children and minors based on their personal data. the platforms must not have a financial incentive to collect massive amounts of data about our children and young people and potentially sell them on. and by making this ban, we actually make it safer for children and young people to be online, and it also gives us parents more peace of mind. next, we prohibit the platforms from using sensitive information about users, regardless of age, to target advertising. and we prohibit dark patterns that manipulate us into making certain choices in various dialog boxes. and now the platforms' money machine has to give way to democracy. democracy must set the framework for the tech giants, not the other way around. this also applies to our online marketplaces. today, it is all too easy to click illegal and dangerous products into the virtual shopping cart. it undermines consumer protection and product safety and is therefore pleased that we have come closer to equating online shopping with offline shopping. in future, the online marketplaces must, among other things, know their sellers, and they must carry out random checks of the goods offered on the platform, where the goods must be held up against existing databases and illegal products. it's no secret that i would have liked to go further myself, but i think we're taking a good first step here. and now i want to switch to english. i would like to thank all the colleagues who made this new legislation possible. thanks to all my shadow rapporteurs and all the associated committees for the cooperation, and a big thanks to the eu commission and also to the french presidency for a fruitful and constructive negotiation. it wasn't always easy, but i do believe that we can all be proud of the outcome. and finally, i would also like to thank our very hard-working and dedicated staff, and especially mathias, alexandra and atanaska for their hard work. they've been working night and day to help us make this legislation possible. with the dsa, we will create a safer, fairer and more transparent online environment. we take back control from the tech giants and we establish a level playing field for businesses. i think that we can all be very proud of the agreement, and i do hope that a big majority here tomorrow will vote in favor of the dsa. with that, we have made history and we will make the online world much safer.

subject_of_business_title: Mental health in the digital world of work (debate)
paragraph: mr president, mr commissioner, unfortunately we have had to go through an unprecedented health crisis to become aware of a problem that has been brewing in europe for some time. another type of pandemic, more silent, that affects the mental health of people, especially the most vulnerable groups, such as women and young people, and that is directly related to precariousness at work, job instability and digitalization. and it is that, when we talk about the digital transition, we also have to talk about the consequences that a misuse of artificial intelligence systems and automation have on the health and safety of workers, including their mental health. mass control and surveillance, the increase in hours worked, the lack of clarity and transparency in labor relations, the absence of separation between professional life and private life or the clear violation of privacy rights are just some of the the examples that increase psychosocial risks and have a negative impact on the mental health of workers, but also on society in general, due to the high cost of public spending that they cause and an increase in the risk of social exclusion and poverty in the medium term . it is for these psychosocial risks for the prevention and management of which we have been demanding a directive for some time, as well as the recognition that certain mental disorders, such as anxiety, depression and burnout, are associated with working conditions and must be recognized as occupational diseases. is the moment to act. i am sure, commissioner, that you share the opinion that it is necessary to legislate and ensure that the employer assumes its responsibility in protecting the mental health of workers. the agreement reached last week on teleworking and the right to disconnect is a step forward. we hope that the signatories are up to the task and that we will soon find new regulatory frameworks on artificial intelligence in the workplace and on the prevention and management of psychosocial risks.

subject_of_business_title: Mental health in the digital world of work (debate)
paragraph: mr president, dear rapporteur, dear commissioner, imagine going to work at zara. you enter the shop in the morning, pick up a tablet, put an earpiece in and, for hours on end, you are tracked and have an algorithm tell you exactly what you need to do. and if you don’t do it fast enough, because a customer asks you something, this might lead to not getting your contract renewed. it might sound futuristic, but this is already the reality for a growing group of workers. bosses are treating them like robots and new technologies allow them to constantly surveil them and micro-manage people, under huge time pressure. but constant monitoring also happens to office workers and civil servants. with the help of software, your boss can know exactly how many emails you send, how many keystrokes you make per hour, and even where your gaze is fixed. in a world like this, workers can’t thrive. the stress of being surveyed and the loss of autonomy leads to lower wellbeing of workers and impacts their mental health. we urgently need rules for the entire labour market to ban surveillance and constant monitoring of workers and regulate algorithmic management for all. and i’m happy to report calls for this. i’m now looking at the commission to take action and make our workplaces safer, healthier and happier again.

subject_of_business_title: Access to water as a human right – the external dimension (debate)
paragraph: madam president, many of us europeans cannot even imagine what life without water means. however, we all have the experience of complications if the water in our homes and apartments were to be disconnected, even for just one day. unfortunately, the situation in the world is dire. billions of people, especially from third world countries, don't have the same thing that we do, they simply don't have access to drinking water. if we do not change the effects of global warming, climate change, the consequences of which we are already experiencing today, some parts of the world will literally dry up. in front of the gates of europe, there will be millions of migrants who will not beg for a better life in the union, but for a glass of drinking water. however, we also have a problem with access to drinking water directly in the european union, where millions of roma living in poor roma settlements drink water from the stream. we cannot, on the one hand, be a leader in the field of digitization or artificial intelligence and, on the other hand, turn a blind eye to the millions of europeans and billions of people in the world who cannot get a glass of clean and safe water all day long.

paragraph: mr president, algorithms do exactly what they are supposed to do, and that is dangerous. imagine: a tax authority is instructed by the government to crack down on fraud and this must be done as efficiently as possible by means of automation. according to the tax authorities, it is most efficient to deal with people with a low income or migration background. based on this, the service decides to build such an algorithm. and this algorithm does exactly what it is supposed to do. it finds so-called fraudsters, especially those with a migration background or low income. for example, the dutch government destroyed the lives of 70,000 children and their parents. no one could explain to their parents what was going on or why certain decisions were made. civil servants blindly followed the computers, because algorithms must be right. an important lesson from the benefits scandal is that digitization without standards and rules can have life-devastating consequences. fortunately, we see this in europe. with the first ai law in the world, i want to ensure that a new surcharge affair can never happen again, but then we have to dare to take action. as a negotiator for the ai ​​regulation, i am committed to strengthening human rights in the use of algorithms. we must prohibit the use of algorithms to label people as criminals or fraudsters based on their personal data. we must ensure that systems do not discriminate. we must introduce a human rights test, so that it is mandatory to look at how we use algorithms. people deserve transparency and the systems should be designed in such a way that we can see what is going wrong. and people should never, ever again be left empty-handed in front of a computer, with a strong right to explanation and mandatory human supervision. let us learn lessons from this terrible scandal and intervene now with ambitious rules.

paragraph: mr. president, in recent decades there has been a transition from the promise of the future that digital emancipation implied to a kind of new civilization based on the algorithmic organization of society. companies and administrations around the world hide behind a technological mind so that their decisions are more objective and efficient. but in that mind lie the prejudices and aberrations that they try to hide. the machines that we ourselves create are no better than we are, because most of the data available to them is biased and reproduces discriminatory patterns for which no one is usually responsible. predictive policing, the allocation of social benefits or the collection of biometric data, for example, are racialized and the structural discrimination they generate hinders the access of certain people to rights, goods and services. artificial intelligence reinforces the privileged place of whites and marginalizes blacks and gypsies, for example, in such a way that it plays a key role in power relations. behind an appearance of neutrality from the point of view of the machines, there are people who are persecuted for who they are and not for what they do, although many of them neither know nor would know how to point to the guilty. it is clear that all this could be put to good use, but in europe we do not have the instruments to demand it. from parliament we have called for many measures: incorporate the intersectional approach in algorithms, collect data disaggregated by racial and ethnic origin, prohibit racial profiling, carry out human rights impact studies, implement compliance controls and human supervision or accountability. however, we are still running after our own shadow.

paragraph: mr president, commissioner, colleagues, the dutch childcare benefit scandal epitomises what the former un special rapporteur on extreme poverty and human rights, philip alston, calls a digital welfare dystopia. it specifically targets poorer citizens rather than rich people evading taxes, where in case of fraud, the sums to recover would be much higher. the system is racist. there is no simple redress and the system targets people who can’t afford to – or are unlikely to – go to court. the principle of innocent until proven guilty is overturned. innocent people are treated like criminals. fundamental principles of the rule of law are overturned. artificial intelligence systems targeting people need very, very strong safeguards and these safeguards are currently not provided by the ai act. and here we need to change, we need to improve the ai act. and furthermore, public administrations should support low-income citizens rather than harassing them and giving millions to big-tech companies to build what virginia eubanks calls the digital poorhouse.

paragraph: mr president, we live in a world where digital surveillance has become common. cctv and face recognition are part of our daily lives, whether we want it or not. however, we fail to understand and address how these already uncomfortable circumstances can become very dangerous for members of racialised groups. there is ample evidence that artificial intelligence tools heavily discriminate against black people and people of colour in general, and women of colour in particular. after all, ai is built by humans and deployed in systems and institutions that have been marked by entrenched discrimination, from law enforcement to housing, to the workplace, to our financial systems. and this racial bias is even in the data used to train the ai data that is often discriminatory or unrepresentative for people of colour, women and other marginalised groups and can rear its head throughout the ai’s design, development, implementation and use. therefore, i want to state that the monitoring of racial bias as proposed in this report is not enough. we need a clear directive that specifically states that institutional racism is unlawful. only then we can make sure that victims of unlawful discrimination get justice.

paragraph: mr president, i feel compelled to come back to the stages of this dossier, so little debate has it given rise to, whereas it contains a concentrate of the debates that drive us in this house: artificial intelligence, mass surveillance, indiscriminate collection of data, including non-suspects, exchange of such data with third countries and private companies. the starting point of the reform is the discovery by the european data protection board of the massive analysis of personal data by the agency outside any legal framework. the commission then presents us with a reform that legalizes illegal practices and considerably strengthens the powers of the agency at its request. all this without evaluation or impact study. dear colleagues, this is far from being a technical file. the exchange of data with private parties and third states has consequences in terms of fundamental rights and data protection. funding of europol projects by third countries may have consequences in terms of foreign interference. giving executive power to the agency to insert security alerts directly into the schengen information system is an eminently political question. authorizing it to develop research and innovation projects, artificial intelligence for experimental and police purposes, and to promote facial recognition technologies when our parliament opposed them a fortnight ago, are highly political issues. ensuring the protection of fundamental rights is an eminently political issue. however, faced with the expansion of the missions and powers entrusted to the agency, we do not find the essential safeguards and independent mechanisms of democratic control. ladies and gentlemen, europol must ensure the safety of all citizens and without weakening their fundamental rights. i therefore urge you to oppose this text, these developments which do not make europe a safer continent for all.

subject_of_business_title: An intellectual property action plan to support the EU’s recovery and resilience (short presentation)
paragraph: dear mr. president, dear colleagues! without innovative solutions, we cannot meet our upcoming goals of the green deal, digitization and industry 4.0. it is therefore important to strengthen intellectual property rights such as patents, designs and trademarks and to improve their enforcement. this report identifies existing problem situations and proposes solutions. for example, the efficient use of intellectual property rights can help corona-stricken companies get back on their feet, making them more competitive and resilient. but only nine percent of smes use such rights across europe. we must therefore support smes with advice, financial resources and user-friendly application procedures to better protect their intellectual property. the uniform patent will result in immense administrative simplification and also cost savings. this makes it possible to obtain patent protection in 25 member states with one application. expensive, parallel lawsuits are prevented by the unified patent court and at the same time legal certainty is increased. for these reasons, all member states involved should make increased efforts to ratify the convention on the unified patent jurisdiction so that the unitary patent package can finally enter into force. furthermore, the enforcement of intellectual property rights needs to be significantly improved. counterfeit goods result in around 416,000 direct job losses every year. counterfeit products can not only significantly affect the health of citizens - for example in the case of counterfeit masks. they are also often linked to organized crime. it is all the worse that brand and product piracy is rarely uncovered. therefore, on the one hand, increased cooperation between the national enforcement authorities with euipo, europol, eurojust and olaf is necessary so that detection and punishment are made more efficient. on the other hand, member states should provide for effective and dissuasive penalties for the production and distribution of counterfeits. and last but not least, technologies such as artificial intelligence or blockchain can be used much more for detection. another important point is the protection of geographical indications. the product with its regional characteristics, the production and the know-how are protected. there is already a european protection system for agricultural products, with which - if you will forgive me and allow the regional connection - the thuringian bratwurst, for example, is protected. not only do consumers benefit from this protection system, as they recognize authentic products across europe, but it also contributes to the preservation of cultural and regional heritage. we call for the existing protection system for agricultural products to become more precise and effective, with less red tape. we also think that such a sui generis protection system should also be created for non-agricultural products, so that regional smes that produce handicrafts and the like should also benefit from such protection throughout europe. finally, a heartfelt thank you goes to all the shadow rapporteurs and their staff. we worked together on what i think is an excellent text.

subject_of_business_title: An intellectual property action plan to support the EU’s recovery and resilience (short presentation)
paragraph: mr president, first, we would like to thank parliament for its report on an intellectual property action plan to support the eu’s recovery and resilience. the report has well captured the importance of a balanced protection of intellectual property rights for the eu’s recovery and resilience, but also for the european economy and in particular smes. as requested by parliament, the commission will step up efforts in the areas of smes and ip management. the commission and the european union intellectual property office will launch a new european sme fund for the next three years – 2022 to 2024 – and this fund will offer more services such as the reimbursement of international trademark and national registration fees for patents. on patents, the commission is pleased with the strong support expressed by parliament on the rolling—out of the unitary patent system, which is expected to start operating by the end of next year, 2022. the commission will continue working on improving the european patent framework. first, the commission agrees that the equitable distribution of vaccines around the globe is essential for effectively combating the spread of covid—19 and that, to address supply chains, the way forward is to facilitate cross—border trade and support technology transfer based on the voluntary licensing of ip rights. the commission also stands ready to take the necessary steps to ensure access to critical ip in times of crisis, including by facilitating the use of compulsory licensing in the absence of voluntary licenses. second, to correct the fragmentation issues identified by the european parliament report as regards the need for a unitary supplementary protection certificate to be on par with the unitary patent, the commission has announced a legislative initiative for next year. the commission will analyse the most adequate institutional actors for the examination and granting. finally, as regards standard essential patents, the commission welcomes the european parliament’s call for enhancing transparency and fostering good faith licensing negotiations. the reform announced by the commission will aim at addressing those issues. in the field of geographical indications, we take note of the call for simplification and not to overburden farmers with administration. in this regard, we aim to make the scheme more attractive and accessible to farmers across the union and boost protection of geographical indications on the internet, in particular. for non—agricultural products or so—called craft and industrial products, the commission welcomes parliament’s support for the establishment of efficient and transparent europeansui generisprotection of geographical indications at european level for craft and industrial products. let me reassure you that the commission is working at full steam on finalising a thorough impact assessment, which is a prerequisite to a proposal in this field. next year, we will also present proposals on designs to modernise design protection systems, to support the digital and green transitions and become more accessible and efficient, in particular for smes. one of our main objectives is to complete the single market for repair spare parts to the benefit of competition and lower prices for consumers. let me also reassure you that the fight against counterfeit goods, such as pharmaceutical and medical devices and toys, remains very high on the commission’s agenda. counterfeit goods not only have negative economic impacts on european economic growth, they also mislead consumers and puts their health and safety at risk and could be detrimental to the environment. organised crime groups are also heavily involved in counterfeiting. the eu toolbox against counterfeiting is a unique opportunity for the eu to single out an overarching, effective policy for all relevant stakeholders and public authorities, to curb counterfeiting both online and offline. the toolbox will build on the existing and future horizontal european initiatives, in particular the digital services act, the eu strategy to tackle organised crime and the european customs action plan. it will also build on existing industry—led initiatives. the european parliament report highlights new challenges for ip policymaking, such as the use of artificial intelligence technologies in supporting the creation of new designs, medicines or vaccines. while we believe that the overall system is fit for these challenges, the commission will continue to assess the issues presented by parliament. the commission welcomes parliament’s call for the transposition of the directive on copyright in the digital single market without delay. the swift implementation of the new directive will benefit creative industries and citizens and ensure more fairness and clarity when copyrighted content is used online. so far, only a few member states have communicated national transposition measures, and the commission has opened infringement procedures. the commission also welcomes parliament’s support for the review of the database directive. the commission has announced a review alongside the upcoming data act. through a targeted review of the database directive, the commission wants to make sure that the directive will not pose an obstacle to data use and sharing, primarily by clarifying the status of machine—generated data. so i’d like to thank you again for the thorough assessment of our ip action plan and the valuable and supportive comments you provided. we are looking forward to continuing our excellent collaboration with you on this ambitious agenda that we have set for the european ip framework.

subject_of_business_title: The outcome of the EU-US Trade and Technology Council (TTC) (debate)
paragraph: mr president, vice-presidents, ladies and gentlemen, having an open forum for discussions with the united states after years of closure and misunderstanding is a great step forward, for which i congratulate the commission. however, i have some questions on which i hope the vice-presidents will want to express themselves, because almost a month after the first meeting i continue to wonder about the true nature of this trade and technology council. is this a forum to mediate on thorny legislative issues, or simply a place to discuss? is it a tool for exchanging ideas or do you want a basis for a future transatlantic agreement? in short, if the commitments made are not binding, as has been repeatedly reiterated, then what is the level of commitment of the partners, especially vis-à-vis some collective challenges such as measures to limit emissions or artificial intelligence ? and finally, what role does the commission see for parliament in all of this? as we have not been particularly involved in this forum so far.

subject_of_business_title: The outcome of the EU-US Trade and Technology Council (TTC) (debate)
paragraph: mr president, i was also in washington last week as chair of the special committee on artificial intelligence in a digital age (aida) and with colleagues from across this aisle – an outreach mission, which we had wanted to do since the inception of the aida mandate. our aim was to set the basis of a dialogue with the us congress on artificial intelligence in the impact of frontier tech on the world of tomorrow. but the launch of the trade and technology council (ttc) just weeks before opened up a broader perspective of transatlantic leadership on technology, on a shared realisation that the future of our relationship will be more and more dominated by tech cooperation, by what we will accomplish in converging standards, research, data governance and on developing mutually beneficial projects. and i congratulate the commission for the launch and for how the ttc was organised. there are many commonalities at the heart ttc: common values, same challenges and opportunities, and most importantly, we see the geopolitics of technology in the same way. but there are also differences, which we need to acknowledge and learn to work with. we see the urgency in the form of regulating and digital platforms differently. we also have a different approach to how to prepare standards. we are more top-down while they work more bottom-up, co-creating together with the industry. we must accept these different regulatory cultures and in fact take the best from each other. i think we can and should work more with the business sector like the americans do, while we can share with them the very good work that you the commission has done in preparing the legislative landscape on digital issues. and most importantly, and we have made this point very forcefully, we must build a parliamentary dimension of the ttc, one where we can come together as legislators and exercise oversight and political guidance on the evolution of the council.

paragraph: chairman, i think we all agree that after trump we need to work with the current biden administration on a positive agenda for the future. this means not only solving problems, for example in the areas of steel and aluminium, but also setting a positive agenda on issues that are important for our future. the eu-us trade and technology council is therefore very important. we all know that technology such as artificial intelligence can be used for the success of our future and the well-being of our people. however, this technology can also be used for a variety of other purposes. it is therefore essential that democratic societies such as the united states and europe cooperate in this area and not leave it to societies that use the relevant technology for espionage or large-scale surveillance of their populations. this democratic control must also be able to take place from the european parliament. this is very important to further strengthen support.

paragraph: mr president, today is 11 november, it’s remembrance day, the day that weapons stood still in europe. i think it is time to remember that, because working together on trade and technology is also about peace, not only about the economy. it will help us win an international competition with china and neutralise its ever-expanding power on the world stage. it is time we fought together unfair trade practices such as theft of intellectual property. it is time we established clear and strategic standards for the use of artificial intelligence so that we have to fight human rights violations through mass surveillance. the covid-19 pandemic has shown us how fragile the global production systems are, and we need to build resilient and sustainable supply chains for tomorrow. i’d like to paraphrase the 1992 us elections by saying ‘it’s not only the economy, stupid, it’s also peace’.

paragraph: mr president, madam vice president, the united states, by history and values, is a natural ally of europe. our economies are already very intertwined, but the need to strengthen that relationship has become greater as the world has become more global; the trade and technology council has opened up new expectations to strengthen this alliance, especially in an area as decisive as digitization. i want to influence five areas in which it is urgent to develop a common effort: seeking solutions to the semiconductor supply crisis; promote the development of artificial intelligence that generates confidence; develop policies and coordinated actions on cybersecurity; work in an area as crucial, as decisive, as standards, and move towards a transatlantic data space that allows our researchers and our companies to take advantage of their full potential. a few days ago, a delegation from the committee on industry, research and energy was in washington, d.c., and the renewed interest there was evident: madam vice president, this momentum cannot be lost, and the council of commerce and technology has to start give results.

paragraph: dialogue with the united states on major global challenges such as cybersecurity, artificial intelligence or data protection is essential. it is through collaboration with our atlantic partners that we will be able to carve out a leading role in the international technological scenario. however, there are issues to reflect on. although you find it positive that there have been openings on the subject of duties on steel and aluminum, i believe that they would only benefit some exporters and would risk aggravating the supply problem, now characteristic of the post-pandemic era. then we must not be hypocritical: a case like the one that emerged in recent days involving german engines sold to china for its military ships makes us appear inconsistent and risks nullifying important actions such as the visit of our delegates to taiwan. i hope that the next meetings will also be characterized by collaboration, for our interests and to face the growing market power of china. finally, i reiterate what i have already said in the past: dialogue with the united states must be carried out on an ongoing and coherent basis, untied by democratic or republican fans.

subject_of_business_title: A pharmaceutical strategy for Europe (debate)
paragraph: madam president, madam commissioner, madam speaker, how many citizens were familiar with the messenger rna technique two years ago? or who knew who biotech was a few months before the pandemic? the importance of the pharmaceutical sector and biotechnological innovation is beyond any debate. its success in recent months has gone hand in hand with ours, and the development of a vaccine in record time, which has freed us from the worst of the pandemic, has not been the result of chance: it has been years of research far from the spotlights, close collaboration and public-private investment and the work of some of the best researchers in the world vaccine ingredients. in this house we have discussed talent, innovation and technology on numerous occasions. today, with this pharmaceutical strategy, we are taking another step to protect the companies and researchers who have shown their faces and to recover the competitiveness of a strategic industry in which europe was once the leader, because, today, we are very far from being autonomous in the pharmaceutical field: only 60% of the medicines we consume are produced in the european union and 80% of the active ingredients come from china and india. to resume this leadership we need, first of all, to provide the industry with sufficient legal certainty to encourage it to invest the time and enormous resources necessary to develop new medicines. and protecting innovative smes is essential because, after all, for many years their only asset has been intellectual property. we must also bet on the technologies of the future, on nanotechnology, on gene therapy, on artificial intelligence and on creating a european health data space that reflects the excellence of our health systems. my second point brings me to drugs that are not profitable, such as pediatric drugs or those that treat diseases like als. from europe, we do not forget those who suffer from these diseases, and this is where it is necessary to solve the deficiencies of the market, bet on a system of incentives that works and, above all, support research with public investment. let's use recovery plans, cohesion funds and innovation programs like horizon europe. of course, we have to put the citizen at the center of all this debate. two-speed europe must be avoided at all costs. a very illustrative example: a patient today, in northern europe, takes on average between 100 and 200 days to have access to a new medicine; that same patient in eastern europe would take between 600 and 1,000 days. we have to tackle this problem because, in healthcare, these disparities cost lives. finally, this strategy must serve to learn from the mistakes of the past, to make sure that we are prepared to face future crises, and now is the time for the commission to come up with an early warning mechanism to avoid medicine shortages and that we bet for administrative solutions that have proven to be helpful, such as quick approvals or joint purchasing of critical materials. let's continue to show that the european union provides solutions. dear colleagues, europe is the continent with the longest life expectancy, a great achievement that says a lot about our healthcare and pharmaceutical systems. it is essential to ensure the sustainability of this system and that the next health crisis finds us with our homework done. this is the best favor we can do for future generations.

subject_of_business_title: European framework for employees' participation rights and the revision of the European Works Council Directive (debate)
paragraph: mr president, ladies and gentlemen, dear colleagues, commissioner! it is a pleasure for me to speak in this house today on an issue that is very, very close to my heart and, i believe, to most of those in this room. and i am also pleased, dear nicolas, that you are taking part in our debate today, because that is an important signal from the commission. we all know that we really are living in a time of quite some upheaval. and we see that digitization is progressing in many work areas, that work steps and jobs are being replaced by automation, that the role of artificial intelligence is increasing, also in the awarding or evaluation of work. the list could be greatly expanded here. at the same time, we agreed on a green deal, with the paris agreement we really set ourselves big goals. and this, like digitization, involves enormous transformations. and it is also the case that they cause concerns and fears in certain regions and also in certain sectors, because we know that millions of people are affected by these transformations. we have also talked a lot about democracy in the past few months, especially in connection with the future conference - how important it is that we involve people and involve them in really creating solutions and helping to shape their own future. and of course that also applies to the world of work. and that is why it is so important, as in the report, that we give employees a voice, that they participate in decisions, and that is – i would like to emphasize once again – part of the dna of the social market economy and thus also part of the dna of social europe . and there are good examples in europe that both sides, capital and labour, benefit from the fact that companies are better off if they involve employees early and appropriately. for example, last week i had the opportunity to speak to the european works council at unilever. the company recently signed a european framework agreement on the future of work with the european works council. and there are two remarkable things that i would like to emphasize here: one is that this agreement once again underlines that the pursuit of pure profit, without regard for the employees, creates companies that are not sustainable. and what goes further with this agreement is that it provides for really concrete further training plans for the employees with retraining, with further training, with an individual right to advice, specifically where we have digital disruptions, where new technologies are used. and that gives the employees security in the face of change and the opportunity to participate in the change. and that's why it's worth seeing - and many studies show this - that companies are more sustainable and come through crises better if they involve their employees. they also educate more. when it comes to female employment, too, one can see that there is more equal pay for equal work or work of equal value than in other companies. and that's why it's important that we strengthen this voice, and that's where the report comes in. that is why, in view of these really massive challenges, we are calling on the commission to take a horizontal approach and to present a european framework guideline for participation, for the codetermination rights of employees, but also to revise the european works council guideline and codetermination within the framework of the european company . we need minimum standards in all areas that cannot be circumvented, regardless of whether you are restructuring the company, changing the form of your company or moving your company headquarters to another country. we want to enable employees to actively shape these transitions and not just be the object of these changes. we also want to make companies more sustainable. and i am therefore asking for broad support for this report, so that it really sends a strong signal to the commission to submit proposals here before the end of this legislative period. and i would also like to thank the shadow rapporteurs from the bottom of my heart for their constructive work. we negotiated really hard on the matter, but we found compromises on everything, and it is therefore good that the committee really did support this report with a large majority. and i think the millions of workers we have here in europe are waiting for a signal that we will say: yes, we will have workers' rights, we will strengthen participation. and we will get through this change, this transformation, together and ensure that in the end no one is left behind and that this does not just remain an empty phrase, but that we create the instruments and the processes for this, and where they are , let's strengthen and improve them. on that note, thank you very much.

subject_of_business_title: European framework for employees' participation rights and the revision of the European Works Council Directive (debate)
paragraph: mr. president, much has been said in recent years about the need to move towards a sustainable and inclusive transition in europe, but we continue to see multinationals that relocate and de-industrialise, impoverishing entire regions after having taken advantage of public aid for years: this is not just sustainability. to fight against inequalities and face an unfair economic model, we must ensure greater participation of workers in their organizations and strengthen democracy at work: this will ensure profitable companies and a return on investment and public aid in the form higher wages and better working conditions. this report is therefore key to ensuring that workers' rights are respected in restructuring processes, to combat instability in the labor market and to end existing cases of exploitation and abuse. we need a legislative framework on information, consultation and participation in the workplace that strengthens social dialogue and brings us closer to the target of up to 90% collective bargaining coverage by 2030; that guarantees the participation of workers in the boards of directors, respecting, in addition, parity, and that ensures that the use of artificial intelligence in the workplace is done in a manner agreed with the unions and ensuring that the benefits of the increase in productivity are shared fairly. in order to achieve truly sustainable development and social progress, social agents, political parties and civil society have to be united and defend solidarity at work: guarantee the right to information and consultation of employees, give them a voice, it is essential to build a equitable, egalitarian and fair economic model. the rights of workers to organize, to be represented, to freedom of assembly and association and to collectively demand reforms in their workplaces are fundamental aspects of the european project and basic principles of a social model that we must defend and reinforce now. and in the future.

subject_of_business_title: Question Time (VPC/HR) - Strengthening the Trans-Atlantic ties in an ever challenging multilateral world
paragraph: mr president, high representative, ladies and gentlemen, in this century we know that a single national security strategy can do little, that a european security strategy is not enough: we need an ever stronger transatlantic security strategy. and in the context of the transatlantic dialogue, we know that for our greatest and most important ally, the united states, the concept has become a matter of national security according to which, whoever will be at the helm of enabling and emerging technologies, from energy to biomedical sciences, from artificial intelligence to quantum computing, it will emerge as a world leader and be able to wield soft power and hard power better than others. so i ask you: is there perfect harmony between europe and the united states in this doctrinal assessment? do you find weaknesses, vulnerabilities in implementing this doctrine?

subject_of_business_title: Conclusions of the European Council meeting of 23-24 March 2023 (debate)
paragraph: madam president, mr president charles michel, for general macarthur, the battles lost can be summed up in two words: too late. for two decades now, our dependence on china has grown steadily. initially confined to the role of craftsman of a cheap economy and low-end products, the chinese empire has now become a global must. it is, since we were talking about energy, a must for the manufacture of wind turbines and photovoltaic panels, which the european union has almost made the only pillars of its energy transition. it has become a leading predator for the most strategic european companies. the spectacular takeover in 2016 of the german kuka, leader in industrial robotics, of the port of piraeus in greece the same year, are only illustrious symbols and perhaps the tree that hides the forest. it is one of the fiercest competitors in the knowledge economy and the technologies of tomorrow, from artificial intelligence to electric cars. carlos tavares, the highly respected boss of stellantis, recently lamented that the red carpet had been rolled out to chinese manufacturers. faced with this reality, the time is no longer for observation but for action. we must preserve our public markets, which are now more open than those of china, favor european companies in public procurement, protect our strategic assets, invest in both innovation and education. the protection of our sovereignty also requires an in-depth investigation into the suspicions of espionage which weigh on tiktok, its links with the chinese power and the manipulation of the precious data of european users by hands which are not ours. europe is not destined to remain the prey of beijing. our future, our freedom, our sovereignty, our independence and our power are at stake.

subject_of_business_title: Roadmap on a Social Europe: two years after Porto (debate)
paragraph: mr president, commissioner, minister, ladies and gentlemen, two years after the porto social summit, we are faced with new challenges, but we are faced with the same debate: how to build a more social europe? we still have a lot of work ahead of us if we want to live in a europe where people can afford decent housing and pay the bills, a europe in which poverty is reduced and access to a quality labour market is enhanced. once again in porto, another opportunity opens up to set new objectives and design mechanisms, which must be binding, to combat all this challenge. because to promote inclusion and fight poverty, ensure people's well-being and create safe and well-equipped workplaces, legislation is needed. the creation of a directive on adequate minimum incomes in europe must be a priority in this new agenda in porto, to meet the poverty reduction commitments already set at the last summit, in addition to helping vulnerable groups to access a good job. and, on the other hand, if wages and working conditions should be on the list of priorities, this includes health and, in particular, mental health. we have already debated a lot in this house about the need to regulate teleworking, guarantee the right to disconnect and curb the mass control and surveillance of workers through the misuse of artificial intelligence. all these factors, as a result of digitalization, increase psychosocial risks and have a negative impact on the mental health of workers. this new roadmap in porto can fill legal gaps and also advocate for directives to prevent psychosocial risks in the workplace and regulate algorithmic management and the use of artificial intelligence in workplaces. ultimately, we have work to do to ensure that social is the guiding principle of all policy and guides any transition, whether green or digital.

subject_of_business_title: Foreign interference in all democratic processes in the European Union, including disinformation - Election integrity and resilience build-up towards European elections 2024 (debate)
paragraph: madam president, dear colleagues, today it is my great honour to present my second report on foreign interference in all democratic processes in the european union, including disinformation. i often hear that democracy around the world is in retreat. i would say that is an incorrect statement. democracy is not simply in retreat; democracy is under attack. in today’s intervention, i would like to especially focus on two overarching aims of the report. first, link our work in the ing2 committee with following up the implementation of the recommendations of the first report, which was approved last year. second, we must examine the issues under the mandate of our committee vis-a-vis russia’s ongoing brutal war against ukraine and to build on the lessons learned. our assessment shows that we have significantly increased our situational awareness, and several necessary steps have been launched and progress has been attained (digital services act, democracy defence package is on the way, growing expertise acquired). however, in view of the upcoming eu elections in 2024, we still should urge for stronger measures and more coordination to protect our european democracy. allow me to outline some of the priorities from our report, which would make a significant difference in making our union more resilient. first of all, we need to move beyond a reactive approach centred on fact-checking, debunking, etc., and instead focus on resilience-building and ‘vaccination’ of our societies against disinformation. therefore, we need to establish a dedicated eu programme to invest in our democracy in a sustainable way. it will not give a solution tomorrow and it will be expensive, but it is certainly a worthwhile long-term investment. another important conclusion of our report is that in tackling disinformation, the eu is still suffering from a fragmented approach, without a clear coordination mechanism and goals. we simply cannot afford splintering our resources when our democracy is at stake. third, we should also greatly raise the costs for perpetrators. therefore, i reiterate that the toolbox of the eu countermeasures should include a specific sanctions regime on foreign information manipulation and interference. russia’s imperial war of aggression against ukraine has clearly exposed the interconnection between hostile information warfare, weaponisation of energy, attacks on critical infrastructure, and threats to the eu, to our immediate neighbourhood, as well as to global security and stability. europe now understands that the cold war logic of buffer states is over. today, grey zones in european security only create instability, risk and opportunities for hostile interference. the eu must invest in closing these grey zones and supporting the resilience and integration of ukraine, moldova and georgia into our european family and nato. to strengthen our resilience, we must learn both from our partners like ukraine, in building resilience and tackling disinformation, but also from our own misjudgement allowing to fall into the trap of energy dependency and elite capture in the past. when i recall the state of affairs even three years ago, i am glad to say that, today, europe is far less naive about russia, china, and other adversaries. a few words about structural priorities and the new challenges we are facing. for years, we have been following a country-agnostic approach that treats all foreign influence efforts in the same way, regardless of their source country and thus the aim, scale and the impact. we should not be afraid to call out those seeking intentionally and in a coordinated way to manipulate our democracy. therefore, we are suggesting moving towards a risk-based approach based on objective criteria. a similar approach already has been used in the eu legislation in money laundering and terrorist financing. an immense challenge is presented by the rapid development of artificial intelligence tools. if so far we still are able to identify what is fake, artificial intelligence will make creating disinformation at scale much easier and cheaper, and much more difficult to recognise. we await the artificial intelligence act with great expectation. another challenge is the speed of decision-making process. we must face the fact that today’s legislation concerning consequences of the digital revolution already addresses the problems of yesterday. this is not only the eu challenge. it is a global problem to be addressed together with like—minded partners. moreover, i am convinced that this house in the next legislation will need a dedicated, cross-sectoral committee dealing with foreign interference and information manipulation issues, including new technological challenges. in conclusion, i would like to thank my shadows for the excellent cooperation through this entire process, and also the secretariat and our political advisors. working on the challenges of the inge1 and inge2 committees has certainly been one of the most important missions throughout my time as a member of the european parliament. i truly hope that all of you can support the report.

first report, which was approved last year. second, we must examine the issues under the mandate of our committee vis-a-vis russia’s ongoing brutal war against ukraine and to build on the lessons learned. our assessment shows that we have significantly increased our situational awareness, and several necessary steps have been launched and progress has been attained (digital services act, democracy defence package is on the way, growing expertise acquired). however, in view of the upcoming eu elections in 2024, we still should urge for stronger measures and more coordination to protect our european democracy. allow me to outline some of the priorities from our report, which would make a significant difference in making our union more resilient. first of all, we need to move beyond a reactive approach centred on fact-checking, debunking, etc., and instead focus on resilience-building and ‘vaccination’ of our societies against disinformation. therefore, we need to establish a dedicated eu programme to invest in our democracy in a sustainable way. it will not give a solution tomorrow and it will be expensive, but it is certainly a worthwhile long-term investment. another important conclusion of our report is that in tackling disinformation, the eu is still suffering from a fragmented approach, without a clear coordination mechanism and goals. we simply cannot afford splintering our resources when our democracy is at stake. third, we should also greatly raise the costs for perpetrators. therefore, i reiterate that the toolbox of the eu countermeasures should include a specific sanctions regime on foreign information manipulation and interference. russia’s imperial war of aggression against ukraine has clearly exposed the interconnection between hostile information warfare, weaponisation of energy, attacks on critical infrastructure, and threats to the eu, to our immediate neighbourhood, as well as to global security and stability. europe now understands that the cold war logic of buffer states is over. today, grey zones in european security only create instability, risk and opportunities for hostile interference. the eu must invest in closing these grey zones and supporting the resilience and integration of ukraine, moldova and georgia into our european family and nato. to strengthen our resilience, we must learn both from our partners like ukraine, in building resilience and tackling disinformation, but also from our own misjudgement allowing to fall into the trap of energy dependency and elite capture in the past. when i recall the state of affairs even three years ago, i am glad to say that, today, europe is far less naive about russia, china, and other adversaries. a few words about structural priorities and the new challenges we are facing. for years, we have been following a country-agnostic approach that treats all foreign influence efforts in the same way, regardless of their source country and thus the aim, scale and the impact. we should not be afraid to call out those seeking intentionally and in a coordinated way to manipulate our democracy. therefore, we are suggesting moving towards a risk-based approach based on objective criteria. a similar approach already has been used in the eu legislation in money laundering and terrorist financing. an immense challenge is presented by the rapid development of artificial intelligence tools. if so far we still are able to identify what is fake, artificial intelligence will make creating disinformation at scale much easier and cheaper, and much more difficult to recognise. we await the artificial intelligence act with great expectation. another challenge is the speed of decision-making process. we must face the fact that today’s legislation concerning consequences of the digital revolution already addresses the problems of yesterday. this is not only the eu challenge. it is a global problem to be addressed together with like—minded partners. moreover, i am convinced that this house in the next legislation will need a dedicated, cross-sectoral committee dealing with foreign interference and information manipulation issues, including new technological challenges. in conclusion, i would like to thank my shadows for the excellent cooperation through this entire process, and also the secretariat and our political advisors. working on the challenges of the inge1 and inge2 committees has certainly been one of the most important missions throughout my time as a member of the european parliament. i truly hope that all of you can support the report.

paragraph: madam president, the content of the second inge report shows that while the threat of foreign interference remains high and ever present, the methods and techniques of our adversaries are evolving. and now, on the day of adopting the updated report, we are already facing a new challenge: misinformation and disinformation fuelled by artificial intelligence, most famously the recent example of chatgpt. we cannot be naive: technology will keep evolving and we are already starting to witness ai-created fake photos and videos that are nearly indistinguishable from reality. as their creation and distribution becomes easier and cheaper, bad actors will become more sophisticated in their use, just like they had mastered the use of fake news before. this time we cannot be just reactive. it is crucial that the defence of democracy package and the artificial intelligence act not only cover existing and known issues, but also are forward—looking enough so that new laws and regulations will not become obsolete the day they are adopted. the health of our democracies depends on it.

paragraph: (it) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the whole world is watching us while alarms are being raised about artificial intelligence in general, the risk of extinction of the human race by sentient algorithms, alarms often launched by the same big tech that fears what they have created. in the meantime, europe has moved forward, without stopping, and in recent months has worked hard to propose a concrete response to the risks that already exist, not those that can be futured, of powerful technologies such as artificial intelligence. they told us: in this way you will curb innovation, so europe will never be competitive. while today many of these same people agree with us: rules are necessary. today, therefore, we are here to ask parliament for a mandate to start negotiations on the world's first law on the subject. our position contains many improvements to the commission's proposal, which clarify and update the text, promote legal certainty, avoid duplication with existing laws, stimulate innovation, while keeping human beings and their fundamental rights as a fixed point. it must remain at the heart of the european approach to artificial intelligence. i will mention just a few of the key points of our proposal: a clear and balanced definition, in line with the work of international organisations; a chapter to regulate systems such as chatgpt, previously excluded from the text, to achieve transparency and mitigate the risks of discrimination and generation of illegal content; in addition to watermarking, to make identifiable the content produced by generative ai which, although already provided for in fact by article 52, i think will be even more clearly specified in the trialogue. but we also haven't forgotten the risks to the environment in training algorithms with billions of data and parameters. we have introduced an obligation for companies and public authorities using high-risk artificial intelligence to carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment based on the specific context of use, as an additional safeguard for vulnerable groups. mention should also be made of the addition of the right to a judicial remedy, to an explanation, to be represented by collective action in the event of a negative impact on health, safety or fundamental rights, and the addition of the environment, democracy and the rule of law among the objectives to be protected, as well as the obligation to discuss the use of artificial intelligence in the workplace with trade unions and to inform the workers involved,  in addition to the expansion of practices considered unacceptable, such as predictive policing, biometric categorization, indiscriminate collection of facial images from the web, emotional recognition in some contexts and opposition to the use of biometric recognition in public spaces for surveillance purposes. the use of these cameras has no proven benefit on the safety of citizens, while the risks of abuse, discrimination and inaccuracy are proven, especially on some people, women, non-white people, children. the introduction of these technologies presents risks for the stability of our countries, for its democratic stability, and for this reason we will fight with the council in the coming months to defend this approach and counter dangers to our freedom. i am thinking of the worrying words of some ministers of the interior, including the italian piantedosi. we want artificial intelligence to unfold its full positive potential for creativity, productivity and improving daily life. for this reason, we have also engaged in an intense work of confrontation with legislators from all over the world to find common approaches. this is why we support the work on the ai pact to anticipate the effects of the regulation and the ai code of conduct for generative artificial intelligence. but let us also issue a clear warning: all approximation and adaptation activities are useful, provided that they do not think of replacing the binding rules that we are going to establish. we will not be influenced by attempts that may come from large corporations or government institutions and not to dilute and weaken this effort to make our democracies stronger in the context of technological transformation. we will do our best in the interests of europeans together with the commission, whom i thank, together with the council, together with all my colleagues.

subject_of_business_title: Artificial Intelligence Act (debate)
paragraph: mr president, executive vice-president, commissioner, dear colleagues, regulating artificial intelligence may at first sound like a very technical matter, but it is so much more than that. it is about asking ourselves the big question: what kind of society do we actually want to live in? and to me, the answer is very clear. a society in which ai enables our democracy and not one in which it undermines it. but, of course, this is much more easier said than it is actually done in practice. for us to get there, i think we should not be playing whac-a-mole or regulating the next big thing. it is about putting in place effective guardrails. it is about putting principles and mechanisms that will last for at least the next couple of years to come. but it is also about working with our partners. it is about working with international partners to shape a global governance framework. it is about maximising the potential of ai, while at the same time addressing the existing and looming concerns. so no, it is not technical. it is about the future of our democracy.

subject_of_business_title: Artificial Intelligence Act (debate)
paragraph: mr president, commissioner, this is historic legislation. europe is a pioneer in having an artificial intelligence law. a technology that can bring many benefits, but that also poses clear risks in fundamental rights, security or disinformation. that is why i welcome the approach that this law has taken, because i believe it is vital to distinguish between technology and use. we do not condemn artificial intelligence itself, but risky practices. we are very clear about what is unacceptable for europe – prohibited uses, as intrusive and discriminatory – and that exceptions should only be given under judicial authorization. we want secure and transparent systems subject to rules, limits and accountability for high-risk uses such as health, environment, transportation, education or justice applications. we are also clear that we need a flexible law that encourages innovation, that gives certainty to companies and that can adapt quickly to the spectacular advance of technology, as we have seen in the development of generative ai with chat gpt, where time is pressing for us to establish transparency and safe use requirements. today in europe we are taking an important step. this law will help citizens build trust in technology and position us at the forefront of artificial intelligence.

intervention_header_en: Svenja Hahn, on behalf of the Renew Group
subject_of_business_title: Artificial Intelligence Act (debate)
paragraph: mr president! the potential of artificial intelligence is so great that we can hardly imagine it today – for all areas of life, be it education, work or health. that's why it's so important that we want to use the artificial intelligence act today to lay the foundation for what kind of artificial intelligence we want to have in a liberal democracy. after all, the opportunity and risk always lie in the application. facial recognition − super handy for unlocking a mobile phone, but biometric facial recognition for surveillance in public spaces, dear colleagues, we know this from china. that has no place in a european union. we need to put a clear stop to such dangers and at the same time promote innovation made in europe. to this end, we are strengthening experimentation in real-world laboratories, for example. that's why we decided to focus on quality standards for general-purpose ai and generative ai, such as chatgpt, and not on bans or a high-risk classification. after all, we must not follow fantasies of surveillance or over-regulation in the artificial intelligence act. our goal must be to strengthen citizens' rights, boost business and innovation, so that we can make the european union a hotspot for progress and artificial intelligence.
