paragraph: mr. president, madam commissioner, esteemed colleagues! a nightmare that became a reality for taylor swift a few weeks ago - nude images generated by artificial intelligence that are forever available online for the whole world to see. but it could happen to any of us. and many of the women who are victims of this abuse suffer from anxiety disorders, depression, or even take their own lives. that is why it is such a great success that the new directive to combat violence against women now clearly states: publishing nude images without the consent of the person involved is a crime. however, what shocks me is that the council has set the bar so high that the protection for the affected women is once again limited. now, a serious harm must be proven. ladies and gentlemen, every woman knows that the publication of nude images against her will is the definition of serious harm! what else is there to prove? let us therefore now fight at the national level to put an end to this insidious form of violence against women! let us fight for a europe where women can live freely and safely!

paragraph: mr president, the strategic technologies platform for europe that we are discussing today is a very good idea. step seeks to facilitate investment in industries that are going to be key to our future, such as artificial intelligence and green technologies. it also seeks to react to the evident loss of competitiveness of our companies and put an end to the dangerous dependencies that have been exposed since the pandemic and the war in ukraine. but, like so many other good ideas, step has come to nothing. it lacks the most important thing: money. while the united states, with its inflation reduction act, injects some €400 billion to support its industry, in the european union we respond with a pyrrhic €1.5 billion to finance strategic projects. we're making a fool of ourselves. the solution is no less europe, it is not a "every man for himself" in which countries that can afford it irrigate their industries with national subsidies, but quite the opposite. we need to strengthen our internal market. we need to find joint solutions to problems that affect us all. you can't be strategic at the national level. it is high time that we had a proper european union budget, which would enable us to solve common problems and finance our priorities.

paragraph: mr president, commissioner breton, ladies and gentlemen, here we are, after two years of intense work, we have finally managed to approve the world's first binding law on artificial intelligence, aimed at reducing risks and increasing opportunities, combating discrimination, providing transparency, bringing our democratic values of freedom and equality into the development of these new technologies, while supporting innovation and competitiveness. thanks to us, in the european parliament, after tough negotiations, unacceptable practices in europe will be banned by the end of the year, such as the recognition of emotions in the workplace and in places of study, such as inferring a person's ethnic, religious or political affiliation on the basis of biometric data. an algorithm will not be able to predict whether a specific person will commit a crime by violating the presumption of innocence; workers will always need to be informed and unions involved in the use of artificial intelligence in the workplace. in short, we fight discrimination, we protect the rights of citizens and workers. these are some important examples of what we have achieved. in the final text, we confirmed the framework of risk reduction for all the most sensitive areas, such as the use of ai in the medical field, in the administration of justice, in the workplace, in democratic procedures, thanks to the verification of compliance on the quality and appropriateness of data, cybersecurity, human control. let's say enough of an artificial intelligence that systematically discriminates against women or non-white people when it has to select resumes or exposes patients to risks on the management of their health data. these are cases that we are familiar with and that we want to counter with a law that is finally able to act on this front. we want to increase the conscious use of artificial intelligence systems, not discourage it. people will know that thanks to these rules, they will be able to use the systems with the greatest possible protection. but thanks to the work of the european parliament, we have also achieved a lot on the transparency front: we say no more to the indiscriminate use of deep fakes that will be made recognizable directly by devices through the so-called watermarking, an invisible labeling, and we say no more to the use of copyrighted content without protection for its owners, because the right to see the economic value of creativity and of what is created by people recognized is a a right that must also be protected within the context of the development of artificial intelligence. we still have a lot to do. to start this implementation work, the ai office, the european artificial intelligence office, is being built, and we will have to accompany institutions and companies in voluntary early compliance, in supporting them to apply the rules before they are fully mandatory; a gradual process of accompaniment that will also focus, for example, on the development of what we wanted, as a parliament, and that is the verification of fundamental rights, the impact assessment – something that will be essential so that users of artificial intelligence also do their part to reduce the risks. i would like to thank you for this great work, which puts europe at the forefront and which sets out a path that we will have to continue with the planned directives, for example on artificial intelligence in the world of work, and i would like to thank my fellow rapporteurs, mr tudorache and my colleagues from the other political groups for that. we have achieved a great deal because parliament, parliament's team, has been able to be united in negotiating according to our vision, which is to really put the human being and european values at the heart of the development of artificial intelligence.

medico, nell'amministrazione della giustizia, nei luoghi di lavoro, nelle procedure democratiche, grazie alla verifica di conformità sulla qualità e appropriatezza dei dati, la cibersicurezza, il controllo umano. diciamo così basta a un'intelligenza artificiale che discrimina sistematicamente le donne o le persone non bianche quando deve selezionare i curriculum o espone pazienti a rischi sulla gestione dei loro dati sanitari. sono casi che conosciamo e che vogliamo contrastare con una norma finalmente in grado di agire su questo fronte. vogliamo aumentare l'uso consapevole dei sistemi di intelligenza artificiale, non disincentivarlo. le persone sapranno che grazie a queste norme potranno utilizzare i sistemi con la massima tutela possibile. ma grazie al lavoro del parlamento europeo abbiamo ottenuto molto anche sul fronte della trasparenza: diciamo basta all'uso indiscriminato di deep fake che saranno resi riconoscibili direttamente dai device tramite il cosiddetto "watermarking", una etichettatura invisibile, e diciamo basta all'uso di contenuti protetti dal copyright senza tutele per i loro detentori, perché il diritto a veder riconosciuto il valore economico della creatività e di quello che viene realizzato dalle persone è un diritto che deve essere tutelato anche dentro il contesto dello sviluppo dell'intelligenza artificiale. noi abbiamo ancora molto da fare. per l'avvio di questo lavoro di implementazione si sta costruendo l'ai office, l'ufficio europeo dell'intelligenza artificiale, e dovremo accompagnare le istituzioni e le imprese nella compliance anticipata volontaria, nel sostegno ad applicare le norme prima che saranno pienamente obbligatorie; un percorso graduale di accompagnamento che metterà al centro anche, per esempio, lo sviluppo di quello che noi abbiamo voluto, come parlamento, e cioè la verifica dei diritti fondamentali, la verifica di impatto – qualcosa che sarà fondamentale affinché anche gli utilizzatori dell'intelligenza artificiale facciano la loro parte per ridurre i rischi. voglio ringraziare per questo grande lavoro, che pone l'europa in prima linea e che traccia una strada che dovremo proseguire con le previste direttive, ad esempio sull'intelligenza artificiale nel mondo del lavoro, voglio ringraziare per questo i colleghi relatori, il collega relatore tudorache e i colleghi degli altri gruppi politici. abbiamo ottenuto molto perché il parlamento, il team del parlamento, ha saputo essere unito nel negoziare secondo la nostra visione, quella di mettere davvero l'essere umano e i valori europei al centro dello sviluppo dell'intelligenza artificiale.

paragraph: mr president, mr commissioner, dear colleagues! the legislation that we have on the table here is complex, complicated legislation and, in my opinion, actually the right thing to do for a leading ai nation – but we are not. that's why the mood outside the eu bubble isn't very good either. we protect everything and everyone, but in doing so, we miss out on a bit of value creation through innovation. we should also be careful that we, as the european union, do not somehow become the world's global authority for fines. that is why we in the group of the european people's party (christian democrats) and european democrats are convinced that the artificial intelligence act is basically only sensible if further points and measures are taken or points are added and the whole thing can then lead to success. in addition to the harmonised technical standards, we also need a flexible approach to all these problems that can arise. nor should we believe – as the rapporteur has already said – that our work will suddenly end with this law. no, i think it's just beginning. unlike other laws, we need to find quick answers and adaptations to problems and developments. we should urgently clarify legal uncertainties through the ai authority, also due to this unclear wording in the text. we need the guidelines as soon as possible. we also need to find out the overlaps with other laws, we need to minimize and clarify. we need the interpretation of the rules for the whole of the european union, in other words, a uniform interpretation. we also need a design for these andboxes so that we can allow for industry- and sector-specific sandboxes accordingly. we need access to quality data for training, including personal data, and in particular we need to adapt to the general data protection regulation. we need extreme help for small and medium-sized enterprises here, especially in order to meet the prerequisites. in any case, when it comes to staffing the ai authority, i hope that they get the right talents there, because that is also necessary.

paragraph: mr president, commissioner, today we are giving the green light to the artificial intelligence act, a law that is unique in the world. a law that allows or prohibits its uses depending on the risk to people and provides penalties for non-compliance. a law that includes transparency criteria so that we know if a text or a photograph has been artificially generated or manipulated and to ensure that the data that has been used respects copyright. in short, with this law, european citizens can be sure that our fundamental rights are always respected. but today we should not talk only about risks. this technology offers great benefits for society and 80% of the uses are low-risk. protecting citizens' rights and promoting innovation must be compatible in the european union, otherwise we will drive innovators out of europe. we now have a good umbrella law. we have said here that this is the beginning. we need to develop flexible, agile industry regulations so that our companies can adapt to the speed of this technology. without over-regulating. in short, it is about taking advantage of the benefits of artificial intelligence, not about being slaves. because it's about europe leading the race for artificial intelligence because our competitiveness is at stake.

paragraph: mr president, commissioner, dear colleagues, tomorrow’s ai act’s adoption is pivotal for european policymaking as it guarantees our rights and fosters innovation. as the tran committee, we prioritise the safety and privacy of public transport users, as well as flexibility for small- and medium-sized enterprises. therefore, we warmly welcome the establishment of stringent conditions for the further processing of personal data pertaining to the safety and resilience of transport systems and mobility within ai regulatory sandboxes. moreover, granting priority access to regulatory sandboxes at minimal or proportionate costs for smes and aiming to minimise the administrative burden and compliance costs demonstrates our commitment to their success. the ai act will facilitate artificial intelligence development in sectors that directly bolster our citizens’ quality of life, especially in sectors like transport. i would like to congratulate the rapporteurs, and all the shadows and the commission, for this important legislative act.

paragraph: mr president, thank you, commissioner, and thank you to our rapporteurs and all the teams that brought us to this point. the final adoption of the artificial intelligence act today is a historic moment. this landmark legislation is a significant step forward in our commitment to responsible digital leadership and creating an ethical future for artificial intelligence in europe. it provides a robust regulatory framework, promoting trust and transparency in ai systems, establishing clear rules for deployment and for use and development. we are fostering accountability and responsibility across the sectors and along our value chains, and this ensures that ai technologies serve the best interests of our citizens. crucially, this legislation upholds fundamental rights in the digital age, with strong requirements for fairness, accountability and non-discrimination. we safeguard against unfair biases and injustices that may arise from unchecked ai systems. we can – and we will – unlock the potential of ai in healthcare, climate solutions and for economic productivity, but we also set clear guardrails, a ban on social scoring, discriminatory algorithms and manipulative techniques, and this ensures ai serves humanity and not the other way around. in addition, this act will encourage innovation and competitiveness by providing legal certainty and a level playing field, and we create an environment that is conducive to breakthroughs in ai technology, positioning europe in this way at the forefront of global innovation. so this is not the last post; the ai act is the foundation. and now comes the crucial task of implementation and increasing international cooperation. and that is the establishment of the ai area. we welcome that, commissioner, and we look forward to continuing our engagement with our international partners to ensure that we have a global response to artificial intelligence.

paragraph: mr president! three and a half years ago, we discussed here: what should the european law on artificial intelligence actually look like? my three demands are still my benchmark today. at the time, i called for us to promote innovation, strengthen citizens' rights and harmonise the internal market. let's take a look at what's available now! the definition of ai is international, real-world labs are coming, and there are clear responsibilities in value creation. but bureaucracy and ambiguities remain, which will be easier for big tech companies to cope with than for smes. i believe that it will be important for the commission to provide clarity in its implementation, because the artificial intelligence act must not become a brake on innovation. as far as citizens' rights are concerned, we have not been able to achieve a ban on real-time biometric surveillance against the member states, but we have been able to remove important hurdles from the rule of law. i have also fought for stronger rules on retrograde biometric identification and predictive policing. i can say that we have improved the commission's proposal; but i would have liked to see more joy in innovation and even stronger protection of civil rights. but ai progress and regulation won't end with the artificial intelligence act. for our democratic and economic future, it is important to continue to work to ensure that governments do not misuse artificial intelligence for surveillance and that innovation has a home in europe.

paragraph: mr president, colleagues, let’s first state what this is: this vote is a revolutionary step, and from left to right, we bridged our differences – and there were some – and we fought together an unprecedented lobby against rules. today, the eu is taking the lead worldwide with binding rules for artificial intelligence, including for chatgpt. and with clear rules on how to design and use ai, we’re putting people and society first, and i’m particularly proud that we already managed to learn from mistakes that were made with the use of ai before. we will make sure nobody’s ever classified as a criminal or fraudster purely based on a calculation again. we will make sure people always get an answer to questions they have about certain decisions made by governments, instead of facing a computer that says ‘no’ and leaving people empty-handed. we will make sure a human is always in the loop, so your human rights are protected and you’re not discriminated against. and i’m proud of the clear limits we put to unethical technologies, such as predictive policing, facial recognition in public space, and so-called sexuality recognition. i would have wanted to go even further, with stronger bans closing every loophole, binding environmental standards and mandatory testing for all large language models and image generators instead of only the largest ones. but my fight for this will continue. let me use my last seconds to once again thank the amazing staff, also from the commission and the council, that stayed with us for 38 hours, which was ridiculous and it should not have been that long. but we did it. and thanks for your commitment to staying and keeping us sharp all night long.

paragraph: dear! commissioner, i would like to thank you for your comments. mr president, i would like to thank you for your comments. artificial intelligence is changing our reality. its capabilities are constantly growing, and the areas in which it can be successfully used are constantly increasing. however, there are risks associated with this that we cannot ignore. not only do we need clear criteria for assessing the safety of products and services that use ai, but we also need a list of prohibited uses of this technology, especially where it is used by public institutions. over the course of the long work on this regulation, it has been possible to take into account the priorities of the ecr, such as the exemption for the research and development phase, fewer requirements and burdens for small and medium-sized enterprises, the strengthening of the role of regulatory sandboxes and real guarantees for the protection of citizens' rights and privacy. whether this legislation will be effective now depends on the competence and commitment of the member states and the authorities that will implement it. europe cannot only regulate, but must educate, invest and innovate. hopefullyai actwon't get in the way of that.

paragraph: mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, for the first time legislation has been introduced to regulate the new environment of artificial intelligence. this legislation was necessary given the impact of artificial intelligence in all areas and the dangers it entails. i am thinking in particular of one example, the spokesperson of the renaissance party, emmanuel macron's party, who posted on social networks a montage of a mock video of marine le pen claiming that she was speaking in russian and defaming her. i am delighted that, through our work, our group has been able to contribute to this text with proposals such as the enhanced control of artificial intelligence by humans – and not by machines – or the use of artificial intelligence by our law enforcement agencies to search for victims of kidnapping, investigate the risk of an islamist attack or combat child pornography. i also welcome the rejection of the scandalous proposals of the left. i am thinking, for example, of their desire to prohibit the anticipation of illegal immigrants crossing borders or the obligation for artificial intelligence to promote diversity. of course, we are realistic. there are still significant shortcomings in this text, and we will remain vigilant. we have lost the fight for the creation of the european gafams, so let's try to win the battle of artificial intelligence so that we are no longer in the digital vice between china and the united states and to advance our nations and our companies in the digital world of tomorrow.

paragraph: mr president, commissioner, artificial intelligence is here to stay. how digital services are here to stay. the digital services regulation or the digital markets regulation are necessary, but they came late. for the first time, the european union is a pioneer in the digital field. with the artificial intelligence act, we created the world's first standard for this revolutionary technology. in the 2000s, we bet on a future that was not digital, without knowing that we would pay dearly for it. this law shows that we have learned from the mistakes of the past. however, we must not be naïve. regular is not enough. in this sector, we compete, among others, with the united states, a country without regulatory limitations when it comes to innovation. that's why we have to keep working to position ourselves in the global digital race. to this end, it is essential to support our smes, reduce the bureaucratic barriers faced by our companies, retain european talent by creating an attractive ecosystem and avoid over-regulation by inviting public-private collaboration. and, of course, putting the citizen at the centre. all of this is based on values and principles, on the european way of doing things. only in this way will we be able to exploit the potential of the digital single market and ultimately increase the competitiveness of the european union. we cannot and should not leave something that continues to change our lives and our society in the hands of private companies alone.

paragraph: artificial intelligence is one of the new challenges of the present and the future. and, like any new challenge, it comes with many positive aspects but also with potential negative consequences. i am sure that most of us have discovered with enthusiasm how useful artificial intelligence can be when we need to compose a text, and then with concern when we learned how it can falsify photos or speeches that are then used in electoral campaigns. it is evident that we need harmonized rules for the development, placement on the market, and use of high-risk ai systems, that we need strict rules regarding transparency. i welcome the initiative of the european commission to regulate this field and establish a clear list of ai practices that are prohibited because they pose unacceptable risks; to strictly limit the situations in which real-time biometric identification ai systems are allowed, such as searching for missing persons, identifying individuals suspected of committing a serious crime, or preventing terrorist attacks. and because artificial intelligence is a field in continuous and rapid development, i recommend that the european commission ensure flexible, easily and quickly activatable control and verification mechanisms.

paragraph: today, europe once again shows the way to the world. this time with the first legislation on artificial intelligence, which is largely the success of the socialist and democrat group. with this, the eu has proven to be a first-rate actor, aware of the speed of development of artificial intelligence, its exceptional effects on society, and all the challenges it brings. the increasing presence of artificial intelligence in everyone's life arouses both interest and concern regarding ethics and data privacy, and ultimately its impact on the future of jobs. the key contribution of the legislation is to protect people and their fundamental rights regardless of technological development. we consider this a great victory! we have protected workers and unions, who must be informed in advance about the use of ai in the workplace. with the law, we aim to prevent any possible abuse by authorities who would infer an individual's ethical, religious, or political affiliation based on biometric data. people, consumers have the right to complain and demand explanations in case of any violations or misuse of ai. we have banned any social or societal scoring. with this historic legislation, we have sided with the people and their demands that individuals must be protected from risky or unethical use of digital technologies, including artificial intelligence.

paragraph: on wednesday, the european parliament approved the agreement between the ep and the council on the regulation concerning the world's first comprehensive rules on artificial intelligence (ai). this is an important step today, as it marks the end of a legislative process that ensures the legal framework for the use of artificial intelligence, serving the interests of eu citizens. the expansion of artificial intelligence is unprecedented in the history of technologies, so i welcome that europe has taken the lead and put forward concrete proposals for managing the risks of ai. it is important that the development and application of ai within europe comply with fundamental rights, remain under human supervision, be safe, transparent, non-discriminatory, and serve the well-being of society and the environment. i welcome the establishment of human-centered regulations, which emphasize consumer protection while also allowing room for innovation and economic opportunities to be exploited. throughout, it has been a key consideration that eu regulation of artificial intelligence not only prioritizes people's safety and addresses the risks associated with ai use but also ensures equal competition conditions for digital smes.

paragraph: the artificial intelligence act is one of the main pillars of the legislative package included in the digital decade and is a precursor, in global terms, of a conceptual and legal approach focused on the inclusive digital transition and a focus on people. this regulation, in conjunction with core pieces of legislation such as the general data protection regulation, the digital markets act, the digital services act and the cybersecurity act, among others, creates competitive advantages for the european industrial and digital ecosystem and will allow citizens in general to access more products and services and under better conditions. the regulation sets out risk standards and rules to mitigate it, including rules for scientific and practical scrutiny of general-purpose ai models, generative ai applications that can generate systemic risks, and the use of biometric identification. i emphasise that this regulation is designed to be applied in an open and democratic political and social ecosystem. without this assumption, it will quickly be crushed and manipulated, and the security of people's data will be called into question. upholding the shared values of the union is a key condition for the success of the regulation under discussion and its objectives.

subject_of_business_title: Presentation by the Council of its position on the draft general budget - 2020 financial year (debate)
paragraph: madam president, dear president-in-office of the council, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen! with the council's position and today's discussion, we are on schedule. all those responsible - parliament, the council, the commission - are concerned to ensure that the 2020 budget can be adopted by mid-november at a difficult time, so that clarity can be created for programs, projects and people for the next year. we in the commission are assuming that we too will maintain continuity and that my possible successor, commissioner johannes hahn, will be able to take over the task here as a service provider for you immediately from november 1st. there is the extraordinary and open development of the uk's exit from the european union alongside the normal issues and questions. if there is a resignation, a resignation at the end of october and there are no regulations, then next year we will have a gap that we will have to talk about here in due course. nor do we expect the uk to accept all the rights and obligations of the end-2020 budgetary framework in the final year of the 2020 budgetary framework. just thinking ahead: if there is no agreement and the kingdom were to leave automatically without an extension, there would be a net gap of around eleven billion euros next year. and since the european union, unlike all other institutions - member states, regions, local authorities - has a comprehensive ban on debt, we should immediately close the gap together. the commission would then make a proposal for this before the conciliation phase, which begins at the end of october. it could be that the eleven billion are provided comprehensively through cuts. it could be that the eleven billion are generated comprehensively through higher deposits. presumably a middle ground between reasonable cuts that don't do us much harm and slightly higher deposits will be the wise path. we will come back to this in three weeks if necessary. we consider it important that the council, parliament and the commission share the same priorities in principle: employment, stabilizing growth, strengthening our competitiveness, innovation, the possible measures for climate protection at european level, which, in addition to emission reduction pathways, in addition to setting standards, also investments mean, and strengthening our internal and external security. the council shares the commission's proposal on some successful programmes: erasmus+, copernicus and other infrastructure projects; on the defense industrial development project, we see ourselves very well in the council proposal and the council's position. we are concerned about some cuts and i will want to talk to you more deeply during the deliberations about the concerns or the damage that cuts would cause. for many, many years we have been talking about 3⁰% of our gdp for research, it is 2⁰%. horizon 2020 is only part of the research investment, but an important part, because in the digital age we do the best research in europe in many areas. that is why we do not consider the reduction of 410 million to be justifiable. and i believe that the council also finds it difficult to represent this in public, because these are concrete examples. we would have to cut key technologies of the future such as nano, micro, laser and biotech by 20⁰% ​​- in areas where we can no longer follow america and china enough. is this really wise, i ask. when it comes to artificial intelligence and technologies for the digitization of the european economy, significant cuts would have to be made, or 118 million less for the european research council. in concrete terms, this means: 80⁰research projects are canceled or not carried out, although we are already unable to co-finance a large number of meaningful research projects because our funds are limited. we believe that there are good reasons for every euro at european level in health research, in the digital transformation of health and care, in the development of artificial intelligence in healthcare. we have joint undertakings in the field of transport research, and they are now to be cut by 80⁰%: shift2rail, single european sky, air traffic management research and others. and that would mean, in part, that we would have to end programs and projects outright. we should talk about this with an open mind over the next few weeks. because all projects make sense - better european than in 28 fragmented silos - and all projects would be at risk if the cuts had to be implemented as proposed by the council. connecting europe, the cross-border infrastructure: 200⁰million cuts. in concrete terms, this means that we will not be able to tackle some projects next year, including safe action – austria, finland, france, germany, the netherlands. here we want to introduce the free emergency call service e-call. this should go away. or the seine-scheldt project, a waterway project that aims to link the french inland waterway network with those in belgium, the netherlands and germany - a viable alternative to road and road freight transport. or the eastern baltic hub – improving the port connection and hinterland connection of the hamina-kotka port in the scan-med corridor. and one thing is clear: if we don't tackle these programs, don't carry out the projects, this is not a saving - we'll just start a year later - but a postponement, a shift in sensible investments. i will fight for every project in the council and ask both budgetary authorities - council and parliament - to follow these good arguments in the end. at cef, as i said, these are measures for competitiveness and for environmentally friendly transport, and i think everything would therefore point the way if it could start next year. the same applies to measures in the field of cosme for small and medium-sized enterprises. the cuts would mean that europe cannot become a contact and funding partner for many start-ups and small companies. the reduction of 25 million in the area of ​​combating cross-border organized crime, terrorism, cybercrime - we have good arguments here for not supporting the cuts, and the citizens are behind us on these issues. europe and the world – heading four: here a cut of 200⁰million is proposed; 70 relate to development aid cooperation, 50 to humanitarian aid. already, if we take it in all honesty, europe is falling short of its obligations to its neighbors and to the world. we must do more to ensure that human dignity develops in these regions – in the sahel, maghreb and sub-sahel zones – so that disaster relief can be provided. with the cuts, europe will not be the partner for human dignity and civil protection in many areas. cuts are proposed in the agencies - frontex, the european center for the development of vocational training, the medicines agency, the asylum office. the cuts mean that our service is getting worse. here, too, i want to openly tell you about my concerns and then come back to them in the deliberations. and despite the difficult time with the exit of the kingdom, we should do everything possible not to increase the rituals that we always perform. with the good will of all three parties involved, an agreement should actually be possible within a few days before the end of the mediation phase. as a commission, we want to do everything we can to achieve this. in difficult times, good governance for a budget would be a clear message that europe is capable of acting and wants to remain a service provider for our fellow citizens.

subject_of_business_title: Commission Work Programme 2020 (debate)
paragraph: madam president, it’s a real pleasure for me to be here today to discuss with you the first commission work programme under the mandate of president ursula von der leyen, which we adopted yesterday. this 2020 work programme is important for two reasons. first, because it will not just be the basis of our work for the first year of the mandate but also because it sets the vision, institutions and in close cooperation with national parliaments and our partners to organise a conference on the future of europe. we are in the process of building the scope and the structure. by the end of 2020, we will present the european democracy action plan to address disinformation, political campaigning, free and independent media, and freedom of speech. with regard to fundamental rights, technology needs to serve the people, not the other way around. therefore, the commission will update the charter of fundamental rights to address emerging issues such as artificial intelligence and facial recognition. last but not least, on the rule of law, the commission will intensify its preventive work, for example, with its first rule of law report, which will assess the situation in all member states. this report will have a sound methodology and form the basis for future work on the rule of law. we are also already working on embedding strategic foresight across all commission policies by using all data at our disposal as regards the long—term trends and major shifts on the horizon to be able to design future—proof policies. to this end, i have already established a strategic foresight network within the european commission and i am fine-tuning together with eu member states and partners our coordination on this. i count a lot on cooperation with you. the european parliament, as i already found out, has a wealth of data and intelligence in all its committees. this was a very quick overview of the initiatives included in our 2020 work programme. it took me a little bit more than 10 minutes, but i wanted to demonstrate to you that we are really delivering on what we promised to you: an ambitious yet realistic agenda of our shared priorities for the first year of this commission. the future partnership with the uk will, of course, be one of our main challenges for the next months and years, and i was here yesterday with you on the emotional farewell to our british colleagues, but this was the case during the negotiation of the withdrawal agreement. we want to reassure you that we have committed to the maximum level of transparency as regards the negotiation process towards the european parliament. together with my colleagues in the commission, we are looking forward to working together on our special partnership of trust and turning our agenda into concrete actions. we first have to join forces to ensure an appropriate, modern long-term budget that rises to our common challenges and from now on, we will all have to intensify the work on legislative decision-making with a view to delivering our priorities. the joint declaration on legislative priorities that will follow will serve as a concrete roadmap for our joint work, truly engaging all three institutions, and this will be followed by our first ever multi-annual programming that should capture our common strategic agenda for europe. thank you very much, madam president, and i’m looking forward to the intervention of the honourable members of this house. (applause)

intervention_header: Maroš Šefčovič, Vice-President of the Commission
intervention_header_en: Maroš Šefčovič, Vice-President of the Commission
subject_of_business_title: Commission Work Programme 2020 (debate)
paragraph: mr president, honourable members of the european parliament, thank you very much for this very rich debate, for all your interventions and i’m glad that i can say that also this discussion has reconfirmed that our work programme reflects our common priorities. i really would like to thank you for all the words of encouragement, for pointing out certain details upon which we have to work even more and also on some of the things that you believe that are missing in the programme and upon which we will do our utmost to work together. i think that the motive with which our president presented her new commission is that this would be the geopolitical commission, which would strive for more, and i believe that with your help, with your support, we can really achieve that. i would like to echo the words of ms niebler and mr marques, who said that to have an ambitious programme is a very good thing, but what would be even more important now is its proper implementation. i found an echo of this call in many of your interventions and i really would like to tell you that we take it very seriously and we hope that with the close cooperation with co-legislators, with you and the council, we can deliver on this programme. ms keller made a very emotional reference to yesterday’s discussion and we’ve all been here and i think that the emotions and the farewell bids to our british friends is still with us. therefore, i think that her question on how to respond to the challenge of yesterday is clearly that we have to build an even better europe, which would be more efficient, more competitive, greener, closer to the citizens. i believe that starting the constructive work on this joint ambitious programme would be the right first step forward to meet these ambitions. to my compatriots, ms ďuriš nicholsonová, who was highlighting the challenges around minimum wage setting, i would like to underline once again that what we are going to propose is to set a framework for minimum wage setting and that we are going to consult widely with the social partners, with our member states, and we would respect, one hundred percent, the national tradition and collective bargaining, but we believe that everyone in the european union deserves a fair wage and that we have to be socially just if it comes to this very basic human right, which is so important for europeans on our continent. on the infringement case against austria, it’s ongoing. we are currently studying the response of austria to our reasoned opinion and we will inform this parliament accordingly once this study is completed. ms aubry made reference to the carbon adjustment mechanism. i would like to reassure her that it’s already in our commission’s work programme for 2021. as i’m sure many of you know, this is a rather complex task. it would require a lot of preparation, a proper mechanism and we have to be ready for quite intense international debate on this issue. we would like to see countries like china and many others who have an emissions-trading (et) system as ambitious as we have, but if this would not be the case, we simply would have to consider a mechanism like carbon adjustment to make sure that we have a level playing field and that we would motivate also other big economies to make sure that they would work on lowering their carbon footprint for their economy and for their products. many of you insisted on the importance of the rule of law and i cannot agree with you more. i think that it’s quite clear that this commission is really committed to ensuring respect for the rule of law equally in all member states. ms de sutter, i also would like to assure you on one very important fact – that the commission will also ensure full respect – and i would like to underline both words – of the charter of fundamental rights in addressing emerging issues such as artificial intelligence and facial recognition. in the context of the statement of mr azmani, thank you very much for your intervention. among other and different constructive observations, you also referred to anti-semitism, which again, we were debating yesterday and witnessing very emotional testimony of holocaust survivors, and i am sure that i do not need to say how much i agree with you and how important this would be for the work of the european commission. mr garicano was referring to the work programme and to the fact that, with the uk leaving, a lot of the universities which have been part of the european union educational area are going as well. but i also would like to assure him that we are looking for ways to maintain good contacts with our british friends within the framework of erasmus, within the framework of research programmes. but on top of that, we want to make sure that the european education area becomes a reality by 2025, and we will work with equal intensity on our skills agenda, where we are going to present our programme and proposal already this year. to ms hayer, i would like to reassure you that, for us, the impact assessment is a very important one. i’m responsible for that and there will be no important legislative proposals without a proper impact assessment being done – because we know that the impact assessment offers very often the best answers to the proper argumentation and the debates we would have, especially with those who are opposing our proposals. to make sure that we will respect full transparency, we are going to establish the interinstitutional evidence register by the end of this year – just to make sure that we will share this information with all of you. when it comes to the issue of poverty, which was raised by several colleagues, we are going to address it through the social roadmap, through the framework for minimum wage setting, as i said, and we are going to work on the children guarantee, which several of you referred to as a very important measure. i hope that with your help and with proper funding, we will restart a renovation wave across the european union. this would not only help us to tackle greenhouse gas emissions but increase the quality of life, especially for all those who are living in social housing, and that through this measure, thanks to energy efficiency, we would reduce the bills they have to pay electricity at the end of every month for heating, cooling or simply using. to mr belka, i would like to say that we are very serious about tax evasion and we will be working very closely with our organisation for economic co-operation and development (oecd) partners and, if there will be a deal within the oecd, we will do all necessary and take all necessary steps to implement it. however, i also would like to assure you that in the absence of such agreement on the global level by 2020, the eu shall act alone. we just simply will not have more patience to wait for the continuation of avoiding paying proper taxes on the european territories. i know, mr president, that time is limited, but to ms fritzon i would like to say that we will consult very thoroughly with the social partners and respect all prerogatives of this social dialogue because this is how we know we will get the best results. on enlargement, i think that we have been very clear on making sure that we will come with a new methodology. we will have a very important summit in zagreb, organised thanks to the croatian presidency, where we want to bring a new impetus, new energy into this process and our commitment to northern macedonia and albania is very clear, and that’s a priority for this european commission. on the transition fund and the multiannual financial framework (mff), to conclude, mr president, that was the point made by ms bonafè, by mr hajšel and many others, i want to assure you that when you are talking about eur 7.5 billion for the just transition fund, we are talking about fresh money. this is how the european commission presented its proposal. it’s on top of the mff proposals which you already tabled and with which you are so familiar and for which the commission is ready to battle with the council to make sure that we have proper financing for all the ambitious items which we have in our programme. of course, it would be on all of us to make sure that we would use the just transition money where it’s most needed, for the people who need to be retrained, where we need to find new jobs for coal miners, for the people working in energy—intensive industries, to make sure that this transition is fair and that nobody is left behind, whether a person or a city, or a region. i cannot agree more with all of you who’ve been highlighting the importance of an ambitious multiannual financial perspective. mr olbrycht, ms dalli, mr lópez aguilar, ms niebler, all of you have been referring to the importance to have a proper multiannual financial perspective. as you know, we will have an extraordinary summit where this would be the item on the agenda, so let’s hope and let’s make strong arguments towards our heads of state and government that we need an agreement, we need it very soon – because every month that we are late with the mff, we are already putting our programmes in serious danger. once again, mr president, honourable members, thank you very much for all your points. i’m sure that now in the way of structured dialogues with your committees, you will have even more chance to debate all the programmes and all the items in greater detail, and we are very much looking forward to it.

intervention_header_en: Thierry Breton, member of the commission
subject_of_business_title: Automated decision-making processes: Ensuring consumer protection, and free movement of goods and services (debate)
paragraph: mr president, president de sutter, thank you for your question, which is more than a question, since in fact it covers the whole panorama of what we have been working on for several weeks and even months now in the commission, concerning the issues that you have raised, and in particular, of course, behind, underlying, everything to do with artificial intelligence, data management in a digital economy which is going to radically change our internal market. the question you are asking, in fact, consists in asking us how this evolution – this revolution, some will say – will effectively modify consumer behavior, but also allow us – this is what we are working on – to consolidate the our entire domestic market. for this, obviously, the first word, the key word which was, moreover, quite present in your speech, madam president, is obviously to establish a climate of trust. it is true that today, there is distrust of artificial intelligence. our fellow citizens ask questions, often legitimate ones, and we are here to try to provide answers – effective answers. it is in this spirit that, as you have recalled, the commission is going to present a white paper on 19 february which will be a kind of targeted consultation, on which we will obviously express our positions, but which is also the means of pursuing the debate that we are having this evening and to extend it to listen to all of you, but also to be able to find solutions together to this absolutely essential development which now marks our era. first, it is obviously a question of properly framing the rules for the development of artificial intelligence in europe. on the other hand, it is also a question of ensuring that these rules allow us to promote the emergence of a european artificial intelligence industry. we have worked a lot, with my collaborators, with all of my colleagues, over the last few weeks, and we really must, together, ask ourselves the question – you reminded us of this earlier – of course, algorithms, when we talk about artificial intelligence, but also the question of data. it is obviously the data which is, i was going to say, the fuel which will allow us precisely, by training them through specific algorithms, to develop specific applications which will obviously intervene in the lives of our fellow citizens. the interest that we will therefore take in data, in value-added data, will be very important in the communication that we will do. i would nevertheless like to remind you, in particular to answer a number of your questions, madam president, that obviously we are not starting from scratch. a lot of work has been done, including legislative work, including in this parliament, of course. first, consumer protection legislation. it also covers commercial practices, as you referred to, involving automated decision-making processes, which can also be invoked in the case of discrimination. similarly, the regulatory framework now requires professionals to inform consumers, when the price is personalized – you mentioned this earlier – on the basis of an automated decision system. i would also like to mention, of course, the gdpr, which we have rightly talked about a lot, and which requires that an impact assessment be carried out when the processing of personal data is likely to present a high risk for the rights and people's freedoms. there are still other requirements that apply in the case of automated decisions taken in the context of, for example, e-recruitment. it is obvious that we will have to ensure that there is no discrimination, and therefore understand how these algorithms work, quite simply so that they respect the whole body of european values ​​to which we are so attached. and obviously, all that concerns human interventions which must, once again, be able to allow us to possibly challenge the decision, allow our fellow citizens to challenge the decision if they consider that they are entitled to do so. finally, i remind you of the so-called platform to business regulation, which was adopted last year and which imposes obligations of transparency on the ranking produced by the algorithms of online platforms and search engines. many things exist but, of course, we will have to move forward and i would finally like to say that we are obviously going to make use of all this. we are also going to reflect together on the adaptation of the directive relating to general product safety, the directive relating to machines, as well as the directive relating to radioelectric equipment. the automotive sector is also going to be a very important subject with regard to artificial intelligence and automatic decision-making. the legislator, as you know, has already instructed the commission to look into the question of the approval of connected autonomous cars, so we will continue in this direction. it may also be necessary to make certain clarifications to the general product liability directive in the light of the development of emerging technologies and the circular economy. finally, as you know, the preparation of the digital services act, on which we are working, will allow us to examine with greater attention a series of algorithmic processes, for example recommendation systems, moderation algorithms , or, of course, a very important subject which has been debated extensively in this parliament, online advertising. a point also, if i may, on services to professionals. the expertise offered must not only be based on traditional qualifications, but also on a new kind of combination of skills bringing together information technology, knowledge and, of course, expertise in each sector. i would also like to tell you that the white paper on which we are going to work, which will be brought to your attention, will be followed by action in the fourth quarter, as planned in the commission's work programme, and that, of course, this it is in this perspective that we really wish to be able to work with you. i know that many of you, ladies and gentlemen parliamentarians, have been working for several months now, even several years, on these issues. it is quite enriching for us, and for me in particular, and therefore through the white paper, we will have a platform to continue these exchanges.

intervention_header_en: Thierry Breton, member of the commission
subject_of_business_title: Automated decision-making processes: Ensuring consumer protection, and free movement of goods and services (debate)
paragraph: mr president, ladies and gentlemen parliamentarians, very honestly, i do not know many parliaments in the world where we can have a debate of this quality on these subjects today. beyond our partisan differences, we all basically shared the same questions, the same feelings, the same desires, the same wishes. basically, i remember one thing. in this evolution – this evolution which will last, i am not afraid to say, for years, even decades, i remember that what your whole parliament shares, and with it the commission, is the place of man, the place of the human, respect for our values, respect for what we are, the integrity of our decisions, understanding of the phenomena that surround us, understanding of situations: what is going on? who makes the decisions? will this change my life? can i still continue to intervene? can i still turn against a body that has made a decision that does not suit me? all these questions, ladies and gentlemen, are indeed addressed in this white paper. i repeat, it is called the white paper on artificial intelligence, but it is only the beginning of our reflection on what i myself called reflection, the structuring of a new space in which we now work, in which we train, in which we have fun, in which we exchange, which is the information space. it is superimposed, basically, on the three other spaces which have gradually contributed to forming what we are today, to also organizing our life in society: the territorial space, first, obviously, then, with the conquests, maritime space and airspace. and today, the information space. so yes, artificial intelligence is one of the first elements. i share a second observation, which you all share, and which pleases me because it was a fight that i also led myself. through the applications that we are going to have to manage, which are going to shape our decisions and our lives a little, the applications of artificial intelligence, or, as you have called it yourself, madam president, of automated decision-making , there is data. this too, we all share: no data, no artificial intelligence. we tended to focus a little too much on the algorithms, these lines of code, as you said. it's not vintage, the lines of code (maybe tomorrow, moreover, it will no longer be lines of code, when we will be in quantum computing, it will be different processes). today, this is what allows us to work, with this intimate relationship between a modeling of our environment still in the form of 1s and 0s (soon, these will be desqubit) and, precisely, the decisions that we are ready to take. but behind that, there are obviously data – this has been mentioned, moreover, by some of you, with the parable or the metaphor of the wolf and the dog in the forest. but what did you mean by that? you obviously wanted to say that, when we take data that characterizes an animal in its natural environment, if we take the same animal in another environment, obviously, you will have differences as to the application resulting from the algorithm and therefore of the process of what is called the learning phase, machine learning, which will integrate all this data. yes, data is essential, and it is also the fight that we want to wage at the commission, with you, to define how to characterize this data and our european data. some say, i heard it on the benches of your assembly, that this turn should not be missed. we may have been late, but i don't think so. i don't believe we are behind in technology. but in any case, this bend there, of these data, we must not miss it. you are right, because the data which is in front of us and which will precisely enable us to feed intelligently, with data which contains our values, is obviously all the new processes in front of us, the industrial data, what is called the “b2b”, public data, data that will obviously come from the world of health – so important for all of us –, from transport. all of this data is in front of us. every 18 months, the amount of data that today constitutes the information portfolio of the planet doubles. so, obviously, this wave should not be missed. this wave is precisely all that we want to do at the commission. several elements: first, obviously, not to regulate too much at the exit. it's too early. today, we are talking about artificial intelligence, a specific exploitation of this data, tomorrow we will be talking about something else. on the other hand, we will have to be careful that everything that comes out is totally compatible with our values ​​and gives citizens the freedom to choose. remember what i just said: choose. the freedom of choice. do not be a prisoner of an algorithm, a system, a data manager, a platform. having the possibility to maintain this choice is a fundamental value in the world of information. we have to work on it. to have the possibility of finding, in these solutions, what we are attached to. finally, obviously, having the possibility of doing it in complete security – legal security of course, ethical security, but also information security, cybersecurity. these topics are absolutely essential. through the reflection that we are proposing to you, there will also be a reflection on infrastructures. we need infrastructures that allow us to store this data, to house the applications – selective applications, intelligent applications. it is also necessary to have control of our information systems, supercomputers, learning machines that will train, month after month, this data.

intervention_header: Helena Dalli, Member of the Commission
intervention_header_en: Helena Dalli, Member of the Commission
subject_of_business_title: Gender Equality Strategy (debate)
paragraph: madam president, honourable members, thank you for putting the gender equality strategy on today’s agenda. the first months since the start of the commission mandate i have had the opportunity to meet many of you already. all the exchanges we have had have confirmed that all of us, together, have so much work to do in this area of policy. i am grateful for the support you have shown me and this commission on many occasions. the european union and its citizens need your full support in making europe an equal place for women and men in all their diversity. gender equality is a founding principle of the european union. europe is a good place to live for many, but it would be an understatement to say that we are still not there yet when it comes to gender equality. women are still being underpaid compared to men. one in three women in the eu have experienced physical or sexual violence, or both since the age of 15 – and that’s millions of women. we cannot accept these appalling inequalities. president von der leyen, vice-president jourová, and the whole college support me and this fight for equality. gender equality is a key theme in the mandate of this commission and the first key milestone will be the launch of the gender equality strategy. the adoption is foreseen for the week of international women’s day in early march. the strategy will underpin the political commitment to gender equality and support strategic and systematic work for gender equality in the union and beyond. we are aiming at an ambitious strategy. in the context of a visible and organised movement opposing progress in women’s rights and gender equality which has emerged in recent years in europe and internationally, it is more important now than ever to restate in the strongest of terms the commission’s continuing commitment to gender equality. there has been a wide consultation on the strategy, including a public consultation that gathered more than 1 300 responses. as gender equality is a cross-cutting issue, the strategy will strengthen the commission’s dual approach of gender mainstreaming combined with targeted actions on specific topics. we aim to introduce a more systematic approach at an early stage of policy design to include a gender perspective in all eu policy areas. as regards content, we intend to present a positive future-oriented vision for a gender equal europe – a europe where women and men, girls and boys, in all their diversity, are free from gender-based violence and gender stereotypes, where they have the opportunity to thrive in the labour market, lead our businesses, politics and participate equally in all sectors. important horizontal considerations that will be emphasised in the strategy are challenging gender stereotypes and intersectionality. in terms of topics, the strategy will address the priorities highlighted in the president’s political guidelines – increasing women’s economic-empowerment by closing the gender pay gap, including by introducing binding pay-transparency measures, getting better gender balance on company boards and improving parents’ and carers’ work-life balance. we also continue our efforts to combat violence against women. eu accession to the istanbul convention therefore remains a priority. if eu accession remains blocked in the council, despite our joint efforts, we will table legislative proposals to strengthen the victims’ rights directive and include or add specific forms of gender-based violence to the list of eu crimes. we shall also address other important and emerging aspects of gender equality, such as online violence against women or the gender perspective in digitalisation, including an artificial intelligence to avoid bias. together with the adoption of the strategy, we will launch a wide-ranging and inclusive consultation process on binding pay transparency measures which we aim to table by the end of the year. i am aware that introducing binding pay-transparency measures can be challenging, and i want to find the right balance for such eu intervention, taking into account the interests of employers, employees and national administrations. i look forward to hearing your views and discussing with you. i sincerely hope to get your support so we, as the eu, can make the so much needed leap towards a gender equal europe in a more gender equal world.

intervention_header_en: Margrethe Vestager, Executive Vice—President of the Commission
subject_of_business_title: Digital Services Act: Improving the functioning of the Single Market - Digital Services Act: adapting commercial and civil law rules for commercial entities operating online - Digital Services Act and fundamental rights issues posed - Framework of ethical aspects of artificial intelligence, robotics and related technologies - Civil liability regime for artificial intelligence - Intellectual property rights for the development of artificial intelligence technologies (debate)
paragraph: madam president, i think it is kind of strange: we are few here because this is a digital debate, and yet the energy and the enthusiasm is to be felt. i think that comes from the fact that the work done is truly impressive, because it’s work that has involved so many colleagues in this assembly, so many colleagues who have done the effort to study the subjects, to form opinions and to discuss. even though it will be, i think, a truly amazing debate today, it will in no way do justice to what has gone before this debate, because it is truly a thing that includes the entire parliament. this is also why it’s a bit unfair to start thanking some rapporteurs and leaders in this, but i would say to alex saliba, tiemo wölken and kris peeters that this is outstanding work. we will respond to your initiatives with two legislative proposals: the digital services act and the digital markets act, and this will reflect ideas. fundamentally we share the same goals. i think that is most obvious. we want to better protect citizens when they use the internet, whether that is in protection against illegal goods, services, content online. as it was put, we need to make sure that as we feel safe offline we should feel safe online. also, to better secure the freedom of expression online. this of course, as you have heard already, is a tricky balance to strike. to achieve this, we need to lay down a solid and impactful eu—wide accountability framework. obviously that has to come with enforcement, because words alone will not do it; then it would be just window dressing. the balance we will have to strike here is of course that we will have to say to some of the gatekeepers, the largest platforms, that things will change. europe is open and we will do this in full compliance with our international obligations, also because we would want to work with the rest of the world to set new standards. in order to do so, we intend to break down legal barriers in the internal market and combat unfair practices by gatekeeper platforms. this will help european innovators, small businesses, to scale, to grow, to be able to compete for our attention, to compete for our business. with the digital services act i think two things have stood the test of time: no general monitoring of user content is one; and, second, a well—balanced system of liability, and the internal market as the core. but things have changed, so obviously we also need to set out in law the responsibilities that platforms must have in relation to their role as societal and economic intervention_header: Margrethe Vestager, Executive Vice-President of the Commission
intervention_header_en: Margrethe Vestager, Executive Vice-President of the Commission
subject_of_business_title: Digital Services Act: Improving the functioning of the Single Market - Digital Services Act: adapting commercial and civil law rules for commercial entities operating online - Digital Services Act and fundamental rights issues posed - Framework of ethical aspects of artificial intelligence, robotics and related technologies - Civil liability regime for artificial intelligence - Intellectual property rights for the development of artificial intelligence technologies (continuation of debate)
paragraph: mr president, this has indeed been a rich, nuanced, very, very good debate. we have come from liability, intellectual property rights, innovation, hate speech, upload filters, consumer protection – i think we have shown the width and the depth of the work that has been ongoing here. but, the thing is that the fundamental question is answered with a ‘yes’. can we have a european model? there are other models, obviously. but the debate tonight has shown with all clarity that no one wants just to leave that to the state. neither will anyone just say, ‘well, let business take care of this’. now this has been a promise: that democracy will shape our society. that promise has been given tonight by everyone who has been taking the floor, that in our democracy we will shape this – for the state, for the business community, to serve the real asset here, which is the individual citizen, and that i find extremely promising. obviously, the level of complexity is quite high. there’s been a lot of very nuanced speeches, trying to balance that on the one hand, there are so obviously things that should not be out there, because it’s illegal in the offline world, while at the same time, no one wants censorship, no one wants the state to control. no one wants to limit a debate that can be free and nurture our democracy and that, of course, is the thing that we will have to grapple with in the months to come. i just read an article in a danish paper, in danish, about artificial intelligence and part of that article was written by ai, in my mother tongue, on a rather complex subject, and i couldn’t distinguish what was written by the authors and what was written by ai. maybe the grammar was slightly better by the ai – i wouldn’t know, but it’s just to say that when we’re in a world where artificial intelligence can write an op-ed, can write a poem, can write music, and we cannot tell the difference anymore, then it’s about time that democracy catches up with technology. otherwise we cannot stand by the promise that the humans are the empowered here and that the machine is a servant. the thing is that now the digital world, the online world, is not another world. it’s our world. for the children who are being bullied, it is just as real as when it was in the schoolyard back in the day. for the people who decide not to participate in democracy because of the hate speech online, it is as real as if someone has threatened them offline. this is our world and this is now, when we went to frame it, because it has matured. back in the digital stone age, in the year 2000, of course, how could we have known any better? but this is the time and with this level of complexity, what a pleasure it is to see that we then discuss the principles. what are the fundamentals? that humans are in control; that transparency, responsibility, accountability, is what we want to work with; that you should know your customer; that you should be able to identify yourself to create the trust that people know who they are dealing with and you know that you are in control of the data that you create. the principle of freedom, of fair markets. i think that is the core of the debate today and then, of course, the obvious: that the legislation that we will discuss and hopefully decide upon, should be implemented, should be enforceable, so that these promises are not empty, that it’s not just more words on paper, but that it’s real rights for citizens, for businesses, in the real world, to make the best possible use of digital technologies. it is, of course, a framework of legislation. it is the digital services act, the digital market act, it’s the legislation on artificial intelligence. it will be the data governance act and the data act and the european digital identity, just to mention the most obvious things. that should create ecosystems of excellence – because europe has so much to offer. we have a culture of doing this and we will do it again. this is how we can create an ecosystem of trust, so that citizens do not feel estranged to a society that they have seen in the movies and found fascinating, but never ever wanted to live in. and obviously, as was just said, this is a european debate that should be rooted in every member state. as we have seen with all the different proposals coming in every member state because this is not just something down in brussels. this is grown from every member state but it needs a european response and this response you have given tonight by a promise that democracy will make sure that we frame this. (applause)

intervention_header: Didier Reynders, membre de la Commission
intervention_header_en: Didier Reynders, member of the commission
subject_of_business_title: Towards a New Consumer Agenda beyond 2020 (debate)
paragraph: mr president, ladies and gentlemen, allow me first of all to thank you again for this invitation to present to you, this time, the new consumer agenda published by the commission on 13 november last. this agenda incorporates many suggestions from the european parliament, whether in reports or in the context of other debates in parliament. for example, on issues such as the sustainability of the internal market, which we have just discussed, or product safety, which will also be on your agenda this week. i think it is important that we can continue to work together on these themes. europe is known for its high level of consumer protection. with the new agenda, we want to uphold this european achievement. the agenda will allow us to ensure that european consumers benefit from the single market, also in a crisis period like the current pandemic. the agenda sets out a political vision and longer-term priorities, aiming to build trust so that consumers can be key actors for the green and digital transitions and also be key to drive the economic recovery out of the covid-19 crisis. the agenda proposes 22 concrete actions. this to address both the immediate challenges of the covid-19 pandemic, as well as longer-term priorities. among our long-term priorities is consumer protection in green and digital transitions. the approach defined in the new agenda will contribute to the implementation of the action plan for the circular economy and the digital strategy, in particular through more sustainable and safer products and services. the new agenda provides for actions in favor of better information on the environmental characteristics of products, such as their lifespan, their environmental impact and their reparability. we will better protect consumers against practices such as greenwashing, early obsolescence or the sale of unviable products. we will also ensure that the need for a solid legal framework on artificial intelligence can be met, in order to guarantee a high level of protection for consumers and fundamental rights online. consumers need to be able to shop securely and confidently online, just as much as in the physical world. the digital transition also has an impact on the consumer credit market. in particular, there are new lenders and new ways of assessing the creditworthiness of consumers based on their data available online. in addition to the environmental and digital transitions, the new consumer agenda addresses three other priorities: the effective application of legislation and effective remedies, raising consumer awareness taking into account the specific needs of different groups and strengthening international cooperation. we must ensure that european citizens can enforce their rights as consumers, regardless of their social or economic situation. consumer empowerment in the green and digital transition must be inclusive. a high level of consumer protection cannot be a privilege available only to some, for example, those with access to online tools and digital skills. let me conclude with a few words on how we want to implement this new policy vision. given the nature and global dimension of the challenges we aim to address, the agenda seeks to foster consumer policy priorities that could be pursued by the eu and its member states. the agenda also suggests a broad partnership, including consumer organisations, but also businesses and all stakeholders, including the european parliament. thank you again for your attention tonight about consumer rights and consumer protection and i'm now looking forward to hearing your remarks and possible questions or proposals.
